examples.professional: We report approximative runtimes, since cluster load changes from hour to hour.
examples.analytical: Such a claim is only approximative, because the underlying measure is itself a proxy for what we actually care about.

nuance.analogy: Like a sketch of a building drawn from a few measurements: useful and close, but not the finished blueprint.
nuance.etymology: From Latin approximare, 'to come near to', through the adjective 'approximative' in modern technical English.
common_mistakes: Using 'approximative' in casual speech, where 'approximate' sounds natural and 'approximative' sounds odd.
Shifting the stress to the last syllable, as in 'uh-prox-uh-MAY-tive'.

senses.definition: Of land, able to be plowed or tilled, capable of growing crops (traditionally contrasted with pasturable lands such as heaths).
senses.example: The county's arable land is mostly flat, which makes wheat and corn easy to plant.

senses.definition: Of land, under cultivation (within any quinquennial period) for the production of crops sown and harvested within the same agricultural year (contrasted with permanently-cropped lands such as orchards).
senses.example: Only a third of the farm was arable this year, since the rest grew apple trees.

senses.definition: Land that can be cropped (i.e. land that is arable); land that is being cropped (i.e. land that is in the cropping phase of a crop rotation, currently being cropped rather than used as pasture or fallow).
senses.example: Most of the estate's arable was planted with soybeans, leaving the orchards untouched.

core.definition: Land that is suitable for plowing and planting crops, rather than pasture or forest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AR, with the vowel of 'cat' plus a clear American r. The last syllable is a reduced 'bul', so do not pronounce a full 'ab-le' ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term used in agriculture, land use, and policy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use arable mainly in farming, environmental, and government contexts, such as 'arable land' or 'arable acreage'. In everyday talk, people say 'farmland' or 'land good for farming'. A natural conversational reply might be to say the land is good for crops.

distinctions.note: Fertile means highly productive soil. Arable means the land can be plowed and farmed, even if it is not especially rich.
Cultivable is a close synonym but is less common in American usage. Arable is the standard term.

examples.everyday: My uncle bought a small piece of arable land so he could grow tomatoes and corn.
examples.professional: The agricultural report shows that only about a third of the county's total area is arable.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that control of arable land shaped the political order of the early agrarian state.

nuance.analogy: Like a garden plot that is ready for planting, not a rocky hillside or a swamp.
nuance.etymology: From Latin arabilis 'able to be plowed', from arare 'to plow'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (uh-RAY-buhl).
Confusing arable with arboreal, which means related to trees.
Using arable to mean fertile in every sense, when it actually refers to suitability for plowing.

arable.etymology: From Middle English *arable*, from Middle French *arable*, from Old French *arable*, from Latin *arābilis*, formed from *arō* (“plow”) + *-bilis* (“able to be”).

senses.definition: Equipped, especially with a weapon.
senses.example: nuclear-armed

senses.definition: Equipped with a gun.
Prepared for use; loaded.
senses.example: The alarm was armed, so the door set off a siren the moment we opened it.

senses.definition: Having an arm or arms, often of a specified number or type.
senses.example: The sculpture shows a Hindu deity, heavily armed and with multiple arms.

senses.definition: Possessing arms of a specified number or type.
senses.example: the four-armed creature

senses.definition: Having prickles or thorns.
senses.example: The thistle is armed with sharp prickles along every stem and leaf.

senses.definition: Having horns, claws, teeth, a beak, etc. in a particular tincture, as contrasted with that of the animal as a whole.
senses.example: The heraldic lion is gules, armed azure, with blue claws and teeth.

core.definition: Carrying or equipped with a weapon, especially a gun.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, with a clear r and a final d. The ending is not pronounced as a separate syllable, so do not say 'ARM-ed'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts, but alarming in news or police reports, as in 'armed suspect'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'armed' mainly for people carrying guns, as in 'armed guard' or 'armed robbery'. It also has a figurative sense, as in 'armed with facts' or 'armed with a plan'. For heavy weapons, Americans say 'armed to the teeth'.

distinctions.note: 'Equipped' is general and can mean any gear, while 'armed' specifically means carrying weapons.
'Loaded' means a gun has ammunition in it, while 'armed' means a person has a weapon.

examples.everyday: The man at the bank said he was armed, so everyone stayed calm and did what he said.
examples.professional: Security will be armed for the event, so please follow their instructions at the gate.
examples.analytical: The argument is armed with statistics but lacks a moral framework, so it persuades only those already convinced.

nuance.analogy: Being armed is like keeping a set of tools in your pocket, ready for trouble.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English armen, from Old French armer, from Latin armare, to arm.
common_mistakes: Using a preposition other than 'with' after 'armed'; say 'armed with' something.
Adding an extra vowel and saying 'ARM-ed'.

senses.definition: A program that reads source code written in assembly language and produces executable machine code, possibly together with information needed by linkers, debuggers and other tools.
senses.example: The assembler converted our hand-written instructions into machine code that the processor could execute.

senses.definition: Assembly language.
senses.example: I wrote that program in assembler.

senses.definition: One who assembles items.
A nanodevice capable of assembling nanodevices, possibly including copies of itself, according to a plan.
senses.example: Researchers designed a nanoscale assembler that could build copies of itself from carbon atoms.

core.definition: In computing, a program that translates assembly language into machine code that a computer can run.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on SEM, and the final syllable is a reduced 'er' sound. The middle b and the l are linked, so the word sounds like 'uh-SEM-bler', not 'uh-SEM-bul-er'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in software engineering, with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use assembler mainly in computer science, programming, and systems work, especially when discussing low-level code. In everyday life, the word means a worker who puts parts together, such as on a factory line. In software contexts, people say assembler or assembly language, and they may run the assembler on a source file.

distinctions.note: A compiler translates high-level languages such as C or Java, while an assembler translates assembly language, which is closer to machine code.
An interpreter runs code line by line without producing a separate machine-code file, while an assembler produces executable machine code.

examples.everyday: My brother works on old video game systems, so he spends his nights with an assembler.
examples.professional: Our build pipeline runs the assembler before linking, so any syntax error stops the release.
examples.analytical: An assembler is a bridge between human-readable instructions and the binary code that hardware executes, and its design reflects the architecture it targets.

nuance.analogy: An assembler is like a translator who turns a detailed set of instructions into the exact steps a machine can follow.
nuance.etymology: From assemble, from Old French assembler, to bring together.
common_mistakes: Confusing assembler with compiler, which handles high-level languages instead.
Using assembler for a factory worker in a technical context without making clear which sense you mean.
Pronouncing the middle b as a separate syllable, as in uh-SEM-bul-er.

senses.definition: A person who is in attendance or in the audience of an event.
(uncommon) A person who is attended.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: A person who attends a meeting, conference, event, or class, usually being physically present or formally registered.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, -DEE, which is long. The first syllable is a weak uh and the middle syllable has light secondary stress; do not say AT-ten-dee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It simply describes someone who is present, with no judgment about their role.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use attendee for people at conferences, webinars, workshops, and professional meetings. At a party they would more often say 'guests,' and in a school setting 'students.' The word appears often in event registration forms and emails, where it sounds slightly formal but perfectly normal.

distinctions.note: A participant actively takes part in an activity, while an attendee is primarily present at it.
An audience watches or listens to a performance or talk, while an attendee may also attend meetings or events where they do not watch anything.
Attender is rare in American usage; attendee is the standard form for people who attend events.

examples.everyday: There were about two hundred attendees at my cousin's wedding.
examples.professional: Please send the updated attendee list to the events team before Friday.
examples.analytical: The survey defined attendees as anyone who registered and checked in, which excludes people who only watched the livestream.

nuance.analogy: An attendee is like a ticket holder in the seats: present for the show, but not performing in it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from attend, from Latin attendere 'to give heed, stretch toward', plus the suffix -ee for a person affected by an action.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in AT-ten-dee; the stress belongs on the last syllable.
Using attendee for someone who only watches a broadcast, when the word usually implies being present or formally registered.

conversation.text: We have over forty attendees on the webinar, so let's keep questions in the chat.
Can you send the slides to all the attendees after the meeting?
Each attendee should bring one idea for next year's plan.

senses.definition: In an audacious manner; bravely, daringly, but not foolhardily.
senses.example: The climber audaciously attempted the steep north face without ropes, drawing gasps from the crowd below.

senses.definition: In a brazen, forthright manner.

core.definition: In a bold, daring way, often in a way that surprises or challenges others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the DAY syllable and keep the 'shus' sound short and unstressed. End with 'lee', not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can describe admirable boldness or rude boldness, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: This adverb is more common in writing than in speech. In conversation, Americans usually say 'boldly' or 'daringly' instead. Use it in a presentation or an essay when you want to stress the boldness of an action.

distinctions.note: Boldly is the everyday choice, while audaciously adds a stronger sense of surprise or daring.
Recklessly is negative and means without thought for danger, while audaciously may be admiring.

examples.everyday: She audaciously asked the chef to remake the dessert, and he did.
examples.professional: The startup audaciously committed to shipping the new API in six weeks.
examples.analytical: Hume audaciously challenged the idea that causation can be observed directly rather than inferred.

nuance.etymology: Formed from 'audacious' plus the adverb ending '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'audaciously' where you mean 'audacity', the noun.
Misplacing the stress on the final syllable.
Using it in casual speech where 'boldly' would sound more natural.

senses.definition: To replace or enhance human labor with machines.
senses.example: Many offices still need to automate.

core.definition: To make a task or process run by machines or software with little or no human effort.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, AW, and the middle syllable is a reduced schwa. Do not stretch the first vowel into 'ah', and do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound positive when it means efficiency, but negative when people worry about losing jobs.
nuance.usage_note: This is common in business and tech meetings, and in everyday talk about personal finances or chores. Americans say 'automate a process' or 'automate something' with no preposition. People also use 'automate away' to mean removing a task from people's work.

distinctions.note: Automatize is a rare variant, and Americans almost always use automate.
Mechanize means equipping work with machines, often in farming or factories, while automate emphasizes control by software or sensors.

examples.everyday: I finally automated my bill payments, so I don't forget them every month anymore.
examples.professional: Can we automate the weekly report so the analysts stop copying numbers into spreadsheets by hand?
examples.analytical: Whether firms should automate complex judgment, and not just routine labor, is a question with serious ethical stakes.

nuance.analogy: Like setting a coffeemaker's timer so it brews every morning without anyone pressing a button.
nuance.etymology: Formed from automation, which comes from automatic, from Greek automatos 'self-acting'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long A as 'AW-tuh-MATE' or stressing the last syllable; the stress is on AW.
Adding a preposition, as in 'automate to the process'; say 'automate the process'.

senses.definition: In an autonomous or self-governing manner.

core.definition: In an autonomous way; by itself, without outside control or step-by-step direction from a person.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TAH, and the rest of the word is reduced. Avoid pronouncing the middle vowels as a long 'oh' like 'no,' which is a common mistake.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds precise and somewhat formal, and it is most often used for machines or processes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'autonomously' mostly for machines, robots, or software that act without human control, as in 'the rover navigates autonomously.' For people, you would more often say 'on their own' or 'independently.' In a business meeting it sounds natural and precise.

distinctions.note: Independently is the everyday adverb for acting apart from others. Autonomously focuses on self-directed operation, especially for systems and machines.
Automatically means by a fixed mechanism or rule. Autonomously implies some ability to choose actions within a broader goal.

examples.everyday: The robot vacuum cleans the whole apartment autonomously, so I just empty the bin once a week.
examples.professional: The batch job should run autonomously overnight and page the on-call engineer only if the data checks fail.
examples.analytical: Whether a machine can decide autonomously is a question about the source of its goals, not merely about the absence of a human hand.

nuance.analogy: Working autonomously is like a self-watering plant system that adjusts itself to the weather without anyone checking the soil each day.
nuance.etymology: Formed from autonomous, from Greek autonomos 'self-governing,' with the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowels as long 'oh' sounds, like aw-toh-NOH-mus-lee, rather than reduced vowels.
Using 'autonomously' to describe people in casual speech, where 'on my own' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A judgment, sentence, or final decision. Specifically: The decision of arbitrators in a case submitted.
senses.example: The court's award in the arbitration case favored the smaller company over its former supplier.

senses.definition: The paper containing the decision of arbitrators; that which is warded.
senses.example: The arbitrators' award was printed on three pages and mailed to both parties.

senses.definition: Funding that has been granted for the conduct of a research project.
senses.example: Our lab received a three-year research award from the National Science Foundation last spring.

senses.definition: A trophy or medal; something that denotes an accomplishment, especially in a competition. A prize or honor based on merit.
senses.example: She was proud of the award she won for best lab presentation at the conference.

senses.definition: To determine; to make or grant an award.
senses.example: The committee will award the scholarship to the student with the strongest research proposal.

senses.definition: To give (an award).
senses.example: Four or five of these medals are awarded every year.

senses.definition: To give (a person) an award.
senses.example: He was awarded with the Nobel Prize for Literature.

senses.definition: To give by sentence or judicial determination; to assign or apportion, after careful regard to the nature of the case.
senses.example: The arbitrators awarded damages to the complainant.

core.definition: A prize, honor, or certificate given in recognition of achievement, or money granted to fund a specific purpose.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WAWRD, one syllable with a rhotic r pronounced clearly. Do not add an extra vowel between the w and the r.

nuance.connotation: Positive. An award signals recognition and prestige, although a grant award is more administrative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use award for honors such as an Oscar, a company prize, or a research grant. In sports and contests, people often say prize or trophy. The verb is used in phrases like be awarded a scholarship, and the legal sense is rare in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: A prize is usually won in a competition. An award is often given for achievement or service, sometimes without a contest.
A grant is money given to fund a project, usually after an application. An award can be an honor or a grant, depending on context.
Honor is a broad word for respect or recognition. An award is a concrete prize or certificate given to mark it.

examples.everyday: She just won an award for best pie at the county fair, so she's insufferable now.
examples.professional: Our team received an award for the best internal tool of the year at the company all-hands.
examples.analytical: The award recognizes sustained contributions to statistical methods in public health over three decades.

nuance.analogy: Like a gold star on a chart, but with public applause and sometimes money.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French awarder, 'to decide', of Germanic origin related to ward.
common_mistakes: Saying awarded with a prize; the usual phrase is awarded a prize.
Using award to mean a competition; a contest is the event, and the award is what you receive.

award.etymology: From Middle English *awarden*, from Anglo-Norman *awarder*, from Medieval Latin, from Latin *ex* (“out”) + Medieval Latin *wardare*, *guardare* (“to observe, regard, guard”); see ward, guard, regard.

senses.definition: A televised ceremony that gives awards, such as the Oscars.
senses.example: The actor thanked her agent during her acceptance speech at the award show.

core.definition: A televised ceremony where prizes are given to people in film, music, television, or other entertainment.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound, the main stress falls on 'award,' so 'show' is lighter. Keep the r in 'award' and avoid saying 'uh-WAHD' with an open vowel, which sounds British.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a popular entertainment event, sometimes with a playful or mildly critical tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use award show in everyday talk about events like the Oscars, Grammys, Emmys, or the MTV awards. People often ask Did you watch the award show last night? and reply I caught part of it or I missed it. Compared with awards ceremony, award show sounds more casual and TV-focused.

distinctions.note: An awards ceremony can be any event that gives prizes, such as a business or academic event, while an award show is usually a televised entertainment event.
A premiere is the first public screening of a film or show, while an award show gives prizes to films, music, or TV.

examples.everyday: Did you watch the award show last night? The host was hilarious.
examples.professional: Our marketing team is pitching a sponsorship for the award show next spring.
examples.analytical: The award show functions as a ritual that reinforces the entertainment industry's image of itself as a meritocracy.

nuance.etymology: Award comes from Anglo-French awarder, meaning to judge or decide; show is the common English noun.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'show' as strongly as 'award,' instead of letting 'award' carry the main stress.
Confusing award show with awards season, which is the months of events leading up to the ceremonies.

conversation.text: I only watch award shows for the outfits.
Award shows are way too long.
Who's hosting the award show this year?

senses.definition: Especially of a calculation, estimation, or other reasoning, or an idea: approximate, rough, simplified.
senses.example: We can do some back-of-the-envelope calculations before all the facts come in.

core.definition: Rough and quick, based on simple math or estimates rather than detailed analysis; used for a quick calculation or idea.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on EN in envelope, and the words run together so the phrase sounds almost like one long word. Reduce of to uhv and the to thee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It signals that a number is an estimate, which is honest and usually welcome, though it can undercut a figure you want people to trust.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in meetings when someone gives a quick estimate, as in 'Just a back-of-the-envelope calculation, we'd need about ten servers.' It is casual but professional, and it is common in business and engineering talk. Hyphenate it before a noun, as in 'a back-of-the-envelope estimate', but not when it follows a verb. A natural follow-up is to ask what assumptions were used.

distinctions.note: A rough estimate is any approximate figure. Back-of-the-envelope adds the idea that it was done quickly with simple math and no tools or data.
A ballpark figure is an approximate number, often used when someone needs an order of magnitude. It says nothing about how the number was produced.
A guesstimate is more informal and suggests little basis at all, while a back-of-the-envelope estimate still rests on some simple reasoning.

examples.everyday: Hey, I did a back-of-the-envelope calculation, and we'd save about forty bucks a month if we switch plans.
examples.professional: Before we commit to the vendor, let's do a back-of-the-envelope estimate of what the migration will cost us.
examples.analytical: A back-of-the-envelope argument can show whether a claim is even plausible before we invest in a formal model.

nuance.analogy: Like sketching a house on a napkin before hiring an architect.
nuance.etymology: Named for the practice of jotting quick figures on the back of an envelope; the idiom is 20th-century.
common_mistakes: Using it for a precise, audited figure. It signals a rough estimate, so calling exact numbers back-of-the-envelope sounds wrong.
Dropping the hyphens before a noun: say a back-of-the-envelope estimate, not a back of the envelope estimate.
Saying on the back envelope instead of back of the envelope.

back-of-the-envelope.etymology: A reference to a calculation or an idea that occurs to one being jotted down on an available scrap of paper, such as the back of an envelope.

conversation.text: I did a back-of-the-envelope calculation, and it looks like we'll save about twenty percent.
This is just back-of-the-envelope math, but the numbers look promising.
A quick back-of-the-envelope estimate says we need two more servers.

senses.definition: The camel with two humps, Camelus bactrianus, native to the steppes of Asia.

core.definition: A camel with two humps, native to the cold, dry steppes and deserts of Central Asia.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BAK on Bactrian and KAM on camel. Say the 'ck' as a clear k, and reduce the final -el to a soft uhl, as in camel, not kuh-MEL.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a factual name for an animal, sometimes used in travel or zoo contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear this name at zoos, in nature documentaries, or in travel writing about Mongolia and China. It is distinguished from the single-humped dromedary, which most Americans picture first when they hear the word camel. Use it when you need to be specific about the two-humped kind.

distinctions.note: A dromedary has one hump and lives mainly in hot deserts such as North Africa and the Middle East; a Bactrian camel has two humps and lives in cold Central Asia.
Camel alone can mean either species; add Bactrian when the two-humped species matters.

examples.everyday: At the zoo we saw a Bactrian camel with two big humps, and my daughter asked why it looked so shaggy.
examples.professional: Our wildlife documentary crew filmed Bactrian camels in the Gobi for the segment on desert adaptation.
examples.analytical: The Bactrian camel's tolerance of cold and drought makes it a useful case study in how large mammals adapt to extreme continental climates.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name for one branch of a tree: Bactrian names the two-humped branch of the camel family.
nuance.etymology: Named after Bactria, an ancient region of Central Asia; Bactria comes from Greek Baktria.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Bactrian' with a long a, as in BAK-tree-an; the vowel is short.
Confusing the species, using Bactrian camel for a one-humped animal.

senses.definition: Having white markings on the face.
senses.example: bald-faced hornet

senses.definition: Shameless and undisguised.
senses.example: a bald-faced lie

core.definition: Shameless and undisguised; done openly and boldly, especially a lie, with no effort to hide it.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound adjective, the main stress usually falls on BALD, the first part, as in red-faced. The second part, face, is a light secondary syllable ending in a clear st sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes dishonesty or rudeness that is open and unashamed, so it is used to criticize.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say bald-faced lie or bald-faced liar when they feel someone is lying openly and without shame. It is informal and emphatic, so it is common in conversation, news, and opinion writing. A natural response is 'Are you serious?' or 'Unbelievable.' Do not confuse it with the literal meaning of having a white face marking on an animal, which is now rare.

distinctions.note: Brazen suggests bold confidence or defiance, while bald-faced stresses open lying or shamelessness.
Flagrant is more formal and is often used for clear violations of rules or laws.

examples.everyday: He told the waiter the order was already paid, which was a bald-faced lie.
examples.professional: She sent the vendor a bald-faced claim that the outage had nothing to do with our update.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that a bald-faced denial of evidence damages public trust more than a careful admission of error.

nuance.analogy: Like a horse with a bright white blaze on its face, impossible to miss and not hidden at all.
nuance.etymology: From bald, describing a white face marking on an animal, combined with face; the figurative sense of shameless developed later.
common_mistakes: Writing it as boldfaced, which means printed in heavy type, such as boldface text.
Using it for mild embarrassment; it describes shamelessness, not awkwardness.
Using it as a noun, when it is an adjective: say a bald-faced liar, not a bald-face.

senses.definition: An unusually large payment due at the end of the term of a loan agreement.

core.definition: A large lump-sum payment due at the end of a loan, after smaller regular payments that do not pay off the full amount.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on PAY in payment, with a lighter stress on balloon. Say the two words as one smooth phrase and keep the final t soft in payment, which is nearly silent between the m and the n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it signals financial risk and a possible need to refinance or pay a large sum at once.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in mortgage, auto and business loan discussions, usually with caution because it can force refinancing or a large payoff. Say it with a loan officer or lawyer, since it sounds technical among friends. A common question is Is there a balloon payment on this loan?

distinctions.note: Installments are regular, roughly equal payments that repay a loan over time, while a balloon payment is one large final payment.

examples.everyday: My cousin's car loan has a balloon payment due next year, and he's stressed about it.
examples.professional: The lender offered a five-year loan with a balloon payment of two million dollars at maturity.
examples.analytical: A balloon payment shifts refinancing risk onto the borrower at maturity, which is why regulators scrutinize such loans.

nuance.analogy: Like paying a small rent for years and then getting one enormous bill on the final day.
nuance.etymology: Balloon (a swelling object) plus payment; the final sum swells above the regular installments.
common_mistakes: Thinking it means a payment made with balloons or as a gift; it is a large final loan payment.
Putting the main stress on balloon; the primary stress falls on PAY in payment.

balloon-payment.etymology: So called because the debt becomes inflated like a balloon as a result of the compound interest accumulating on the large sum.

senses.definition: To rely on someone or something; to count on something; to depend on something.
senses.example: I'm banking on you being there. I don't have your expertise.

core.definition: To rely on someone or something; to count on a person or thing to happen or to be there when needed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'on' in this phrasal verb. The final k of 'bank' links into the vowel of 'on', so it sounds like 'ban-KAHN' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It expresses trust and confidence in someone or something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'you can bank on it' to mean something is certain, as in 'he'll be late, you can bank on it.' It is informal but common in everyday conversation and in business. A natural reply is 'Great, I'll count on that' or simply 'Thanks, I appreciate it.'

distinctions.note: Count on is a near-synonym that sounds slightly more personal and everyday, while bank on often adds a sense of certainty.
Rely on is more neutral and common in formal writing, while bank on is more informal and colloquial.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about the ride tonight, you can bank on me to pick you up at six.
examples.professional: We can't bank on the vendor delivering before the release, so let's build in a buffer.
examples.analytical: A theory that must bank on untested assumptions carries a heavier burden of proof.

nuance.analogy: To bank on someone is like putting money in a bank you trust, knowing it will be there when you need it.
common_mistakes: Using 'bank in' instead of 'bank on' with the same meaning.
Using 'bank on' with a noun that is too abstract, where 'count on' or 'rely on' sounds more natural.
Forgetting that 'you can bank on it' is a common, stand-alone phrase of certainty.

senses.definition: A flag or standard used by a military commander, monarch or nation.
senses.example: The army's commander raised the royal banner above the castle walls as the troops marched in.

senses.definition: The military unit under such a flag or standard.
senses.example: The banner of cavalry rode ahead of the main army through the valley at dawn.

senses.definition: A military or administrative subdivision.
senses.example: The province was divided into three banners, each governed by a regional administrator.

senses.definition: Any large sign, especially when made of soft material or fabric.
senses.example: The mayor hung a banner across Main Street to commemorate the town's 100th anniversary.

senses.definition: A large piece of cloth with a slogan, motto, or emblem carried in a demonstration or other procession or suspended in some conspicuous place.
senses.example: Protesters unfurled a banner reading 'Clean Water Now' outside the city council meeting.

senses.definition: A cause or purpose; a campaign or movement.
senses.example: They usually make their case under the banner of environmentalism.

senses.definition: The title of a newspaper as printed on its front page; the nameplate; masthead.
senses.example: The paper's banner across the top of page one had faded after decades of printing.

senses.definition: A type of advertisement on a web page or on television, usually taking the form of a graphic or animation above or alongside the content.
senses.example: A large banner ad at the top of the news site kept covering the article I wanted.

senses.definition: A type of administrative division in Inner Mongolia and Tuva, made during the Qing dynasty; at that time, Outer Mongolia and part of Xinjiang were also divided into banners.
senses.example: Hanggin Rear Banner, Bayannur, Inner Mongolia, China

senses.definition: A particular pool of specific virtual items or characters, from which the players can draw randomly by paying in-game currency.
senses.example: I'll keep pulling on this banner until I get my favorite character.

senses.definition: One who bans something.
senses.example: The new mayor was a fierce banner of plastic bags, pushing the ordinance through in March.

senses.definition: The principal standard of a knight.
senses.example: The knight rode into the tournament carrying his banner embroidered with the family crest.

senses.definition: Exceptional; very good.
senses.example: The bakery had a banner year, selling twice as many loaves as the year before.

senses.definition: To adorn with a banner.
senses.example: Volunteers bannered the square with bright ribbons and flags for the festival.

senses.definition: To display as a banner headline.
senses.example: The Chronicle bannered the senator's resignation across its front page the next morning.

core.definition: A long piece of cloth with a message or design, hung up or carried on a pole at a parade, protest, event, or building.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BAN. The final -er is unstressed and r-colored, so say it as a soft 'er' sound, not 'ah' or 'ayn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a noun. As an adjective in 'banner year' or 'banner season', it is clearly positive, meaning outstanding.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see banners at parades, school events, sports games, and protests, and online the word also names a wide web ad strip, as in 'banner ad'. The adjective 'banner year' is common in business and sports news to mean a record or outstanding year. As a verb, 'to banner' is rare and sounds literary; Americans more often say 'to hang a banner'.

distinctions.note: A flag is a piece of cloth that represents a nation, state, or group, usually with a fixed design; a banner carries a message or slogan and is often temporary.
A sign is usually a fixed or posted board with information; a banner is a cloth hung or carried, often for a specific event.

examples.everyday: They hung a huge banner over the gym that said Welcome Home, Coach.
examples.professional: Let's run a banner ad on the homepage for the spring webinar and see who signs up.
examples.analytical: The regiment marched behind its banner, and the cloth became a visible symbol of loyalty that men were willing to die to protect.

nuance.analogy: A flag is the face of a country, while a banner is a message stretched across the street for everyone to read.
nuance.etymology: From Old French baniere, from Medieval Latin bandum, meaning a standard or flag.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -er as a full 'ah' or 'ayn' sound; keep it soft and r-colored.
Using 'banner' for a small logo or icon; a banner is a long piece of cloth or a wide web ad, not a small image.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture a banner, Hebrew nes, is a signal pole or standard that gathers people. In Exodus 17:15 Moses builds an altar and names it 'The LORD is my banner' after the victory over Amalek. Song of Solomon 2:4 says the lover's banner over the beloved is love, and Psalm 60:4 says God gives a banner to those who fear him, so that they may rally to it.

banner.etymology: From Middle English *baner*, from Old French *baniere* (Modern *bannière*), of origin.

senses.definition: To make a short, loud, explosive noise with the vocal organs (said of animals, especially dogs).
senses.example: The neighbor's dog is always barking.

senses.definition: To make a clamor; to make importunate outcries.
senses.example: The protesters began to bark at the mayor until security escorted them out of the hall.

senses.definition: To speak sharply.
senses.example: The sergeant barked an order.

senses.definition: To strip the bark from; to peel.
senses.example: Dad showed me how to bark the logs with a drawknife before they dried.

senses.definition: To abrade or rub off any outer covering from.
senses.example: I barked my shins climbing the fence.

senses.definition: To girdle.
senses.example: To kill the invasive trees, the crew barked each trunk in a ring near the base.

senses.definition: To cover or enclose with bark, or as with bark.
senses.example: to bark the roof of a hut

senses.definition: The short, loud, explosive sound uttered by a dog, a fox, and some other animals.
senses.example: The neighbor's dog let out a sharp bark every time the mail carrier walked past.

senses.definition: An abrupt loud vocal utterance.
senses.example: His sudden bark of laughter startled everyone in the crowded elevator.

senses.definition: (video games) A short, repeatable, and unobtrusive voiceline spoken by an NPC.
senses.example: Every time I passed the guard, he repeated the same bark about the locked gate.

senses.definition: The exterior covering of the trunk and branches of a tree or of various other woody plants.
senses.example: The bark of the old oak had deep furrows where years of rain had worn it.

senses.definition: Hard candy made in flat sheets, for instance out of chocolate, peanut butter, toffee or peppermint.
senses.example: She bought a chocolate peanut butter bark at the holiday market for her nephew.

senses.definition: The crust formed on barbecued meat that has had a rub applied to it.
senses.example: The pitmaster let the brisket develop a dark, peppery bark before wrapping it in foil.

senses.definition: The envelopment or outer covering of anything.
senses.example: A tough bark of fried batter encased the fish, keeping the inside moist.

senses.definition: Woodchips.
senses.example: We spread a thick layer of bark around the roses to keep weeds down.

senses.definition: A vessel, typically with three (or more) masts, with the foremasts (or fore- and mainmasts) square-rigged, and mizzenmast schooner-rigged.
senses.example: The three-masted bark sailed out of the harbor with its cargo of coffee.

senses.definition: (music) The quick opening of the hi-hat cymbal as it is hit, followed by its timely closing.
senses.example: The drummer's bark on the hi-hat gave the chorus a crisp, snappy feel.

senses.definition: Peruvian bark or Jesuit's bark, the bark of the cinchona from which quinine is produced.
senses.example: Doctors in the 1800s prescribed Peruvian bark to treat fevers before quinine was isolated.

senses.definition: (poetic) A sailing vessel or boat of any kind.
senses.example: Across the silver sea, the bark carried our hopes toward a distant shore.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: The sound of a dog barking.
senses.example: The dog went Bark at the squirrel, and then sprinted off across the yard.

core.definition: To make a sharp, loud, explosive sound with the voice, especially of a dog; to speak in a sharp, harsh way.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a clear r; it rhymes with park and dark. Do not drop the r, which is pronounced in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for animals; when used of people, it is negative, meaning to speak harshly or give orders aggressively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bark for dogs and for speaking sharply, as in the manager barked orders at the crew. Neighbors often complain about a dog that barks at night. Bark also names the outer covering of a tree, which is pronounced the same, so context shows which meaning is intended.

distinctions.note: Yap describes a small dog's high, repeated barking and is often used for people who talk too much; bark is the general word for the sound.
Woof imitates a dog's bark and is used mostly by children or in cartoons, not as a formal verb.

examples.everyday: The neighbor's dog barks every time someone walks past the fence.
examples.professional: The team lead barked at everyone to finish the release before noon, which made the meeting tense.
examples.analytical: In animal behavior research, a bark is studied as a signal that carries information about threat, identity and emotional state.

nuance.analogy: A dog's bark is like a smoke alarm: short, loud and meant to warn.
nuance.etymology: From Old English beorcan, to bark; the tree-bark noun comes from a different Old Norse source.
common_mistakes: Confusing the tree-bark noun with the sound of a dog; both are spelled bark, so context decides.
Dropping the r and saying BAHK; General American keeps the r clearly.

bark.etymology: From Middle English *barken*, *berken*, *borken*, from Old English *beorcan* (“to bark”), from the **berkan* (“to bark”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰerg-* (“to make a noise, growl, bark”), from **bʰer-* (“to drone, hum, buzz”).

senses.definition: A blow with a stick or cudgel.
senses.example: A bastinade struck across his shoulders left a bruise that lasted weeks.

senses.definition: A sound beating with a stick or cudgel, specifically: A form of punishment among the Turks, Chinese, and others, consisting in beating an offender on the soles of his feet.
senses.example: The colonial official ordered the bastinade for the thief, beaten on the soles of his feet.

senses.definition: To beat in this manner.
senses.example: The guards bastinaded the prisoner until he could no longer stand on his feet.

core.definition: A punishment of repeated blows with a stick on the soles of the feet, used in some past legal systems.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the last syllable, NAYD, which rhymes with 'made' and 'lemonade'. Do not stress the first syllable, and do not pronounce the final -e as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes cruel physical punishment, so it is a grim historical term.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans will never use this word; you will meet it in history books, travel writing, or discussions of past legal systems, especially the Ottoman Empire. In modern American English you would say 'corporal punishment', 'flogging', or 'caning' for similar practices. The spelling bastinado is also common and equally correct.

distinctions.note: Flogging is a general term for whipping or beating, often on the back, while bastinade specifically means blows to the soles of the feet.
Caning uses a thin rod, usually on the hands or buttocks, while bastinade specifically targets the feet.

examples.everyday: I had never heard of the bastinade until my history class described it.
examples.professional: The chapter on Ottoman legal practice mentions the bastinade as a punishment for minor offenses.
examples.analytical: European travelers' accounts of the bastinade reveal as much about their own anxieties as about Ottoman justice.

nuance.analogy: Like a drummer hitting one precise spot again and again until the rhythm becomes pain.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish bastonada, a blow with a stick, from bastón, stick.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with baton or bastion because of the similar sounds.
Using it for any beating; the word specifically refers to blows on the soles of the feet.

senses.definition: In a bathetic manner.

core.definition: In a way that drops suddenly from serious or grand to trivial or silly, usually without the speaker intending it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -THET-, with a reduced first syllable and a short i in the middle. Keep the ending -klee light, and avoid stressing the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a writer or speaker's failed attempt at grandeur.
nuance.usage_note: This adverb is rare and appears mainly in literary criticism, reviews, and academic writing. Americans would not use it in casual speech, where they would say 'the ending fell completely flat' instead. It works best to describe how a passage or speech moved from serious to silly.

distinctions.note: Pathetically means in a pitiful or inadequate way, while bathetically means in an anticlimactic drop from grandeur.
Sentimentally describes excessive emotion, while bathetically describes a sudden fall in tone or seriousness.
Absurdly means ridiculously, while bathetically specifically refers to a drop from a serious or grand tone.

examples.professional: Her presentation opened with a bold vision for the platform, then bathetically moved into a slide about printer maintenance.
examples.analytical: The novel's climax collapses bathetically, undermining the tragic stakes the author has carefully established.

nuance.analogy: Like a grand speech that trips on the last step and lands in a puddle.
nuance.etymology: From bathetic, from bathos, from Greek bathos, meaning depth.
common_mistakes: Confusing bathetically with pathetically, which means in a pitiful way.
Using bathetically to mean deeply or intensely, which changes the meaning entirely.
Stressing the final syllable instead of the -THET- syllable.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the material making up the edge of a seashore, as with pebbles, gravel, and sand.
Pertaining to a beach or something beach-like.

core.definition: Having the casual, sunny look or feel of a beach, or resembling a beach in style or atmosphere.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BEECH, and end with a clear long e, like 'ee', not a short 'ih'. The ch is a single sound, so say beech, not beetch.

nuance.connotation: Positive and relaxed, suggesting a breezy, laid-back style.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use beachy in fashion, interior design, music and hair styling, often in phrases like beachy waves. It is informal and sounds upbeat, so it suits shopping, lifestyle and social media talk. For a more neutral description, Americans often say beach-like or coastal.

distinctions.note: Coastal describes a location near the sea, while beachy describes a relaxed, sunny style or feel.
Beach-like is neutral and literal, while beachy is more informal and often used to describe style.

examples.everyday: Her hair has those beachy waves that look effortless after a day in the sun.
examples.professional: The marketing team wants a beachy, relaxed look for the summer campaign.
examples.analytical: Critics describe the album's beachy sound as a deliberate nostalgia for 1960s California pop.

nuance.analogy: Beachy is like a sun-faded cotton shirt: relaxed, a little worn, and full of warm summer memories.
nuance.etymology: Beach plus the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using beachy to mean the physical sand or shore, when in everyday American English it usually means a style or feel.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a short 'ih' instead of a long 'ee'.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of beans.
senses.example: The soup had a beany, earthy flavor that my kids refused to touch.

core.definition: Tasting or smelling of cooked beans, usually in an unpleasant way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BEE. The second syllable is a short 'ee' like the one in beanie, so don't add a y sound between the syllables.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, describing an unpleasant flavor; it is neutral when simply describing a dish.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use beany most often for a flavor, such as some soy milks, protein drinks, or plant-based products, that tastes like cooked beans. It is usually a complaint or a warning about taste. For a neutral description, say it has a bean flavor. Do not use it to describe people.

distinctions.note: Earthy often suggests a rich, natural flavor and can be positive, while beany names specifically the taste of beans, usually negative.
Nutty is a positive flavor like almonds; beany suggests the raw, cooked-bean taste.

examples.everyday: This oat milk tastes a little beany, so I'll switch to almond.
examples.professional: Our taste panel described the new soy formula as too beany, so the team is testing a roasted version.
examples.analytical: A beany flavor in plant-based products is often traced to enzymes that release aldehydes when beans are crushed.

nuance.analogy: Like the taste of an unseasoned pot of beans that clings to everything in the kitchen.
nuance.etymology: From bean with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing beany as BEAN-ee with a long a; it is BEE-nee.
Using beany as a compliment about food; it is usually negative.

senses.definition: Appropriate, becoming.
senses.example: He moved with a befitting grace.

core.definition: Suitable or appropriate for a particular person, occasion, or status, especially in a dignified or formal way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, FIT. The final 'ing' is short and unstressed, so do not stretch it into 'eeng'. The 'i' in 'fit' is the short vowel of 'sit'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes something that properly honors a person or occasion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use befitting mainly in formal writing, speeches, or ceremonies, such as a 'befitting tribute' or a 'befitting farewell'. In everyday speech, people would say 'appropriate', 'suitable', or 'right for the occasion'. It is a little stiff for casual talk, so it can sound like a deliberate formal choice.

distinctions.note: Appropriate is neutral and common in everyday English, while befitting is more formal and emphasizes dignity or social status.
Fitting is a neutral word for suitable, while befitting is more formal and often used for honors, ceremonies, or a person's rank.
Suitable focuses on practical fit, such as a suitable job, while befitting focuses on what honors or matches a person's status.

examples.everyday: The restaurant had a big sign that said 'Happy Retirement, Frank', which seemed befitting for a man who worked there for forty years.
examples.professional: The company hosted a dinner befitting her thirty years of service, with speeches from the CEO and board members.
examples.analytical: The speech, befitting a state funeral, avoided any mention of the defeat and praised the dead as if they had never failed.

nuance.analogy: Like a suit tailored for a particular event, fitting the person and the moment exactly.
nuance.etymology: From the prefix be- and fit, from Middle English befitten, meaning to suit or become.
common_mistakes: Using befitting in casual speech, where appropriate would sound more natural.
Confusing it with befuddling, which means confusing someone.
Writing 'befitting to' instead of using 'befitting' directly before a noun or as a predicate adjective.

senses.definition: The sound produced when someone or something bellows.
senses.example: The bellowing from the stadium crowd shook the windows of the nearby apartments.

core.definition: A loud, deep, booming sound, usually made by a person shouting in anger or pain or by an animal such as a cow.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BEL, and keep the second syllable short and light. Do not stress the -ing ending, and say the ow sound as 'oh' in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, suggesting loud anger, pain or distress.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bellowing' to describe a deep, loud roar, especially from an angry person, a foreman, a farm animal or a coach. The noun is less common than 'yelling' or 'shouting' in everyday talk, but it is natural in writing. In conversation people more often use 'bellow' as a verb, as in 'he bellowed at us'.

distinctions.note: Yelling is the everyday word for loud shouting, while bellowing is deeper and more booming, often suggesting an animal or a large person.
Roaring is a long, powerful sound, as of a lion or a crowd, while bellowing is a shorter, more forceful shout.

examples.everyday: I heard bellowing from the neighbor's yard, so I went over to see what was wrong.
examples.professional: The foreman's bellowing across the warehouse floor made everyone stop what they were doing.
examples.analytical: The philosopher's bellowing rebuttal filled the room, though his argument was thinner than his voice.

nuance.analogy: Like a foghorn that carries across the harbor and makes everyone turn toward the sound.
nuance.etymology: From Old English belgan, meaning to swell up or be angry.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'be-LOH-ing'.
Confusing 'bellowing' with 'bellows', which is a device for blowing air.
Using 'bellowing' as an everyday word for ordinary talking, when it means loud and deep.

senses.definition: A traitor.

core.definition: A person who betrays their own side, friends, team or country; a traitor.

pronunciation.tip: Both names carry stress, on BEN and AR, and the last syllable of Arnold is a weak -uld, not a long o. Americans link the two names smoothly, as one phrase, with the r in AR clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. Calling someone a Benedict Arnold is a serious accusation of betrayal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this name as a common noun for someone who betrays people who trusted them, such as a teammate, coworker or friend, as well as a country. You hear it in sports, school and politics, as in 'He pulled a Benedict Arnold on the team.' It is rarely used for a stranger, because it implies someone once trusted. Natural alternatives are traitor or turncoat.

distinctions.note: Traitor is the general word for someone who betrays a country or cause; Benedict Arnold is sharper and more personal, implying betrayal of a trusted group.
A turncoat switches loyalty, often for convenience; Benedict Arnold suggests a deliberate betrayal of people who trusted you.

collocations: accuse someone of being a Benedict Arnold
the Benedict Arnold of the team

examples.everyday: Don't pull a Benedict Arnold on me and tell the coach about our plan.
examples.professional: If anyone on the team leaks the roadmap to a competitor, that is basically a Benedict Arnold move.
examples.analytical: Historians still debate whether Benedict Arnold's defection was driven by ideology, grievance or money, yet his name remains the American shorthand for betrayal.

nuance.analogy: It works like a label on a shelf: once someone is put there, the whole story of betrayal comes with them, the way Judas does in other traditions.
nuance.etymology: Named for Benedict Arnold, the American general who tried to hand West Point to the British in 1780; his first name comes from Latin benedictus, 'blessed'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable of Arnold with a long o, like 'nold' in 'old'; Americans say AR-nuld.
Using it for a mild disagreement; it is reserved for serious betrayal.
Forgetting that it is a proper name, so both words are capitalized in formal writing.

benedict-arnold.etymology: From Benedict Arnold, famous for betraying the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War.

senses.definition: Having a disposition to do good.
senses.example: Chinese and Eastern mythologies describe dragons as benevolent.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) Possessing or manifesting love for mankind.
senses.example: The benevolent donor quietly covered tuition for every student who asked.

senses.definition: Altruistic, charitable, good, just and fair.
senses.example: Our manager was benevolent and fair when he reviewed each employee's contract.

core.definition: Kind, generous, and wanting to help others; describing a person, group, or institution with goodwill.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, NEV, and reduce the first and third syllables to schwa. Don't say BEN-uh-vuh-lent, and remember that the final -ent is a short 'uh-nt'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes goodwill, but 'benevolent dictator' can sound ironic or critical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say benevolent in formal writing, business, and nonprofit contexts, such as a benevolent society or a benevolent employer. In everyday conversation they would say nice or kind. The phrase benevolent dictator is a common American way to describe a powerful leader who is kind but not democratic.

distinctions.note: Kind is everyday and describes behavior, while benevolent is formal and describes a general attitude of goodwill.
Generous is about giving, while benevolent can describe goodwill even when nothing is given.
Benevolent describes kind intentions toward people, while benign describes something gentle or not harmful, often a medical condition.

examples.everyday: Our landlord seems pretty benevolent, since he waived the late fee when my paycheck was delayed.
examples.professional: Our benevolent employer matches donations to food banks, so our team can give more without extra cost.
examples.analytical: Hobbes questioned whether a benevolent sovereign could exist, since power tends to corrupt even good intentions.

nuance.analogy: A benevolent person is like a warm host who makes sure every guest has a chair before sitting down.
nuance.etymology: From Latin benevolens, present participle of benevolere, 'to wish well', from bene 'well' and velle 'to wish'.
common_mistakes: Confusing benevolent with benign when describing a person; say 'a benevolent person', not 'a benign person'.
Using benevolent for simple politeness, which sounds stiff in casual conversation.

benevolent.etymology: From Old French *benevolent*, borrowed from Latin *benevolēns*.

senses.definition: Lacking education or knowledge; unenlightened; also, lacking morality; immoral, unscrupulous.

core.definition: Lacking education, knowledge, or enlightenment, often in a condescending way; also, caught by nightfall while traveling.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NY, the second syllable, which rhymes with 'sky'. The final -ed is pronounced 'id', and the first syllable is a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It is condescending and can sound insulting, because it suggests a whole group or era is unenlightened.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use benighted in everyday speech; it appears mostly in literature, history writing, and opinion pieces. Calling someone benighted is a strong and patronizing insult, so use ignorant, uninformed, or old-fashioned in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Ignorant is a plain, common word for lacking knowledge, while benighted is literary and often describes whole cultures or eras.
Uninformed is neutral and means not up to date on facts, while benighted suggests deeper moral or intellectual darkness.
Unenlightened is close in meaning but less dated, and it is more likely in modern prose.

examples.everyday: My uncle still has benighted ideas about vaccines, and it drives my mom crazy.
examples.professional: Our old reporting process was benighted, and it took three months to find errors that a simple dashboard would have caught.
examples.analytical: Critics called the policy benighted, arguing that it rested on superstition rather than on the available evidence.

nuance.analogy: A benighted mind is like a room with the lights off: the person cannot see what is right in front of them.
nuance.etymology: From benight, formed from be- and night, meaning overtaken by darkness; the sense of ignorance developed later.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as BEN-ighted, with stress on the first syllable.
Using benighted as a neutral word for not knowing a fact, which sounds insulting.

core.definition: The father of Balaam the prophet, and also the name of an early king of Edom in Genesis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BEE. The second syllable has an r-colored vowel, so pronounce the final sound as a clear "or" as in "door".

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: This name is used in Bible study and religious writing. Americans typically say it as "BEE-or," and when you mention Balaam, say "Balaam son of Beor" so the listener can identify him.

examples.everyday: My Bible class got stuck on the name Beor because it shows up in the story of Balaam.
examples.professional: When I taught Numbers 22, I pointed out that Balaam is always identified as the son of Beor.
examples.analytical: The repeated identification of Balaam as the son of Beor links the prophet to a family of Mesopotamian diviners, which shapes his ambiguous role in Numbers.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name printed on a passport, Beor is the label that identifies whose son Balaam was.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew name of uncertain meaning; some scholars connect it to a root meaning "to burn" or "torch," but this is not settled.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like "bee-ur" with two equal syllables.
Confusing it with Bethor or Bosor, which are different names in other texts.
nuance.biblical_note: Beor is the father of Balaam, the non-Israelite prophet hired by Balak of Moab to curse Israel (Numbers 22:5). Deuteronomy 23:4 identifies Balaam as the son of Beor of Pethor. Genesis 36:32 names a king of Edom called Bela son of Beor, so the name also appears in the list of Edomite kings.

senses.definition: One who fights as if frenzied, like a berserker.
A type of von Neumann probe whose mission is to exterminate alien lifeforms.
senses.example: In the science fiction novel, a berserker probe roams the galaxy destroying every alien civilization it finds.

senses.definition: (historical) A Norse warrior who purportedly fought in a trance-like frenzy; a berserk.
senses.example: The saga describes a berserker who bit his shield and charged into battle without fear.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A person who fights or acts with wild, frenzied rage; someone who is intensely and violently aggressive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BUR. The middle and final syllables are both reduced r-colored vowels, so do not pronounce the final -er as 'kair'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting out-of-control aggression; in sports or gaming talk it can be playful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say go berserk to mean losing control with anger or excitement. The noun berserker is informal and often figurative, as when describing someone as a berserker on the basketball court. It also refers to Norse warriors, a topic you may meet in history class.

distinctions.note: Berserk is the adjective, as in 'the crowd went berserk'; berserker is the noun for a person who behaves that way.
A maniac is someone who is crazy, especially in a violent way; berserker is looser and often used for an intense, energetic person.

examples.everyday: My little brother turns into a berserker whenever someone touches his video game controller.
examples.professional: The launch week turned our team into berserkers, fixing bugs day and night.
examples.analytical: The Norse sagas portray the berserker as a figure of terrifying power, yet they also show how such frenzy threatens the community it claims to protect.

nuance.analogy: Like a storm that rises suddenly over calm water, a berserker's rage arrives without warning and sweeps everything aside.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse berserkr, traditionally 'bear-shirt' or 'bare-shirt', though the origin is debated.
common_mistakes: Using berserker as a verb or adjective; the adjective is berserk.
Stressing the middle syllable as 'bur-SER-ker'.

senses.definition: A place for a vessel to lie at anchor or to moor.
senses.example: The cargo ship sailed into its berth at the port just before dawn.

senses.definition: A room in a vessel in which the officers or company mess (“eat together”) and reside; also, a room or other place in a vessel for storage.
senses.example: The crew stored the spare rope in the forward berth beside the galley.

senses.definition: A place on a vessel to sleep, especially a bed on the side of a cabin.
senses.example: I climbed into the top berth and fell asleep to the sound of waves.

senses.definition: A job or position on a vessel.
senses.example: He finally earned a berth as a deckhand on a container ship.

senses.definition: A bunk or other bed for sleeping on in a caravan, a train, etc.
A place for a vehicle on land to park.
senses.example: The delivery truck needed a berth at the loading dock for three hours.

senses.definition: An appointment, job, or position, especially one regarded as comfortable or good.
senses.example: She landed a comfortable berth in the state attorney general's office.

senses.definition: A position or seed in a tournament bracket.
senses.example: The top seed earned a first-round berth against the weakest team in the bracket.

senses.definition: A position on a field of play.
senses.example: The rookie took up a berth in center field for the first time this season.

senses.definition: Chiefly in wide berth: a sufficient space in the water for a ship or other vessel to lie at anchor or maneuver without getting in the way of other vessels, or colliding into rocks or the shore.
senses.example: After the argument, most of the staff gave the new manager a wide berth.

senses.definition: Chiefly in wide berth: a sufficient space for maneuvering or safety.
senses.example: After the argument, most of the staff gave the new manager a wide berth.

senses.definition: A proper place for a thing.
senses.example: Every tool in the garage has its proper berth on the pegboard.

senses.definition: (historical) An assigned place for a person in a horse-drawn coach or other means of transportation, or in a barracks.
senses.example: The passenger secured a berth in the stagecoach bound for Denver.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To use a device to bring (a spacecraft) into its berth or dock.
senses.example: Mission control will berth the cargo capsule with the station's robotic arm tomorrow.

senses.definition: To assign (someone) a berth (noun etymology 1, noun sense 1.3 or etymology 1, noun sense 2.2) or place to sleep on a vessel, a train, etc.
senses.example: The conductor berthed us in a sleeper cabin on the overnight train.

senses.definition: To provide (someone) with a berth (noun etymology 1, noun sense 3.1) or appointment, job, or position.
senses.example: The senator berthed his former aide in a comfortable post at the agency.

senses.definition: Of a person: to occupy a berth.
senses.example: The crew berthed in the forward quarters, sharing bunks by rotation.

senses.definition: To bring (a ship or other vessel) into a berth (noun etymology 1, noun sense 1.1); also, to provide a berth for (a vessel).
Of a vessel: to move into a berth.

core.definition: A bunk or sleeping space on a ship or train; also a safe distance, as in the idiom 'give a wide berth'.

pronunciation.tip: The rhotic r gives the vowel an 'ur' quality, and the th is voiceless, as in 'thin'. In American speech berth sounds identical to birth, so context tells them apart.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the idiom give a wide berth carries a sense of caution or mild disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use berth for a bunk on a train or ship and for the place where a large vessel docks, though boats in a marina are usually said to be at a dock or slip. The idiom give someone or something a wide berth is common in news and everyday talk. Saying you were offered a berth for a job sounds British or literary.

distinctions.note: Birth means the beginning of life; in American speech it sounds the same as berth, so the spelling and context are your only guide.
A dock is a structure for loading or landing boats; a berth is the specific space where one vessel lies.
A slip is a boat's space in a marina, usually for small boats; berth is the general word for a vessel's place.

examples.everyday: Give that guy a wide berth; he's been yelling at the cashier all morning.
examples.professional: The port assigned our container ship to berth 14 as soon as the tide came in.
examples.analytical: The idiom to give a wide berth shows how a sailor's need for room at sea has become a general way of describing social distance.

nuance.analogy: Like a reserved parking space for a boat, a berth is a set place where something waits safely until it moves on.
nuance.etymology: Probably from bear in its nautical sense of keeping away from something; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Writing 'give a wide birth' instead of 'give a wide berth'.
Using berth for a dock or marina slip, when Americans usually say dock or slip for small boats.

berth.etymology: The noun is derived from Late Middle English *birth* (“ bearing away or off, clearance, berth”).

core.definition: Fishing village on the northeast shore of the Sea of Galilee; hometown of Peter, Andrew and Philip.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SAY, which has a long 'ay' vowel. The final syllables are reduced, so 'ih-duh' is quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a place name; in the Gospels it carries a solemn tone because Jesus pronounces a warning against it.
nuance.usage_note: Bethsaida appears mainly in Bible study, sermons and discussions of Holy Land geography. Americans may say it when discussing the disciples' hometowns or Jesus' ministry near the Sea of Galilee. In casual talk, people usually add 'the fishing village' or 'Galilee' so the listener knows which place is meant.
collocations: Bethsaida on the Sea of Galilee

examples.everyday: Our Bible study leader said Peter, Andrew and Philip all came from Bethsaida, near the Sea of Galilee.
examples.professional: The tour guide placed Bethsaida near the Jordan's mouth, so our itinerary needs to show that stop.
examples.analytical: Jesus' woe against Bethsaida in Matthew 11 shows that near proximity to his works increases the responsibility to repent.

nuance.analogy: Like a small harbor town whose fishermen became famous, a place known mostly for the people who came from it.
nuance.etymology: Aramaic bêt-ṣaydā, 'house of fishing'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, BETH-say-duh.
Dropping the middle syllable 'ih' so the word sounds like 'beth-SAY-duh'.
nuance.biblical_note: Bethsaida is Aramaic bêt-ṣaydā, 'house of fishing'. John 1:44 says Andrew, Peter and Philip came from Bethsaida. Mark 8:22-26 describes Jesus healing a blind man at Bethsaida. Matthew 11:20-24 records Jesus' woe against Bethsaida and Chorazin because they did not repent despite his mighty works.

senses.definition: The period or time between two events; interim; meantime; meanwhile.

core.definition: The period of time between two events, while waiting for something else to happen; the interim or meantime.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TIME, and the first word has a lighter stress on twin. The first syllable of between is reduced to a short bih, so the phrase sounds like bih-twin-TIME.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it describes an interval without judgment, though it sounds literary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say between-time in everyday speech and would normally say in the meantime or in the meantime while. You will mostly meet the word in literature, older writing, or formal prose. In conversation, a natural reply to news that you must wait is In the meantime, let's keep in touch.

distinctions.note: Meantime is the everyday American equivalent, usually as the phrase in the meantime.
Interim is a formal word often used for temporary roles or periods, as in an interim director.
In-between is an adjective or adverb, as in in-between jobs, rather than a noun for the period itself.

examples.everyday: Please keep us in your thoughts in the between-time while the test results come back.
examples.professional: In the between-time, we will keep the old system running in parallel with the new one.
examples.analytical: Benjamin's essay treats the between-time of revolution as a space where old institutions fail and new habits form.

nuance.analogy: Like the pause between a flash of lightning and the sound of the thunder.
nuance.etymology: A compound of between and time, both from Old English.
common_mistakes: Writing in between time as one unhyphenated word group when you mean the compound noun; the hyphenated form is between-time.
Using between-time in casual speech where in the meantime sounds natural.

senses.definition: Having two sides.
Involving both sides equally.
Binding on both of the two parties involved.
Having bilateral symmetry.
senses.example: Most animals have bilateral symmetry, with matching left and right halves.

senses.definition: Involving descent or ascent regardless of sex and side of the family (bilateral linearity).
senses.example: Bilateral descent traces ancestry through both the mother's and the father's families.

senses.definition: A meeting between two people or groups.
senses.example: The two countries scheduled a bilateral to discuss the trade dispute next month.

core.definition: Involving or affecting two sides or parties equally, such as a bilateral agreement between two countries.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAT, the second syllable. The t between vowels is a flap, so it sounds like a soft d, and the final -al is an unstressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise descriptive word used in politics, law, business, and medicine.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bilateral mainly in politics, law, business, and medicine, as in bilateral talks or bilateral symmetry. In casual speech they would say two-way or between the two of us. Use it in writing or meetings when you are describing an agreement or relationship between exactly two parties.

distinctions.note: Bipartisan means supported by both major political parties, while bilateral means between two countries or two parties.
Two-sided is plain everyday language, while bilateral is formal and often used for agreements or symmetry.

examples.everyday: We made a bilateral deal: I cover the groceries and you cover the gas for the trip.
examples.professional: The bilateral agreement with our vendor has to be signed before the end of the quarter.
examples.analytical: A bilateral treaty binds each party to obligations that depend on the other's compliance, which shapes how disputes are resolved.

nuance.analogy: A bilateral agreement is like a handshake: it takes two people, and it means little if only one side holds on.
nuance.etymology: From Latin bi- meaning two, and lateralis, of a side, from latus, side.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in bye-luh-TAIR-uhl; the stress belongs on LAT.
Using bilateral for a meeting or agreement among three or more parties; that would be multilateral.

senses.definition: Having the ability to speak two languages fluently.
Spoken or written in two different languages.
senses.example: a bilingual dictionary

senses.definition: Characterized by the use or presence of two languages.
senses.example: bilingual education

senses.definition: A person who is able to use two languages.
senses.example: My grandmother was a bilingual who switched between Spanish and English at the dinner table.

senses.definition: An inscription that includes the same text in two languages.
senses.example: The bilingual on the temple wall, in Greek and Egyptian, helped scholars decode hieroglyphs.

core.definition: Able to speak two languages fluently; also describes text, signs or materials written or presented in two languages.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LING. The spelling 'gual' is pronounced 'gwuhl', with a reduced vowel, not 'gyoo-al'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Being bilingual is seen as a valuable skill in the US, especially in healthcare, schools and customer service.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I'm bilingual' or 'She's bilingual' for someone who speaks two languages well, and use it for signs, forms and schools. It is also used as a noun ('a bilingual' is less common), while 'a native speaker' or 'fluent in two languages' are alternatives for a person. Saying 'I'm a little bilingual' is a casual joke, not a precise claim.

distinctions.note: Multilingual means able to use three or more languages, while bilingual means exactly two.
Bilateral means involving two sides or countries, such as a bilateral trade agreement, and has nothing to do with languages.

examples.everyday: My cousin is bilingual, so she translates for her grandmother at family dinners.
examples.professional: We need a bilingual support agent for Spanish-speaking customers on Tuesday's shift.
examples.analytical: Claims that bilingual children gain cognitive advantages depend heavily on how researchers define bilingual.

nuance.analogy: A bilingual person is like a house with two front doors, each leading to a different community.
nuance.etymology: From Latin bi- (two) and lingua (tongue, language).
common_mistakes: Confusing bilingual with bilateral, which means two-sided.
Stressing the last syllable, as in bi-ling-GWAL.

bite-off-more-than-you-can-chew.phonetic: /ˌbaɪt ˌɔf ˌmɔɹ ðæn ju kæn ˈtʃu/

senses.definition: To try to do too much; to take on or attempt more than one is capable of doing.
senses.example: I think I bit off more than I could chew when I agreed to paint this house by myself.

core.definition: To take on more work or responsibility than you can realistically handle.

pronunciation.respelling: bite awf mor than yoo kan CHOO
pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on chew, and than you can reduces quickly to thn yoo kn. Keep off and more lightly stressed, and keep the r in more clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative or cautionary: it suggests overcommitting and possible failure, though it can be said kindly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this at work, at school, and at home, usually about themselves or a friend who has agreed to a big project. Say I think I bit off more than I can chew with this renovation when you feel overwhelmed. A natural reply is Yeah, but you'll figure it out or Want some help? It is too casual for formal writing.

distinctions.note: Overcommit is more formal and business-like, describing agreeing to too many obligations; bite off more than you can chew is casual and often about one big task.
Stretch yourself is positive and suggests growth through challenge; bite off more is usually a warning about being overwhelmed.

antonyms: take it one step at a time
collocations: I think I bit off more than I can chew
don't bite off more than you can chew
bite off more than you can handle
bit off more than she could chew
realize you've bitten off more than you can chew

examples.everyday: I offered to host Thanksgiving for twenty people, and I think I bit off more than I can chew.
