examples.professional: We promised three new features this sprint, and honestly that's biting off more than we can chew.
examples.analytical: The dissertation tries to bite off more than it can chew, claiming to resolve both the problem of evil and the nature of grace in a single chapter.

nuance.analogy: Like taking a bite so big that you cannot close your mouth.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; the core image is a bite too large to chew.
common_mistakes: Saying bite off more than you can do, which loses the chewing image and sounds unnatural.
Using the wrong past tense: say I bit off more than I could chew, not bited.
Adding a y sound to chew, as in chyoo; the American word is a plain choo.

conversation.text: Don't bite off more than you can chew by signing up for three races this spring.
Taking on two projects plus a new hire? You might bite off more than you can chew.
I think I bit off more than I could chew with this home renovation.

inflections: bites off more than you can chew
bit off more than you can chew
bitten off more than you can chew
biting off more than you can chew

senses.definition: A police patrol car.
senses.example: A black and white pulled up outside the bank just as the alarm went off.

senses.definition: The police, a police officer or the clothing they wear.
senses.example: A black and white stopped us at the corner and asked for my license.

senses.definition: A type of giant cookie (about eight inches in diameter) with icing on the top side: half white, half dark chocolate.
senses.example: At the bakery, I ordered a black and white cookie with frosting split down the middle.

senses.definition: A kind of ice cream soda with chocolate and vanilla flavors.
senses.example: The diner's black and white soda was my favorite treat as a kid.

senses.definition: Day and night (two very different things).
senses.example: Their personalities were black and white, so they never agreed on anything.

senses.definition: Of art, a photograph or photography, using dots or lines that are either black or white (with no other values involved).
senses.example: Using Adobe Photoshop, he opened the images that were grayscale and converted them to be black and white.

senses.definition: Of art, a photograph or photography, using shades of gray rather than shades of any other color.
senses.example: Their photos from that era are all black and white.

senses.definition: Of a television or monitor, displaying images in shades of gray rather than color.
senses.example: Grandpa still watches the old black and white television in his bedroom.

senses.definition: Classifying people, objects or concepts as two polar opposites, especially "right" and "wrong"; dichotomous and inflexible.
senses.example: I wish she weren't always so black and white about every single thing.

senses.definition: Easily divided into diametrically opposing categories.
senses.example: Her arguments were too black and white, leaving no room for compromise at all.

core.definition: Using only black, white and shades of gray with no color; figuratively, simple and clear-cut, with no middle ground.

pronunciation.tip: Before a noun, as in a black-and-white photo, the first word gets the stress: BLACK-and-white. Alone, as in a black and white thing, the stress often falls on WHITE. Keep and reduced to uhnd.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for photography and art; in figurative use, it can be negative when it suggests oversimplification, as in black-and-white thinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use black-and-white for old photos, films and art, and they also say black-and-white thinking to criticize simple right-or-wrong views. Writing it with a hyphen before a noun is standard American usage. The word also names a New York style of cookie and an old slang term for a police car, but in everyday talk the adjective is the common use.

distinctions.note: Monochrome means one single color, which can be any hue, while black-and-white means only black, white and gray.
Grayscale is a technical term for digital images using only shades of gray, and it is more precise than black-and-white in computing.
In black and white is an idiom meaning in writing, so it is a different sense from the adjective.

collocations: see things in black and white

examples.everyday: My grandma's wedding photos are all black-and-white, and they still look amazing.
examples.professional: The vendor's contract terms aren't black-and-white, so let's clarify the service levels before we sign.
examples.analytical: Moral questions are rarely black-and-white; the ethics of the study depend on context and consent.

nuance.analogy: Like a grayscale photo, it keeps the shapes clear but removes the colors that help you see the subtleties.
nuance.etymology: From black (Old English blæc) and white (Old English hwit), joined by and.
common_mistakes: Writing black and white before a noun without a hyphen, when the standard form is black-and-white photo.
Using black and white as a noun for in writing without the preposition in; say in black and white.

senses.definition: To produce an air current.
senses.example: Open the window so the breeze can blow through the room.

senses.definition: To propel by an air current (or, if under water, a water current), usually with the mouth.
senses.example: Blow the dust off that book and open it up.

senses.definition: To be propelled by an air current.
senses.example: The leaves blow through the streets in the fall.

senses.definition: To direct or move, usually of a person to a particular location.
senses.example: The gale blew us straight into the harbor before dawn.

senses.definition: To create or shape by blowing.
senses.example: to blow bubbles

senses.definition: To force a current of air upon with the mouth, or by other means.
senses.example: to blow the fire

senses.definition: To clear of contents by forcing air through.
senses.example: to blow an egg

senses.definition: To cause to make sound by blowing (as a musical instrument).
senses.example: Blow your horn! That car is about to hit us!

senses.definition: To make a sound as a result of being blown.
senses.example: In the harbor, the ships’ horns blew.

senses.definition: To exhale visibly through the spout the seawater which it has taken in while feeding.
senses.example: There’s nothing more thrilling to the whale watcher than to see a whale surface and blow.

senses.definition: To burst or explode; to occur suddenly.
senses.example: Get away from that burning gas tank! It’s about to blow!

senses.definition: To cause to explode, shatter, or be utterly destroyed.
senses.example: The demolition squad neatly blew the old hotel up.

senses.definition: To cause the sudden destruction of.
senses.example: He blew the tires and the engine.

senses.definition: To suddenly fail or give way destructively.
senses.example: He tried to sprint, but his ligaments blew and he was barely able to walk to the finish line.

senses.definition: Of a vein, to suffer a rupture or puncture in the wall as a result of an injection or cannula, causing fluid (blood, medication, or saline) to leak into the surrounding tissue.
senses.example: The nurse stopped the IV right away because the vein had blown and the saline was leaking.

senses.definition: To melt away because of overcurrent, creating a gap in a wire, thus stopping a circuit from operating.
senses.example: The fuse blew when the space heater drew too much current from the circuit.

senses.definition: To recklessly squander.
senses.example: I managed to blow $1000 at blackjack in under an hour.

senses.definition: To fail at; to mess up; to make a mistake in.
senses.example: I blew it and forgot to start the spaghetti, so I had plenty of sauce and no pasta.

senses.definition: To be very undesirable.
senses.example: This blows!

senses.definition: To perform oral sex on (someone); to fellate.
senses.example: Who did you have to blow to get those backstage passes?

senses.definition: To leave, especially suddenly or in a hurry.
senses.example: Let’s blow this joint.

senses.definition: To leave the Church of Scientology in an unauthorized manner.
senses.example: After two decades in the church, he finally blew without telling anyone in his family.

senses.definition: To make flyblown; to defile or spoil, especially with fly eggs.
senses.example: The butcher's counter had been left uncovered, and the meat was blown by flies by noon.

senses.definition: (of a fly) To lay eggs; to breed (in flesh or meat).
senses.example: Flies will blow the exposed carcass within hours if nobody covers it.

senses.definition: To breathe hard or quick; to pant; to puff.
senses.example: He was blowing hard after climbing four flights of stairs to the office.

senses.definition: To put out of breath; to cause to blow from fatigue.
senses.example: The steep hill blew the runners, and several slowed to a walk.

senses.definition: To sing.
senses.example: That girl has a wonderful voice; just listen to her blow!

senses.definition: To flatulate or defecate.
senses.example: Uh, oh! I gotta blow!

senses.definition: To generate (a reading) on a breath alcohol meter.
senses.example: I blew a zero, so the cop let me drive on.

senses.definition: To blossom; to cause to bloom or blossom.
senses.example: The apple trees blew early this year after the unusually warm March.

senses.definition: (dated) To talk loudly; boast; brag.
senses.example: Grandpa would blow about his fishing catches at every holiday dinner.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To slander, insult, critique or discredit (someone); to reprimand or scold (someone).
senses.example: The coach blew him for missing practice again, and the whole team went quiet.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (historical) To blow from a gun.
senses.example: The gunner blew the lock off the door with a single shot.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: A strong wind.
senses.example: We’re having a bit of a blow this afternoon.

senses.definition: A chance to catch one's breath.
senses.example: The players were able to get a blow during the last timeout.

senses.definition: Powder cocaine.
senses.example: Police found a small bag of blow hidden under the seat of the car.

senses.definition: A blowjob; fellatio.
senses.example: His girlfriend gave him a blow.

senses.definition: An instance of the act of striking or hitting.
senses.example: A fabricator is used to direct a sharp blow to the surface of the stone.

senses.definition: A sudden or forcible act or effort; an assault.
senses.example: The boxer landed a crushing blow to the jaw in the final round.

senses.definition: A damaging occurrence.
senses.example: A further blow to the group came in 1917 when Thomson died while canoeing in Algonquin Park.

senses.definition: An outcrop of quartz from surrounding rock, thought to indicate mineral deposits below.
senses.example: Prospectors followed a white quartz blow up the ridge, hoping to find gold below.

senses.definition: Synonym of button (“the punchy or suspenseful line of dialogue that concludes a scene”).
A state of flowering; a bloom.
senses.example: roses in full blow

senses.definition: A display or mass of flowers; a yield.
A display of anything bright or brilliant.
An instance of using high-pressure air to empty water from the ballast tanks of a submarine, increasing the submarine's buoyancy and causing it to surface.
(historical) A cut made to a sheep's fleece by a shearer using hand-shears.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Used to express displeasure or frustration.
senses.example: Blow the expense!

core.definition: To push air out of your mouth, or to make air move, so that something is moved or cooled.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long 'oh' vowel that glides into an 'oo' sound. Remember the forms: blow, blew (/bluː/), blown (/bloʊn/).

nuance.connotation: Neutral: the verb describes ordinary actions like blowing out a candle or blowing on hot food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blow in everyday talk for actions such as blowing out candles, blowing your nose, or blowing on soup to cool it. In slang, blow can also mean to waste money or ruin a chance, as in 'blow an opportunity'. Its meaning depends heavily on the object and the particle that follows it.

distinctions.note: Breathing is involuntary air movement in and out, while blow is an intentional push of air out in a direction.
Puff is a short, quick burst of air, while blow can be longer and more controlled.

examples.everyday: Blow on your coffee before you drink it; it's still really hot.
examples.professional: I'll blow up the chart on the projector so everyone can read the axis labels.
examples.analytical: The author uses blow to suggest breath as a source of life, a sense older than the modern idiom about wind.

nuance.analogy: Blowing is like using a straw in reverse: you push air out instead of drawing it in.
nuance.etymology: From Old English blāwan, to blow, with cognates in other Germanic languages.
common_mistakes: Using blew as the past participle, as in 'I have blew it'; the correct form is 'I have blown it'.
Confusing blow with blew in past-tense sentences, such as 'Yesterday the wind blow hard'.

blow.etymology: From Middle English *blowen*, from Old English *blāwan* (“to blow, breathe, inflate, sound”), from **blāan*, from Proto-Germanic **blēaną* (“to blow”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰleh₁-* (“to swell, blow up”).

senses.definition: All the creative or academic works produced by someone.

core.definition: The complete set of creative, artistic or scholarly works that a person has produced over their career.

pronunciation.tip: The word 'of' reduces to a weak 'uhv' in fast speech. The 'work' is pronounced with an American r-colored vowel, like 'wurk', and the 'o' in 'body' is a short 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises the overall quality and quantity of someone's accomplishments.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in reviews, job interviews, awards and portfolio discussions for artists, writers, architects, scientists and scholars. It is a compliment to judge a person by their overall achievements. A natural reply is 'Thank you, I'm proud of it', or 'Thanks, it means a lot'.

distinctions.note: A portfolio is a selected set of samples chosen to show ability, while a body of work is the full record of everything produced.
Oeuvre is a formal, mostly literary or art-world term for a creator's entire output; Americans use body of work in ordinary speech.

collocations: a body of work speaks for itself

examples.everyday: After the gallery show, everyone kept talking about the artist's body of work.
examples.professional: Before we make an offer, let's review her body of work from the last three product launches.
examples.analytical: A scholar's body of work should be judged by its coherence over decades, not by one landmark book.

nuance.analogy: A body of work is like a garden: each piece is a plant, but people judge the whole garden over the years.
nuance.etymology: Body from Old English bodig, meaning trunk or person; work from Old English weorc, meaning deed or labor.
common_mistakes: Saying 'body of works' in the plural; the phrase is normally singular, with 'bodies of work' for several people or fields.
Using the phrase for a single piece of work, where 'work' or 'project' is more natural.

senses.definition: A person who loves reading books.

core.definition: A person who loves reading books and enjoys spending time with them.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable of 'lover', with 'book' a little weaker. End with a clear American r-colored vowel, not a strong second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm. Calling someone a book lover is a compliment about their curiosity and taste.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'book lover' casually, often as a self-description: 'I'm a total book lover.' It is friendly and not usually a criticism, unlike 'bookworm' or 'bookish', which can suggest awkwardness. A natural reply to 'You're a book lover too?' is 'Guilty!' or 'Me too, what are you reading?'

distinctions.note: A bookworm is a more playful, sometimes teasing term for someone who reads voraciously; 'book lover' is warmer and more neutral.
A reader is simply someone who reads; 'book lover' adds enthusiasm and pleasure in books as objects.
A bibliophile is a formal, literary term for someone who collects and treasures books, especially rare ones.

examples.everyday: Oh, you're a book lover too? Then you have to try the mystery series I just finished.
examples.professional: We're looking for a book lover who can help curate the children's section of the new library branch.
examples.analytical: To call oneself a book lover implies a bond with the physical object as well as with its contents, a distinction that scholars of print culture often examine.

nuance.analogy: A book lover is to books what a music lover is to songs: someone who finds pleasure in them, not only in what they say.
nuance.etymology: Compound of book (from Old English bōc) and lover (from love, Old English lufu, with the agent suffix -er).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'lover' with a long o, as in 'LOH-ver', instead of the short vowel in 'luv'
Using 'book lover' for a bookseller or store employee; it means someone who enjoys reading

core.definition: The Old Testament book about Daniel, a Jewish exile in Babylon who stays faithful to God, interprets dreams, and receives visions of future kingdoms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DAN in Daniel; the last syllable is a weak 'yul', not 'yel' or 'EEL'. In speech 'of' reduces to 'uv' and links: 'book-uv'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to reverent; it is a sacred text, though 'Daniel in the lions' den' is also a familiar cultural reference.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the book of Daniel' or just 'Daniel' in church and Bible study ('turn to Daniel 3'). The title is capitalized. Written references use the form Daniel 6:16.

distinctions.note: Both are apocalyptic, but Daniel is in the Old Testament and Revelation is the final New Testament book.
Ezekiel is a prophet in exile with visions, while Daniel combines court stories with visions.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study group is working through the Book of Daniel this fall.
examples.professional: Today I'll teach on Daniel 3, where three young men refuse to worship the golden statue.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the Book of Daniel was composed in the sixth century BC or during the Maccabean crisis.

nuance.analogy: Like a two-part story: first court tales of faithful living in a foreign empire, then dreamlike visions of history's end.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew name Daniyyel, meaning 'God is my judge'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the name as 'Dan-YEL' or 'DAN-ee-el'; it is 'DAN-yul'.
Writing 'Daniels' instead of 'Daniel'.
Saying 'Book from Daniel' instead of 'Book of Daniel'.
nuance.biblical_note: Daniel (Hebrew Daniyyel, 'God is my judge') is in the RSV Old Testament and is partly written in Aramaic (chapters 2:4b-7:28). Daniel 3 tells of three friends who are delivered from the fiery furnace for refusing idolatry. Daniel 6 tells how Daniel is saved from the lions' den after continuing to pray to God. Daniel 7 describes a vision of four beasts and one 'like a son of man' who receives an everlasting dominion.

traditions.view: Orthodox Bibles include additions to Daniel: the Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three, Susanna, and Bel and the Dragon, all read as Scripture.
Catholic Bibles also include these additions as deuterocanonical parts of Daniel and accept them as inspired.
Protestants generally follow the Hebrew text and place the additions in the Apocrypha, if included at all; the RSV prints them separately.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or coming from the north.
senses.example: boreal forests

core.definition: Of or relating to the cold northern regions of the Earth, especially the northern forests of Canada, Alaska and Russia.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a long 'ee' in the middle and a reduced final syllable. Don't stress the second syllable as in 'bo-REAL'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive, sometimes evocative of cold northern landscapes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'boreal' mostly in science, ecology, geography and nature writing, especially for the boreal forest or taiga of Alaska, Canada and northern Europe. In everyday talk, people say 'northern' or 'up north' instead. It is not a casual synonym for 'northern' in ordinary weather conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Arctic' refers to the polar region itself; 'boreal' refers to the northern forest zone just south of the tundra.
'Northern' is common and general; 'boreal' is precise and used mainly in ecology and geography.

examples.everyday: We drove for hours through boreal forest on the way to Alaska, and I didn't see a single house.
examples.professional: Climate models predict faster warming in the boreal zone, so our team is adding northern sites to the study.
examples.analytical: The novel's boreal imagery, with its silence and frozen lakes, becomes a symbol of spiritual isolation.

nuance.analogy: Like a dark green scarf wrapped around the top of the Northern Hemisphere, dense with spruce and pine.
nuance.etymology: From Latin borealis, northern, from Greek Boreas, the north wind.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable: say BOR-ee-ul, not bo-REE-ul.
Using 'boreal' as a casual synonym for 'northern' in everyday weather talk.

boreal.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *boreālis* (“northern”), from *Boreās*, from Ancient Greek *Βορέᾱς* (“personification of the north wind”).

senses.definition: To perform (a task) in an incompetent or unacceptable manner; to make a mess of something.
senses.example: A botched haircut seems to take forever to grow out.

senses.definition: To do (something) without care or skill, or clumsily.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: To mend or repair (something) clumsily.
senses.example: I tried to botch the broken hinge, but now the cabinet door won't close.

senses.definition: An action, job, or task that has been performed very badly; a ruined, defective, or clumsy piece of work.
senses.example: The first draft of the report was such a botch that we rewrote it entirely.

senses.definition: A patch put on, or a part of a garment patched or mended in a clumsy manner.
senses.example: Her grandmother's apron had a crooked botch on one pocket where she had sewn it.

senses.definition: A mistake that is very stupid or embarrassing.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: A messy, disorderly or confusing combination; a conglomeration; hodgepodge.
senses.example: The menu was a botch of Thai, Italian, and barbecue dishes with no clear theme.

senses.definition: A tumor or other malignant swelling.
senses.example: The surgeon removed a botch from the patient's shoulder before it could spread.

senses.definition: A case or outbreak of boils or sores.
senses.example: The village physician reported a botch of boils among the children after the flood.

core.definition: To do a job or task so badly that the result is spoiled, or to make a mess of something through carelessness.

pronunciation.tip: Use the open 'ah' vowel of the cot-caught merger, not the 'aw' of 'bawtch'. The 'tch' ending is a single quick sound, like the end of 'catch'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes poor work or a serious mistake and is usually used to criticize.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'botched' very often about jobs, surgeries, repairs, and plans that went badly wrong, such as 'a botched robbery' or 'a botched surgery.' It is stronger than 'mess up,' which can describe small errors. In casual talk, 'I totally botched that' is a natural way to admit a mistake.

distinctions.note: 'Mess up' is casual and can describe small or large errors, while 'botch' suggests the work was done badly and clumsily.
'Bungle' stresses clumsy handling, while 'botch' stresses the poor outcome of the work.
'Ruin' implies damage or destruction, while 'botch' implies a failed attempt at doing something well.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I botched the recipe and the cake came out flat as a pancake.
examples.professional: The vendor botched the migration, so we had to roll back the database overnight.
examples.analytical: The argument shows how a single botched decision can expose a deeper flaw in the whole process.

nuance.analogy: It is like a tailor who sews a seam crooked: the shirt still exists, but it is ruined for its purpose.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly related to an older sense of botch meaning to patch clumsily.
common_mistakes: Using 'botch' for a trivial error, where 'mess up' is more natural.
Pronouncing it with the 'aw' vowel of 'bought', which is British-style.

botch.etymology: From Middle English *bocchen* (“to mend”), of uncertain origin.

senses.definition: The act of enclosing (text, etc.) in brackets.
senses.example: The bracketing of the quotation made it clear which words were added by the editor.

senses.definition: A technique used to display the internal structure of a string of elements, in a similar manner to that used in mathematics and symbolic logic.
senses.example: Linguists use bracketing to show how the words in the sentence group together.

senses.definition: A series or group of brackets; brackets, collectively.
senses.example: The typesetter's document was cluttered with bracketing that made the math unreadable.

core.definition: In philosophy, especially phenomenology, the method of setting aside a belief or assumption so you can examine it without judging whether it is true.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BRAK. The t between vowels is a flap, so it sounds close to a soft 'd', and the second syllable is weak and reduced, not a full 'et'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a careful intellectual procedure.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people say 'let's set that aside' or 'let's put that on hold' for the same idea, and bracketing sounds academic. In philosophy classes and phenomenology discussions, the term is standard and assumed. The physical sense of putting text in brackets is also common in editing and writing.

distinctions.note: Epoché is the Greek term for the same suspension of judgment in ancient skepticism, while bracketing is the term Husserl used for the phenomenological version.
Parenthesizing means putting a phrase in parentheses in writing, a typographic act, whereas bracketing in philosophy is a mental act of setting a belief aside.

collocations: bracketing the existence of the world

examples.everyday: Let's bracket the budget question for now and talk about the venue first.
examples.professional: Before we commit, let's bracket the cost question and focus on whether the timeline works.
examples.analytical: Husserl's method of bracketing asks us to suspend the natural assumption that the world exists independently, so that experience can be described as it appears.

nuance.analogy: Like putting a colored filter over a lamp to see the room without assuming its true color, bracketing lets you examine a belief as it appears.
nuance.etymology: From bracket, a word traced to Spanish and French forms of Latin bracae 'breeches'; the -ing noun is English.
common_mistakes: Using bracketing only for physical brackets, when in philosophy it is a mental suspension of judgment.
Pronouncing the middle t as a hard /t/ instead of an American flap.

senses.definition: A braggart.
Empty boasting.

core.definition: Loud, empty boasting, or a person who boasts this way; often used to describe bragging that is not backed by real achievement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DOH, the third syllable, and the final 'o' is a clear 'oh' sound. The middle 'shee' is short and not a full 'shay'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies pretentious and hollow boasting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in writing and speech to sound witty or literary, but it is less common than 'bragging'. In everyday talk, say 'all talk' or 'bragging'. It is best used to describe a boastful person in an essay or a story.

distinctions.note: Bragging is the everyday word for boasting; braggadocio is more formal and emphasizes empty pretense.
A braggart is a person who boasts; braggadocio can name either the person or the behavior.

examples.everyday: All that talk about his new car is just braggadocio, he bought it used.
examples.professional: His presentation was pure braggadocio, with no data to support the claimed revenue growth.
examples.analytical: Spenser's character embodies braggadocio, whose courage exists only in words and vanishes when tested.

nuance.analogy: Like an empty balloon that looks big but has no air inside.
nuance.etymology: Coined by Edmund Spenser in The Faerie Queene (1590), formed from 'brag' with an Italianate ending.
common_mistakes: Using it as a verb; it is only a noun.
Saying 'braggadocio' with stress on the first syllable instead of DOH.

senses.definition: Detailed categorization, or itemization or listing, of the components of a thing; an instance of this.
senses.example: Looking at the breakdown of the budget, I see a few items we could cut.

senses.definition: A detailed description of a forthcoming project or screenplay which identifies all the required elements, such as the cast, costumes, equipment, props, and special effects.
senses.example: The screenplay breakdown lists every costume, prop, and special effect needed for each scene.

senses.definition: A failure, particularly one which is mechanical in nature.
senses.example: Whenever he was behind the wheel, he would panic at the first sign of a breakdown.

senses.definition: Something, such as a vehicle, that has experienced a mechanical failure.
senses.example: We saw a breakdown by the side of the road.

senses.definition: Separation of a thing into components; decomposition, fragmentation; an instance of this.
senses.example: Looking at the breakdown of the budget, I see a few items we could cut.

senses.definition: A failure in a relationship; a failure or loss of organization in a system.
senses.example: After months of arguments, their marriage reached a breakdown that no counselor could repair.

senses.definition: (Sudden) worsening of physical health or mental stability, resulting in an inability to carry on normal activities; an instance of this.
senses.example: After so much stress, he suffered a breakdown and simply gave up.

senses.definition: Injury to a horse's leg causing lameness; an instance of this.
senses.example: The vet said the mare's breakdown in her foreleg would keep her out of racing for good.

senses.definition: The short period of open play immediately after a tackle and before and during the ensuing ruck.
senses.example: The fly-half took the ball into contact, and the breakdown was messy for both sides.

senses.definition: A part of a piece of music or a song which differs from the other parts in that it features improvisation or is stripped down (for example, played by fewer instruments or a solo performer).
senses.example: During the bridge, the band drops to a quiet breakdown featuring just the bassist and drums.

senses.definition: Synonym of percussion break (“a percussion-focused segment of a song, chosen by a hip-hop DJ to manipulate through cutting, mixing, and other techniques in order to create rhythmic music”).
senses.example: The DJ stretched the breakdown for three minutes, cutting the drums back and forth.

senses.definition: A section of a song, typical in hardcore music and related styles (such as metalcore, grindcore, and deathcore), characterized by a lower tempo and greater heaviness and intensity of sound.
senses.example: The metalcore song slows to a crushing breakdown where the whole crowd starts moshing.

senses.definition: The sudden (and usually damaging) transition of an electrical insulator to a conductor when subjected to a sufficiently strong voltage, caused by the partial or complete ionization of the insulator; an instance of this; also, the minimum voltage at which this occurs.
senses.example: Humidity lowered the air's resistance, so a breakdown arced across the insulator during the storm.

senses.definition: Breaking of chemical bonds within a compound to produce simpler compounds or elements; an instance of this.
senses.example: Heating the compound causes thermal breakdown, splitting it into simpler molecules.

senses.definition: A piece of music played for such a dance, especially a rapid bluegrass tune featuring a five-string banjo.
senses.example: The fiddlers launched into a fast breakdown, and the whole barn started clapping along.

senses.definition: (dated) A noisy, rapid, shuffling dance engaged in competitively by a number of individuals or pairs in succession, common among African-Americans from the Southern United States; also, a lively event, chiefly in a rural setting, at which such dancing is done; a hoedown, a shindig.
senses.example: At the church picnic, the young men competed in a noisy breakdown while the crowd cheered.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A sudden failure of a machine or vehicle to work, or a sudden emotional collapse when someone can no longer cope with stress.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BRAYK, and the second syllable is lighter. Do not stress DOWN as in the verb 'break down.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals failure, whether mechanical or emotional, and is usually heard as bad news.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'my car had a breakdown' or 'she had a nervous breakdown' in everyday talk. For a mental-health event, 'nervous breakdown' is common but dated, and many people now say 'mental health crisis.' A natural reply to a car breakdown is 'Oh no, are you okay?' or 'Do you need a ride?'

distinctions.note: 'Breakdown' is the noun for the event, while 'break down' is the verb: 'the car broke down.'
'Malfunction' is a more technical term for a device not working correctly, while 'breakdown' is the everyday word for a car or appliance stopping.
'Burnout' describes gradual exhaustion from work, while a 'breakdown' is a sudden collapse, often with more acute distress.

collocations: had a breakdown on the highway

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, my car had a breakdown on the way over.
examples.professional: The data pipeline had a breakdown overnight, so the dashboard is stale this morning.
examples.analytical: Durkheim treats the breakdown of social norms as a central cause of anomie, a state in which individuals lose their sense of direction.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge giving way under too much weight: everything looked fine until it suddenly failed.
nuance.etymology: From break plus down, literally the act of breaking something down or into fragments.
common_mistakes: Using 'breakdown' as the verb: say 'the car broke down,' not 'the car breakdowned.'
Stressing DOWN as in the verb; the noun has stress on BRAYK.
Saying 'have a breakdown' for a planned analysis; 'breakdown' in that sense is a detailed list, and that is a different use.

conversation.text: She had a breakdown after months of stress.
We had a breakdown on the highway and waited two hours.
Can you send me a breakdown of the costs?

senses.definition: The point at which the increasing strain in a material causes it to break.
senses.example: The steel beam reached its breaking point under the load and snapped in two.

senses.definition: The point at which a person or system succumbs to stresses or pressures and descends into crisis.

core.definition: The moment when a person or system can no longer cope with stress or pressure and falls into crisis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on POINT, with BREAK-ing secondary. The vowel in point is the diphthong 'oy', and the -ing is short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a state of crisis or overload.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say reach the breaking point or be at the breaking point, often with the, as in 'I'm at the breaking point'. The British form at breaking point is less natural in American speech. It is common in conversation about work, family or money, and a natural reply is 'I know, let's take a break'.

distinctions.note: A limit is a fixed maximum; a breaking point is the moment when stress finally causes collapse.
Threshold is more technical and neutral, often used in science or policy; breaking point is emotional or dramatic.

collocations: push someone to the breaking point

examples.everyday: After three weeks of double shifts, I was at the breaking point.
examples.professional: The on-call rotation reached its breaking point when two engineers left in the same month.
examples.analytical: Many modern accounts of despair describe the self reaching a breaking point, where its effort to hold itself together collapses.

nuance.analogy: A breaking point is like the last drop that makes a full bucket overflow: nothing changes until suddenly everything does.
nuance.etymology: From break (Old English brecan) plus point (Latin punctum, a prick or dot), originally a physical measure of strain.
common_mistakes: Saying at breaking point without the; American speakers normally say at the breaking point.
Pronouncing point with a short vowel instead of the diphthong 'oy'.

senses.definition: To cook by direct, radiant heat.
To expose to great heat.
To be exposed to great heat.
(archaic) To cause a rowdy disturbance; embroil.
senses.example: Do not broil the congregation with your petty quarrels, brother.
senses.label: archaic

senses.definition: Food prepared by broiling.
senses.example: The restaurant's signature broil was a thick ribeye with garlic butter.

core.definition: To cook food by exposing it directly to intense heat from above, as under the top element of an oven.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the oy diphthong of boy. It rhymes with oil and soil, so avoid saying brawl or bril.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a common everyday cooking term.
nuance.usage_note: In American kitchens, broil refers to cooking under the top heating element of an oven, and many ovens have a broil setting. It differs from grilling, which uses heat from below. Americans say broil the steak for five minutes and usually warn to keep an eye on it because it burns quickly.
word_family: broiler (noun, a cooking element or a chicken)

distinctions.note: Grilling uses heat from below over a grate; broiling uses heat from above, usually in an oven.
Roasting cooks food in an oven with moderate, even heat; broiling is fast and intense.

examples.everyday: Can you broil the chicken for a few minutes so the top gets crispy?
examples.professional: The kitchen manager asked the line cooks to broil the vegetables to order during the dinner rush.
examples.analytical: Broiling depends on radiant heat from above, which is why it browns surfaces rapidly while leaving the interior comparatively moist.

nuance.analogy: Like afternoon sun beating straight down on a sidewalk, browning everything from above.
nuance.etymology: From Old French bruler, meaning to burn.
common_mistakes: Confusing broil with boil; broiling uses dry, intense heat, while boiling uses water.
Pronouncing it as brawl or bril instead of BROYL.

broil.etymology: From Middle English *broylen*, *brulen* (“to broil, cook”), from Anglo-Norman *bruiller*, *broiller* (“to broil, roast”), Old French *brusler*, *bruller* (“to broil, roast, char”), a blend of two Old French verbs:

conversation.text: Broil the salmon for a few minutes to crisp the top.
Broil it for two minutes, but watch it closely so it doesn't burn.
I broiled the cheese until it was bubbly.

related: broiler (noun, a cooking element or a chicken)

senses.definition: A garment worn over the torso that protects against projectiles.

core.definition: A garment of layered strong material, worn under or over clothing, that protects the torso from bullets.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BUL in bulletproof, with a weaker stress on proof, and vest is stressed as the noun. The t in bullet is a quick flap, so it sounds close to 'BUL-ih-proof'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and factual; it refers to safety equipment, so it has no negative shade.
nuance.usage_note: Police officers, security guards, and soldiers wear bulletproof vests, and the term is common in American news. 'Body armor' is a broader, more formal term that also covers plates and other protection. Americans usually write the term as one word, 'bulletproof', without a hyphen.

distinctions.note: Body armor is the broader and more formal category, including vests, plates, and armored clothing.
A flak jacket is an older military term for protection against shrapnel, not mainly bullets.
Bulletproof glass protects a barrier or window, while a vest protects a person's body.

examples.everyday: My brother works night security and always wears a bulletproof vest on shift.
examples.professional: Procurement needs to renew the bulletproof vests for the patrol unit before spring.
examples.analytical: A bulletproof vest protects against some threats, but high-velocity rounds can still penetrate it, so its limits must be stated clearly.

nuance.analogy: A bulletproof vest is to a bullet what a helmet is to a falling brick: it absorbs or deflects the impact but cannot stop everything.
nuance.etymology: Bullet comes from Middle French boulette, a small ball; proof comes from Middle English prove, meaning test or resistance.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words or with a hyphen; the usual American spelling is 'bulletproof vest'.
Saying 'bullet proof' with equal stress on both parts instead of stressing BUL.

senses.definition: A person who breaks in to premises with the intent of committing a crime, usually theft.
senses.example: The burglar made off with a large diamond from the museum.

senses.definition: To commit burglary.
senses.example: Two men burglared the pharmacy overnight and fled before the police arrived.

core.definition: A person who unlawfully enters a building to steal or commit another crime.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'ar' is reduced to a light, r-colored 'er', so it sounds like 'BUR-gler', not 'BUR-glar' with a strong 'ar' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. A burglar is a criminal, and the word is always used with disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'burglar' for the person who breaks into a home or business, while 'burglary' is the crime. In conversation people often say 'a burglar broke into our house' or 'the police caught the burglar.' A burglar is different from a robber, who uses force or threats against a person, so be careful with the words in police and news reports.

distinctions.note: A robber takes property from a person using force or threats. A burglar enters a building without the occupants present and steals.
A thief takes things in any setting. A burglar specifically breaks into a building or vehicle to steal.
An intruder is anyone who enters without permission. A burglar intends to steal or commit a crime inside.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor heard a noise in the garage and called 911 because she thought a burglar was inside.
examples.professional: Our security team says the building's access logs show a burglar entered through the loading dock after hours.
examples.analytical: The philosopher's example of a burglar who is caught only by chance raises questions about intention and moral responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Like a thief who has chosen the house itself as the target.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin burgator, meaning housebreaker.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'glar' with a long 'ar' vowel.
Confusing 'burglar' with 'robber' when describing a crime in which no one was threatened.

burglar.etymology: 16th century, from Medieval Latin *burglātor*, British byform of *burgātor* (“burglar”), derived from *burgō* (“to commit burglary”), from Late Latin *burgus* (“fortified town”), itself probably from **burg* (“fortress”), from Proto-Germanic **burgz*,…

senses.definition: Synonym of by far.
senses.example: Our team won the regional final by a wide margin, scoring twice as many points.

core.definition: By a large amount; by far. Used to say that one thing is much greater, better or more than another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of 'margin'. The final syllable is a weak schwa, and the 'g' is pronounced as a soft 'j' sound, as in 'judge'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is common in news, sports and business reporting, and it describes a clear and large difference.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'by a wide margin' very often for elections, games, sales and test scores: 'She won by a wide margin.' It sounds neutral and factual, so it fits both everyday conversation and professional writing. It is usually paired with a verb such as win, lead or beat.

distinctions.note: 'By far' is more general and can describe any comparison, while 'by a wide margin' focuses on the size of a difference in a measured result, such as a vote or score.
'By a long shot' is casual and often negative, while 'by a wide margin' is factual and suitable for reports and analysis.

collocations: beat expectations by a wide margin

examples.everyday: Our team won the game by a wide margin, so everyone was happy.
examples.professional: The new campaign outperformed last quarter by a wide margin, mostly in mobile conversions.
examples.analytical: The model's accuracy exceeds the baseline by a wide margin across all subgroups tested.

nuance.analogy: Like a finish line crossed with daylight between the first runner and the rest of the field.
nuance.etymology: 'Margin' comes from Latin margo, meaning 'edge' or 'border'.
common_mistakes: Using 'with' instead of 'by', as in 'won with a wide margin', which sounds wrong to Americans.
Confusing 'margin' with 'marginal' and using the adjective where the noun is needed.

senses.definition: A fast temporary storage where recently or frequently used information is stored to avoid having to reload it from a slower storage medium.
senses.example: The browser stores frequently visited pages in a cache so they load faster next time.

senses.definition: A store, protected and often hidden in some way, of things that may be required in the future, such that they can be retrieved rapidly.
senses.example: Members of the 29-man Discovery team laid down caches to allow the polar team to travel light, hopping from cache to cache on their return journey.

senses.definition: Such a store of physical supplies, placed by humans or other animals for practical reasons.
senses.example: Members of the 29-man Discovery team laid down caches to allow the polar team to travel light, hopping from cache to cache on their return journey.

senses.definition: A container containing treasure in a global treasure-hunt game.
senses.example: The geocaching kids found a cache hidden beneath a bench in the park.

senses.definition: To store data in a cache.
senses.example: Make sure the application caches the query results so the dashboard loads quickly.

senses.definition: To place in a cache.
senses.example: Before the hike, she cached a spare water bottle under a rock near the trail.

senses.definition: To participate in geocaching.
senses.example: On weekends, my son and I cache around the city and log our finds online.

senses.definition: To hide or seek a geocache.
senses.example: We spent an hour in the rain trying to cache the box that a stranger had hidden.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) to store up, stockpile.
senses.example: Squirrels cache nuts in the autumn to survive the long winter.

core.definition: A hidden or protected store of things, or in computing, a fast temporary storage area holding data that is often used.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it exactly like 'cash', with the 'sh' sound at the end. Americans do not say the final t, and the vowel is the short 'a' of 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday use it can sound adventurous, as in a treasure cache, while in computing it is purely technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say cache for a stash of things, such as a cache of old letters, or for a supply of food hidden for emergencies. In tech, people say the browser cache or the cache is full, usually in the context of slow loading or clearing data. Because cache sounds like cash, avoid writing one for the other.

distinctions.note: A stash is an informal hidden collection of something, often for personal use, while a cache can be formal, technical, or secret and is used for retrieval.
A reserve is a supply kept for a future need and is usually visible or official, while a cache is typically hidden or kept as a fast-access store.

examples.everyday: Our hotel app is slow, so I'm going to clear the cache on my phone.
examples.professional: We store the user profiles in a cache so the API doesn't query the database for every request.
examples.analytical: A cache relies on the assumption of locality, so frequently accessed data is kept close to the processor.

nuance.analogy: A cache is like a desk drawer for the papers you use every day, rather than walking to the archive each time.
nuance.etymology: From French cache, a hiding place, from cacher meaning to hide.
common_mistakes: Confusing cache with cash, which sounds similar but means money.
Using cache as a verb with 'to' in a computing sense; in tech, people usually say store data in the cache or cache the results.

cache.etymology: From French *cache* (as used by French Canadian trappers to mean “hiding place for stores”), from the verb *cacher* (“to hide”).

senses.definition: An event resulting in great loss.
The distress that results from some disaster.
senses.example: The flood brought calamity to the valley, leaving families in grief and poverty.

core.definition: A sudden event causing great damage, loss, or suffering, such as a flood, fire, or famine.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LAM. The -ity ending is unstressed and reduces to a short ih sound followed by tee.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative and serious. Used for large-scale misfortune, though it can be used humorously for small mishaps.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use calamity for large-scale disasters, often in news or serious conversation, as in a natural calamity. For personal troubles, people usually say disaster or nightmare. Calling a small mishap a calamity sounds humorous or dramatic, which works well among friends.

distinctions.note: Disaster is the everyday word; calamity is more formal and often suggests overwhelming, widespread misfortune.
Catastrophe is strongest and often sudden; calamity can also describe prolonged suffering such as famine or war.

examples.everyday: Forgetting the cake at home was a total calamity, but nobody got hurt.
examples.professional: The database outage was a calamity for the reporting team, so we are writing a postmortem.
examples.analytical: Some theologians read the plague not simply as a natural calamity but as a call to moral reflection.

nuance.analogy: Like a flood that carries away the whole valley, not just one building.
nuance.etymology: From Latin calamitas, damage or loss, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as calamety or calimity.
Using calamity for trivial events without a humorous intent.

calamity.etymology: From Middle French *calamité*, from Latin *calamitās* (“loss, damage; disaster”).

senses.definition: The person who makes a telephone call.
senses.example: ―I’ve got someone on the line.―Who’s the caller?

senses.definition: A visitor.
senses.example: a gentleman caller

senses.definition: The person who stands at the front of the hall and announces the numbers.
senses.example: The caller shouted out B-7, and my grandmother dabbed her card with a happy sigh.

senses.definition: A function that calls another (the callee).
senses.example: If the called function throws an exception, the caller should be prepared to handle the error.

senses.definition: (rare) A whistle or similar item used to call foxes.
senses.example: Before dawn, the hunter blew his fox caller, hoping to lure a curious animal into range.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: The person who directs dancers in certain dances, such as American line dances and square dances.
senses.example: The caller kept the square dancers on pace, calling each figure over the fiddle music.

core.definition: The person who makes a telephone call, or in a call center, the customer who phones in.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, KAW. The second syllable is an unstressed American r-colored 'er', so do not pronounce it as a full 'ah' or 'uh' followed by a separate l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, descriptive word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the caller' when describing the person who phoned, such as 'The caller didn't leave a name.' In call centers, staff often say 'caller' for customers. Outside telephone contexts, 'caller' can mean a visitor, but this sense is old-fashioned, so people say 'visitor' instead. A natural reply to 'Who was the caller?' is 'I don't know, it was a blocked number.'

distinctions.note: Caller is the person who places the call, while called party is the technical term for the person who receives it.
Caller refers to someone on the phone or formally announcing a visit, while visitor is the everyday word for someone who comes to your home or office in person.

examples.everyday: The caller didn't leave a name, so I'm not picking up if the number is unknown.
examples.professional: Our support script asks the caller for an account number before we transfer the call.
examples.analytical: The caller and the called party occupy asymmetric positions in the communicative exchange, since one initiates and the other responds.

nuance.analogy: Like the person who rings the doorbell first: they start the interaction, and you respond to it.
nuance.etymology: From 'call' (Old English 'ceallian') with the agent suffix '-er', meaning one who calls.
common_mistakes: Using 'caller' for the person who receives a call, when that person is the called party or recipient.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'kaw-LAR' with heavy stress on the second syllable.

conversation.text: The caller didn't leave a name, just a number.
The radio host took a question from a caller in Ohio.
The caller hung up before I could answer.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or resembling a callithump; riotous.
senses.example: callithumpian band

core.definition: Noisy, riotous and disorderly, like a rowdy mock parade or a boisterous street celebration.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on THUM, the third syllable. The 'th' is the voiceless sound as in 'think', and the final syllables are reduced and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Negative or humorous. It describes noisy disorder, often with a comic tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use this word in everyday talk. It is a rare, old-fashioned term that appears in historical writing and humorous commentary about rowdy celebrations. Using it in conversation would sound playful or deliberately literary, so it works best in writing or storytelling.

distinctions.note: Raucous is a common word for loud and harsh noise, while callithumpian is rare and specifically suggests a mock parade or rowdy procession.
Riotous suggests wild or out-of-control behavior, while callithumpian suggests a noisy, comic street celebration.

examples.professional: The planning meeting turned callithumpian once the budget vote came up, and nobody could be heard.
examples.analytical: The protest, callithumpian in its noise and spectacle, lacked any coherent demand that could be debated.

nuance.analogy: Like a parade of pots, pans and tin whistles marching down a street with no clear route.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'callithump', a 19th-century American term for a noisy mock parade; the exact origin of that element is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it with 'callithumpean' or 'callithumpeon', which are not standard forms.
Using it as a general synonym for loud, when it implies a specific rowdy parade.

can-i-get-you-started-with-anything-to-d.phonetic: /kæn aɪ ˌɡɛt ju ˌstɑɹtɪd wɪð ˌɛniˌθɪŋ tu ˈdɹɪŋk/

senses.definition: The server's usual first question: what you'd like to drink while you look at the menu.

core.definition: A server's opening question asking what you want to drink before you order food, usually while you look at the menu.

pronunciation.respelling: kan eye get yoo STAR-tid with en-ee-thing too DRINK
pronunciation.tip: In fast speech 'can' reduces to 'kun' and the phrase links into 'kun-eye-GET-yoo-STAR-tid'. Stress falls on STAR and DRINK, the 'th' in 'anything' is unvoiced, and the t in 'started' is a soft flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly; it is standard restaurant politeness and carries no pressure.
nuance.usage_note: Servers in American restaurants ask this almost immediately after seating you, so expect it. A natural reply is 'Just water, please' or 'I'll have a Coke.' If you are not ready, say 'Give us a minute' or 'Can we get a few minutes?' Do not answer with a full sentence about the menu.

distinctions.note: Taking the order comes after the drinks question and asks for food; the drinks question is the first step.
This is a shorter, more casual version that covers both food and drinks at once.

examples.everyday: Hi there, can I get you started with anything to drink? Just a sparkling water for me, thanks.
examples.professional: Before the client dinner, the host asked, can I get you started with anything to drink, and offered the wine list.
examples.analytical: The server's question performs a small social ritual: it turns the guest's first decision into a low-stakes choice that signals the meal has begun.

nuance.analogy: It is like the first handshake that opens a meeting: small, expected, and it sets the pace.
nuance.etymology: 'Get' here means to bring or supply; 'start' comes from Old English styrtan, to jump or move suddenly.
common_mistakes: Answering 'Yes' or 'No' instead of naming a drink, which sounds awkward.
Saying 'Can I get you start' without the -ed ending, which drops the past participle.

conversation.text: Hi, I'm Josh. Can I get you started with anything to drink?

senses.definition: A beating with a cane, especially as a form of punishment.

core.definition: A beating with a cane, used as a form of physical punishment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAY, and the second syllable is a short i. The ng at the end is one sound, so do not add a separate g.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes violent physical punishment and is often used in discussions of human rights or law.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use caning in everyday talk because corporal punishment with a cane is uncommon in the United States. The word comes up mainly in news about other countries, in legal or human rights discussions, or in history about schools. Americans would more often say beating or spanking for ordinary physical discipline.

distinctions.note: Spanking is a slap, usually on the buttocks, with the hand, while caning uses a rod and is far more severe.
Flogging uses a whip or lash, while caning uses a rigid cane, so the two are different instruments and degrees of punishment.

examples.everyday: I read about a man being sentenced to caning in Singapore, and it really shocked me.
examples.professional: Our compliance training covers how local laws on caning differ, since the company has offices in several Southeast Asian countries.
examples.analytical: The debate over caning often turns on whether the state can justify physical punishment as a deterrent when it does not reform the offender.

nuance.analogy: Caning is like a punishment that leaves a visible mark on the body, while a warning leaves a mark only on the mind.
nuance.etymology: From cane, from Old French canne, from Latin canna, from Greek kanna.
common_mistakes: Confusing caning with canning, which means preserving food in jars or cans.
Using caning to mean the act of walking with a cane, which is not its meaning.

senses.definition: Any salt or ester of carbonic acid.
To charge (often a beverage) with carbon dioxide.
senses.example: The bottling plant carbonates the sparkling water before it goes into the cans.

core.definition: A chemical salt that contains carbon and oxygen, such as calcium carbonate in limestone and chalk.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHR. The middle vowel is reduced, and the word ends with a clear 'nayt' sound. The noun and verb are pronounced the same.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'carbonate' in chemistry, geology, and medicine. In everyday speech they might say 'baking soda' or 'chalk' instead. The verb form 'to carbonate' is used for drinks, so people often hear it in beverage contexts.

distinctions.note: Bicarbonate, as in baking soda, contains one hydrogen atom, so it is a different ion with a different pH.
Carbonated describes a drink with carbon dioxide dissolved in it, while carbonate is the chemical salt.
Carbonic is the adjective linked to carbonic acid, the parent acid of carbonate salts.

examples.everyday: Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, and washing soda is sodium carbonate, so they're not the same.
examples.professional: The lab found high levels of carbonate in the water sample, which changed the pH reading.
examples.analytical: Carbonate minerals record the chemistry of ancient oceans, so geologists use them to reconstruct past climates.

nuance.analogy: A carbonate is like a shell in the ocean: it is made from carbon and oxygen, and it preserves a record of its environment.
nuance.etymology: From French carbonate, from carbone (carbon) plus the chemical suffix -ate.
common_mistakes: Confusing carbonate with bicarbonate, which is a different chemical.
Saying 'car-BON-ate' with stress on the second syllable; the stress is on the first.

senses.definition: A case for holding cards, as credit cards, bankcards, or business cards.
An authorized user of a card that is used for financial transactions, etc.
senses.example: As a cardholder, she gets two percent back on every grocery purchase.

core.definition: A small case for holding cards, or a person who has been issued a card such as a credit card or library card.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the first syllable, CARD, with a weaker secondary stress on hold. The final -er is a reduced r-colored vowel. Don't put the stress on the end of the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it is used in banking, membership and library contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cardholder for both the physical case and the person authorized to use a card. You will hear it at banks ('Are you the cardholder?') or in talk about rewards programs. In formal writing it is one word, not card holder.

distinctions.note: An account holder owns the bank or service account, while a cardholder is the person authorized to use a card issued on that account.

examples.everyday: I'm a cardholder at the public library, so I can borrow up to twenty books at a time.
examples.professional: Please verify the cardholder's name and billing address before we process the refund.
examples.analytical: The law treats the cardholder and the account holder differently, which matters when a company must cover unauthorized charges.

nuance.analogy: A cardholder is like a key holder: authorized to use the card, even if someone else owns the account.
nuance.etymology: From card, from Latin charta, plus holder, one who holds.
common_mistakes: Confusing cardholder with account holder; the cardholder uses the card, while the account holder owns the account.
Stressing the final syllable; the stress belongs on CARD.

senses.definition: In terms of, or by means of, catalysis.
senses.example: The new enzyme works catalytically, speeding up the reaction without being consumed by it.

core.definition: In a way that causes or speeds up a chemical reaction, or acts as a catalyst does.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'lit', and the ending -ically is pronounced 'ik-lee', with no extra vowel. Do not add a schwa before the final 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical adverb used in science writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in chemistry, biology, and engineering writing, not in speech. In casual talk, they say 'speed up' or 'make it happen faster'. Common verbs with it include 'act', 'promote', and 'accelerate'.

distinctions.note: Chemically is broader; catalytically means specifically through the action of a catalyst.
Enzymatically means by enzymes, which are biological catalysts, while catalytically is the general term.
Thermally means by heat, while catalytically means by a substance that speeds a reaction without being used up.

examples.everyday: Their stories acted catalytically, and suddenly everyone at the table was talking at once.
examples.professional: The new process reacts catalytically at lower temperatures, which cuts our energy costs significantly.
examples.analytical: Enzymes act catalytically by lowering the activation energy of biochemical reactions without being consumed by them.

nuance.analogy: Like a coach who speeds up a team's play without touching the ball herself.
nuance.etymology: Formed from catalytic, from Greek katalysis, 'dissolution'.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'catalyticly', dropping the -al- before -ly.
Using the noun 'catalyst' where the adverb is needed.
Dropping the final -ally sound and saying 'catalytik'.

senses.definition: To assign a category; to divide into classes.
senses.example: First, categorize incoming messages according to the needed actions.

core.definition: To put things into groups or classes based on shared qualities or defined criteria.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable (KAT). The middle syllable -or- is reduced to a weak 'guh', and the ending -ize is pronounced /aɪz/, rhyming with 'rise', not 'ih-zee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound negative when people are sorted into stereotypes, as in 'Don't categorize people like that.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it at work, in school, and in data and research settings: 'Can you categorize these tickets by priority?' In casual talk people more often say 'sort' or 'group' or 'put into groups'. American spelling uses -ize, while British English uses -ise.

distinctions.note: Sort is casual and everyday; categorize implies assigning items according to a deliberate, named system of groups.
Classify is more formal and scientific, usually tied to an established taxonomy; categorize is common in business and everyday work.
Group is loose and informal; categorize implies explicit criteria and labeled categories.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to categorize all my old photos into folders by year.
examples.professional: Can you categorize these support tickets by severity before the standup?
examples.analytical: To categorize an experience is already to interpret it, which is why no classification is entirely neutral.

nuance.analogy: Like sorting laundry into whites, darks, and delicates.
nuance.etymology: From category, ultimately from Greek katēgoria, 'predication, assertion,' from katēgorein, 'to accuse, assert.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'categorize in groups' instead of 'categorize into groups' or 'categorize as'.
Adding an extra syllable and saying 'CAT-ih-gor-ize' instead of 'KAT-uh-guh-rize'.

senses.definition: Relating to the office of a bishop or an archbishop.
senses.example: The cathedral clergy met with the bishop on Monday to plan the diocesan budget.

senses.definition: The principal church serving as the office (and some as place of residence) of an archdiocese's/a diocese's archbishop/bishop which is symbolized by an episcopal throne known as the cathedra.
senses.example: The bishop presided over the ceremony from his seat in the cathedral.

senses.definition: A large or important church building.
senses.example: We toured the cathedral in Chartres, admiring its stained glass windows.

senses.definition: A large, impressive, lofty, and/or important building or place of some other kind.
senses.example: a cathedral of commerce

senses.definition: A large buttressed structure built by certain termites.
senses.example: Termites built a cathedral of mud rising six feet above the savanna.

core.definition: The principal church of a bishop's diocese, where the bishop's official seat, the cathedra, is located.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THEE, the middle syllable. The th is voiceless, as in 'think', and the final syllable is light, so say 'drul', not 'dral'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, and often admiring when applied to large or beautiful buildings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cathedral for a bishop's main church, and also for any very large or impressive building, as in 'a cathedral of pines'. A cathedral ceiling is the American term for a high, peaked ceiling. Most places of worship are called churches; cathedral is reserved for major or famous ones.

distinctions.note: Church is the general word for any Christian place of worship, while cathedral names the main church of a bishop's diocese or a very large building.
A basilica is an honorary title given to a church of special importance, not necessarily a bishop's seat.
A chapel is a small church or worship room, usually much smaller than a cathedral.

examples.everyday: We took the kids downtown to see the cathedral, and the stained glass was amazing.
examples.professional: The cathedral will host the diocesan staff meeting in the parish hall next Tuesday.
examples.analytical: The cathedra in a cathedral signifies the bishop's teaching authority, which is why the church is named for the seat.

nuance.analogy: Like a regional headquarters: the main building where the leader of the whole region works.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin cathedralis, from Greek kathedra, 'seat', from kata, 'down', and hedra, 'seat'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in KATH-uh-drul.
Calling every church a cathedral; Americans reserve the word for a bishop's seat or a very large building.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek kathedra, 'seat', appears in Matthew 23:2, where the scribes and Pharisees are said to sit on Moses' seat. The image of a seat of teaching authority later shaped the church's use of cathedra and cathedral.

cathedral.etymology: From Middle English *cathedral*, *chathedral*, *cathiderall*, from Old French, from Latin *cathedrālis*, from *cathedra* + *ālis*, from Ancient Greek *καθέδρα* (“chair of a teacher, throne”).

senses.definition: The act of causing.
senses.example: Researchers warned that a strong correlation does not prove causation between the two variables.

senses.definition: The act or agency by which an effect is produced.
Cause and effect.

core.definition: The process by which one thing produces an effect, or the relationship of cause and effect between events.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZAY, and the -tion ending is pronounced shun, with the t becoming sh. Don't add an extra syllable like kaw-ZAY-shawn.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a formal term used precisely in science, statistics and philosophy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use causation in science, statistics, law and academic writing, most famously in the phrase correlation does not imply causation. In everyday talk people usually say cause or what caused it. A natural phrase at work is 'We need to establish causation before we make that claim.'

distinctions.note: Cause is the everyday word for the thing that makes something happen; causation is the more formal noun for the process or relationship.
Correlation means two things vary together; causation means one actually produces the other, so the two are not the same.

examples.everyday: My dad said the rain didn't cause our delay; there was no real causation, just bad luck with the traffic.
examples.professional: The report claims the new onboarding flow reduced churn, but we can't claim causation from a simple before-and-after comparison.
examples.analytical: Hume challenged our confidence in causation by arguing that we infer it from repeated experience rather than observing a necessary connection.

nuance.analogy: Like tracing a wet floor back to the crack in the pipe, not just noticing the puddle.
nuance.etymology: From Latin causatio, from causari, to give as a reason, from causa, cause.
common_mistakes: Using causation as the everyday word for cause; say the cause of the problem instead.
Using causation when you mean correlation; they describe different relationships.

senses.definition: Lacking the proper care or concern for something important, reckless, rash, high-handed.
senses.example: It was cavalier of the manager to ignore the safety warnings before launching the product.

senses.definition: High-spirited.
senses.example: The cavalier young colt bucked and galloped across the pasture all morning.

senses.definition: Supercilious.
senses.example: Her cavalier reply made it clear she thought the question was beneath her.

senses.definition: (historical) Of or pertaining to the party of King Charles I of England (1600–1649).
senses.example: Cavalier families in the 1640s often lost their estates after the parliamentary victory.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Someone with an uncircumcised penis.
A defensive work rising from a bastion, etc. and overlooking the surrounding area.
senses.example: The engineers built a cavalier on the bastion to watch the valley below the fortress.

senses.definition: (historical) A military man serving on horse, early modern cavalry officers who had abandoned the heavy armor of medieval knights.
senses.example: The cavalier galloped ahead with his sabre drawn, leading the charge against the infantry line.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A gallant: a sprightly young dashing military man.
senses.example: In the old novel, the young cavalier bowed low and swept the heroine off her feet.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A gentleman of the class of such officers.
senses.example: As a cavalier of the old gentry, he was expected to hunt, ride, and serve the crown.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (dated) Of a man: to act in a gallant and dashing manner toward (women).
senses.example: He cavaliered the local belles all summer, dancing with each one and sending flowers.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Showing careless disregard for something important, such as safety, rules, or other people's feelings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The last syllable is 'leer', not the French 'lee-AY' or 'cah-vah-LYAY'. In American speech the final r is clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a dismissive, careless attitude that can seem arrogant or irresponsible.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cavalier to criticize someone who is too casual about risks, deadlines, rules, or feelings. It is a formal, somewhat literary word, so it is more common in writing and serious discussion than in casual talk. Saying someone is 'cavalier' is a fairly strong criticism.

distinctions.note: Casual describes a relaxed manner; cavalier implies carelessness about consequences that matter.
Arrogant describes an attitude of superiority; cavalier focuses on careless dismissal of what should be taken seriously.

examples.everyday: He was pretty cavalier about the deadline, like it didn't really matter.
examples.professional: Pushing untested code to production is a cavalier approach to risk that our on-call team will pay for.
examples.analytical: Nietzsche's cavalier dismissal of inherited moral categories invites charges that he ignored their historical roots.

nuance.analogy: A cavalier attitude is like a driver who ignores the stop sign because he assumes nothing will happen.
nuance.etymology: From French cavalier 'horseman', from Italian cavaliere, from Late Latin caballarius, from caballus 'horse'.
common_mistakes: Using cavalier to mean friendly or kind; the meaning is usually careless or dismissive.
Pronouncing it with a French stress on the last syllable.

senses.definition: The number and type of cells in a given tissue.

core.definition: The number and types of cells present in a tissue, a term used mainly in pathology and cell biology.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'LAIR', the third-from-last syllable. Reduce the final '-ity' to 'ih-tee', not 'eye-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical, with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Pathologists use cellularity to describe how many cells fill a tissue sample, often in reports as 'high cellularity' or 'low cellularity'. Everyday Americans rarely use the word and would say 'how many cells' instead. Do not confuse it with cellulite, which is a different word about skin.

distinctions.note: Cellularity is a pathology term about cells in tissue, while cellulite is dimpled fat under the skin.
Cellular is the adjective for anything relating to cells, while cellularity is the noun for their number and kinds.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the sample had low cellularity, so they may need to take another biopsy.
examples.professional: The pathology report notes high cellularity in the lymph node, which supports the preliminary diagnosis.
examples.analytical: Assessing cellularity alone can mislead, since a dense tissue may contain mostly inflammatory cells rather than the tumor itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a headcount at a stadium, cellularity tells you how many people are in the seats, though not who they are.
nuance.etymology: From cell, from Latin cella, 'small room', with the noun suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Confusing cellularity with cellulite, which is a completely different word.
Stressing the last syllable as 'ih-TEE' instead of putting the main stress on 'LAIR'.

senses.definition: Intellectual rather than emotional or physical.
Of or relating to the brain, cerebrum, or cerebral cortex.
senses.example: The neurologist explained how damage to the cerebral cortex affected his patient's memory.

core.definition: Relying on reason and intellect rather than emotion or instinct.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on REE, and the first syllable is a weak 'suh', not 'SEE'. The ending is one light syllable, 'bruhl', not 'bray-ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can praise a thoughtful film or book, but it can also suggest someone is cold or detached.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cerebral for ideas, books, films, or people who approach life through logic and analysis. It can be a compliment or a mild criticism that someone is too detached. In medicine, it means relating to the brain, as in cerebral palsy. Calling an ordinary person cerebral to mean smart sounds unusual; thoughtful or smart is more natural.

distinctions.note: Intellectual refers to the mind and ideas broadly, while cerebral stresses detached reasoning over feeling.
Rational describes sound reasoning itself, while cerebral describes a style or approach that prefers thinking to feeling.

examples.everyday: That movie is too cerebral for me; I wanted something with more action and a few laughs.
examples.professional: Her cerebral style means she wants the data before making any decision, which keeps us from rushing.
