Mispronouncing it as 'fah-SEEL' or confusing it with fragile.

senses.definition: A phenomenon that becomes popular for a very short time.

core.definition: A style, interest or activity that becomes very popular for a short time, often with great enthusiasm, and then quickly fades.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short, flat 'a' like in 'cat' and end with a clear voiced 'd.' Don't devoice the final sound to 't' ('fat'), which changes the meaning.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. Calling something a fad suggests it is shallow or will not last.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'it's just a fad' to dismiss a trend, such as a diet, an app or a clothing style. 'Fad diet' is a common term for a weight-loss plan that is popular for a while. The word can sound dismissive if used about someone's serious interests or beliefs.

distinctions.note: A trend can last longer and shows a direction of change; a fad is more intense and shorter-lived.
A craze is a very intense enthusiasm, often more emotional; a fad is more casual and quickly forgotten.
Fashion is broader and can last for years; a fad is brief and often unserious.

examples.everyday: Remember when everyone wore those rubber wristbands? That was a fad, and then nobody cared.
examples.professional: Let's not chase the latest AI tool as a fad; we need a proper evaluation before we commit budget to it.
examples.analytical: Critics often treat religious revivals as fads, but this dismisses the social causes that give them lasting force.

nuance.analogy: A fad is like a sparkler: it burns bright and fast, then it's gone.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'fade' with a long vowel.
Calling a long-lasting tradition a fad, which can sound dismissive to Americans.

core.definition: In Christianity, the question of how trust in God and good deeds relate in salvation, especially in Paul and James.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress falls on 'works,' with secondary stress on 'faith.' 'And' is reduced to 'und' or 'n,' and the 'th' in 'faith' must be voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the debate itself can be sensitive among Christians, especially across denominations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in church, Bible study, and theology classes, and it is often connected with Romans and James. It can sound technical outside religious talk. Say 'the relationship between faith and works' and avoid casual use.

distinctions.note: Faith alone (sola fide) is the Protestant claim that faith alone justifies, while 'faith and works' is the broader question of how they relate.
Works righteousness is the belief that people earn salvation by deeds, which Protestants criticize.
Grace and effort is a more general phrase about gifts and personal work, not the specific Pauline-Jamesian debate.

collocations: the relationship between faith and works

examples.everyday: In our Bible study we've been arguing about faith and works all month.
examples.professional: This lecture covers how Reformation and Catholic traditions differ on faith and works.
examples.analytical: Paul and James are not necessarily in conflict: Paul addresses how one is justified, while James addresses what living faith looks like.

nuance.analogy: Faith and works are like a root and its fruit: the root saves the tree, but the fruit shows that it is alive.
common_mistakes: Saying 'faith and work' without the plural; the theological phrase uses 'works.'
Dropping the 'th' in 'faith' or pronouncing it as 'faiss.'
Assuming Paul and James say exactly the same thing in the same sense.
nuance.biblical_note: Romans 3:28 says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. James 2:14-26 argues that faith without works is dead, using Abraham and Rahab as examples. Ephesians 2:8-10 says believers are saved by grace through faith, and are created for good works.

traditions.view: Faith and works are not opposed but are two aspects of one life in Christ, in which God's grace and human cooperation work together toward theosis.
Justification begins as God's gift, but faith must be active in charity. Good works done in grace merit growth in grace and eternal life, as taught at Trent.

Lutheran and Reformed churches teach justification by faith alone, with works as its necessary fruit, not its cause. Anglicans, Methodists and others also stress that living faith produces holy living.

senses.definition: Loyal; adhering firmly to person or cause.
senses.example: My dog is very faithful: he doesn't like to be petted by anybody else.

senses.definition: Having faith.
senses.example: The faithful congregation prayed together every Sunday morning for the missionaries overseas.

senses.definition: Reliable; worthy of trust.
senses.example: My servant is very faithful.

senses.definition: Consistent with reality.
senses.example: I would consider that a very faithful reproduction.

senses.definition: Engaging in sexual relations only with one's spouse or long-term sexual partner.
senses.example: They had been faithful to each other all of their married life.

senses.definition: Injective in specific contexts, e.g. of representations in representation or functors in category theory.
senses.example: The proof relied on the forgetful functor being faithful, so distinct morphisms stayed distinct.

senses.definition: Of a module, whose annihilator is zero.
senses.example: Every nonzero vector space over a field is faithful, so the proof applies directly.

senses.definition: The practicing members of a religion or followers of a cause.
senses.example: The faithful pray five times a day.

senses.definition: Someone or something that is faithful or reliable.
senses.example: As a loyal reader, I count myself among the faithful who buy every new volume.

core.definition: Loyal and steady in support of a person, cause or promise; reliable and true to what you have committed to.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAITH. The final syllable uses a syllabic l with no separate vowel, so it sounds like 'fayth-f'l'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises reliability and loyalty, though in romance it can be sensitive.
nuance.usage_note: Common in relationships, work and religion to praise someone reliable. 'Faithful' also has a romantic sense, so 'faithful to your partner' can be a sensitive topic. As a noun, 'the faithful' means devoted members of a group, often religious, and can sound formal or ironic when used about fans.

distinctions.note: Loyal emphasizes support toward a person or group; faithful often implies keeping a promise or commitment over time.
Reliable describes someone who does what is expected; faithful adds emotional commitment and steadiness.

examples.everyday: My dog is the most faithful friend I've ever had; he waits by the door every night.
examples.professional: The new dashboard stays faithful to the original data source, so the numbers match the warehouse exactly.
examples.analytical: A translation is faithful when it preserves the meaning of the source, though fidelity to the letter can sometimes betray the spirit.

nuance.analogy: A compass that points north every time you check it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English feithful, from faith, ultimately from Latin fides.
common_mistakes: Saying 'faithful of' instead of 'faithful to'.
Pronouncing the last syllable as a full 'full' rather than the weak 'ful'.
nuance.biblical_note: The key words are Hebrew ne'eman (trustworthy, firm) and Greek pistos (faithful, trustworthy). Scripture uses the word of God and of people who keep their trust. 1 Corinthians 4:2 says stewards must be found faithful, Revelation 2:10 urges believers to be faithful unto death, and Psalm 31:23 says the Lord preserves the faithful.

senses.definition: Of a current that is alternating, as opposed to galvanic.
Of or pertaining to electricity, especially to electrical induction.

core.definition: Relating to an alternating electric current, especially one produced by induction and used in electrotherapy.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'RAD,' with a short a as in 'cat.' Keep the r clear and do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'faradic' outside physics, electrical engineering or medicine, especially in discussions of older electrotherapy equipment. In modern English, people usually say 'alternating current' or 'AC' for the general concept. The term is still used in historical or clinical writing about electrical stimulation.

distinctions.note: 'Galvanic' refers to direct current, which flows in one direction, while 'faradic' refers to alternating current.
'Alternating current' is the standard modern term; 'faradic' is a specialized, mostly historical or clinical adjective.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's old physical therapy machine used a faradic current, but that technology is mostly gone now.
examples.professional: The faradic stimulator is outdated, so we replaced it with a modern electrotherapy unit with adjustable waveform settings.
examples.analytical: The historical debate between galvanic and faradic methods reveals how early physiologists understood the relation between electricity and nerve response.

nuance.analogy: Think of faradic current as electricity that changes direction again and again, like a rope pulled back and forth rather than pulled steadily in one direction.
nuance.etymology: Named after the physicist Michael Faraday (1791–1867), whose work on electromagnetic induction made this kind of current possible.
common_mistakes: Using 'faradic' to mean any electricity; it specifically refers to alternating current produced by induction.
Mispronouncing the stress as 'FAR-a-dik'; the main stress falls on the second syllable.

faradic.etymology: From *Faraday* + *ic*, for Michael Faraday, English chemist and physicist.

senses.definition: A mass of fat stored in the rump of a beast as an adaptation to heat and harsh environmental conditions or selection by man.
senses.example: The Karakul sheep has a large fat tail that stores energy during the desert winter.

senses.definition: The relatively high probability of a relatively extreme outcome.
A tail of a probability distribution with significantly higher kurtosis than a normal distribution (which has kurtosis = 0).
A tail of a probability distribution with infinite variance.

core.definition: In statistics, the long, slowly decaying tail of a probability distribution, which makes extreme outcomes far more likely than a normal distribution predicts.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on tail, with fat getting secondary stress. Keep the short a in fat and the long a in tail, as in tale.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, technical. In finance and risk talk it can carry a warning about rare but severe events.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and statisticians in the United States use fat tail as standard technical vocabulary, often in risk modeling and finance. People say fat-tailed distribution or heavy-tailed when describing the property. In casual conversation, the phrase is rare and needs context.

distinctions.note: Heavy tail is the broader mathematical term, often linked to power laws, while fat tail is common in applied statistics and finance.
An outlier is a single unusual data point, while a fat tail is a property of the whole distribution that makes extremes more likely.
A normal distribution is thin-tailed, so its extremes are rare, while a fat tail allows surprising events to be much more common.

examples.everyday: My brother-in-law keeps saying the stock market has fat tails, which I think means crashes happen more often than people expect.
examples.professional: We should use a Student-t model because our loss data shows fat tails that the normal assumption misses.
examples.analytical: A distribution with fat tails assigns non-negligible probability to extreme events that a Gaussian model would dismiss as impossible.

nuance.analogy: A normal distribution is a bell with short, steep shoulders, while a fat tail is a bell whose edges trail far out, so surprises are not rare.
nuance.etymology: From fat, meaning large or thick, plus tail; the statistical sense is a modern extension of the everyday words.
common_mistakes: Confusing the statistical fat tail with an animal's fat tail, which is a literal store of fat.
Writing fat-tails as a plural noun when the standard phrase is fat tails, or fat-tailed as an adjective.

senses.definition: With smug stupidity or vacuous silliness; idiotically.
senses.example: He fatuously assured the nervous passengers that the flight would be the smoothest ever.

core.definition: In a foolishly self-satisfied way, showing silly complacency or a lack of good sense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The tu in fatuous sounds like 'chew', not 'too', and the final -ly is a light lee.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies contempt or mockery toward someone's smug foolishness.
nuance.usage_note: Fatuously appears mostly in writing, criticism, or formal speech, and it is rarely used in casual American talk. Americans would more often say foolishly, stupidly, or smugly. Using it in conversation may sound pretentious or sarcastic.

distinctions.note: Foolishly is neutral and common, while fatuously adds the idea of smug, self-satisfied silliness.
Inanely means pointlessly silly, while fatuously adds a sense of complacency and self-regard.

examples.everyday: He kept grinning fatuously at his own joke, even after nobody laughed.
examples.professional: The vendor fatuously promised zero downtime without any testing, and we all knew better.
examples.analytical: The essay fatuously assumes that technological progress will automatically cure social inequality.

nuance.analogy: Like a person who keeps clapping at a magic trick that has already been exposed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fatuus, foolish, through the English adjective fatuous and the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as too, as in fa-TOO-us, when the tu sounds like chew.
Confusing fatuous with fatal or fatalistic, which have different meanings.

senses.definition: Highly fertile; able to produce offspring.
Leading to new ideas or innovation.
senses.example: The brainstorming session was fecund, producing dozens of ideas for the new product.

core.definition: Highly fertile, able to produce many offspring or new growth; also productive of new ideas.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced 'und', not 'and' and not a separate syllable. The vowel is short, as in 'fed'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most uses, suggesting abundance and creativity, though it can be neutral in biology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fecund in literary criticism, poetry, nature writing, and formal speech about ideas or creativity. It is not common in casual talk. Everyday speakers would say fertile, productive, or full of ideas.

distinctions.note: Fertile is the everyday word for able to have children or grow plants; fecund is more literary and emphasizes abundance.
Prolific describes high output of work or creations; fecund can also describe biological fertility.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's garden was so fecund that tomatoes spilled over the fence every August.
examples.professional: The brainstorming session was fecund, and we came out with more solid ideas than we expected.
examples.analytical: Scholars describe the fecund decades of the Renaissance as a time when art, science, and philosophy grew together.

nuance.analogy: A fecund mind is like rich soil: whatever you plant there tends to grow quickly and abundantly.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fecundus, fruitful, from fecundare (to make fruitful).
common_mistakes: Confusing fecund with feculent, which means dirty.
Pronouncing it like 'FEE-kund' with a long vowel in most American speech.

fecund.etymology: From Middle French *fécond*, from Latin *fēcundus* (“fertile”), which is related to *fētus* and *fēmina* (“woman”).

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see up,‎ to.
senses.example: She went up to the third floor.

senses.definition: Capable, ready or equipped, having sufficient material preconditions for, possibly willpower (at a particular moment).
senses.example: to feel up to it

senses.definition: As much as; no more than.
senses.example: You can make up to five copies.

senses.definition: Until.
senses.example: Up to that point, I liked her.

senses.definition: Within the responsibility of, to be attributed to the sphere of influence of, having someone or something as authoritative in.
senses.example: It’s up to you whether to get the blue one or the red one.

senses.definition: Doing, involved in.
senses.example: to be up to

senses.definition: Devising, scheming (planning something mischievous or inappropriate).
senses.example: He looked like a man up to no good.

senses.definition: Considering all members of an equivalence class the same.English Wikipedia has an article on:up toWikipedia.
senses.example: There’s only one rooted tree with two leaves, up to ordering.

senses.definition: Taught by; in the class of.
(uncommon) Willing, interested in.
senses.example: Are you up to going to the beach?
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: (uncommon) Willing, interested in.
senses.example: Are you feeling up to joining the team for trivia night on Thursday?
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: To have enough energy, health or willingness to do something, especially something tiring or difficult.

pronunciation.tip: Stress UP, and reduce to before a verb or noun to a quick tuh. The p in up is strongly voiceless, so do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is polite and often used to decline something without blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mainly in the negative, as in I don't feel up to it, to decline politely. It is common with health or energy, as in Do you feel up to a walk? It is usually followed by a noun or -ing form, as in feel up to going out. Do not confuse it with the idiom be up to, which means doing something.

distinctions.note: Be up to means to be doing something or to be capable of something; feel up to focuses on your energy or willingness at the moment.
Be able to states general ability; feel up to suggests you are ready or willing now, often because of health or mood.

examples.everyday: Do you feel up to a short walk after dinner, or should we stay in?
examples.professional: I don't feel up to presenting the forecast today, so could Jamal take my slot on the agenda?
examples.analytical: Whether a patient feels up to decision-making depends on capacity, mood and physical strength, not merely on the presence of symptoms.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone battery at 20 percent: enough charge for one short task, but not for a marathon.
nuance.etymology: From the verb feel, from Old English fēlan, plus the adverb up and the preposition to.
common_mistakes: Using a bare verb after it, as in feel up to go; say feel up to going.
Confusing it with be up to, as in What are you up to?, which asks what someone is doing.

feel-up-to.etymology: From Middle English *up to*, from Old English *up tō*.

conversation.text: Do you feel up to going for a walk?
I don't feel up to cooking tonight, so let's order in.
If you feel up to it, come to dinner on Sunday.

senses.definition: A company of people that share the same interest or aim.
senses.example: The Fellowship of the Ring

senses.definition: A feeling of friendship, relatedness or connection between people.
senses.example: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

senses.definition: A merit-based scholarship.
senses.example: She won a fellowship that covers tuition and a living stipend for three years of doctoral study.

senses.definition: A temporary position at an academic institution with limited teaching duties and ample time for research.
senses.example: After finishing her dissertation, she accepted a postdoctoral fellowship with few teaching duties.

senses.definition: A period of supervised, sub-specialty medical training in the United States and Canada that a physician may undertake after completing a specialty training program or residency.
senses.example: He completed a cardiology fellowship at Johns Hopkins after finishing his internal medicine residency.

senses.definition: (dated) Company, companions; a group of people or things following another.
senses.example: In his old letters, the soldier wrote fondly of the fellowship he had shared with his comrades.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To admit to fellowship, enter into fellowship with; to make feel welcome by showing friendship or building a cordial relationship. Now only in religious use.
senses.example: The Bishop's family fellowshipped the new converts.

senses.definition: To join in fellowship; to associate with.
senses.example: The megachurch he attends is too big for making personal connections, so he also fellowships weekly in one of the church's small groups.

core.definition: A close, friendly association among people who share an interest, purpose or faith.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FEL. The middle syllable is nearly silent, so say it as two syllables with a reduced vowel, not three full syllables. Do not stress the -ship ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests warmth, belonging and shared purpose.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fellowship in church, academic and professional contexts. A fellowship can be a scholarship for graduate study or a group of friends who share a faith. Saying you are part of a fellowship sounds warm and sincere.

distinctions.note: Friendship is personal and between two people, while fellowship describes a wider group who share a purpose or faith.
Community is broader and may be based on geography, while fellowship emphasizes shared belief, interests or relationship.

examples.everyday: Our church dinner on Sunday is a great way to get some fellowship with the neighbors.
examples.professional: I was awarded a postdoctoral fellowship to study machine learning fairness.
examples.analytical: Paul describes the church as a fellowship grounded in shared life in Christ.

nuance.analogy: A fellowship is like a shared campfire where strangers become companions around one warm light.
nuance.etymology: From fellow, from Old English feolaga, partner, plus -ship.
common_mistakes: Using fellowship to mean a single friendship; it usually describes a group.
Saying fellowship with a stress on the final syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is koinonia, meaning sharing, participation, partnership or communion in something held in common. In Acts 2:42 the early believers devote themselves to fellowship along with the apostles' teaching and prayer. In 1 Corinthians 1:9 God calls believers into fellowship with his Son Jesus Christ our Lord. In Philippians 2:1 Paul appeals to any fellowship in the Spirit as a basis for unity.

fellowship.etymology: From Middle English *felowschipe*, *felawshipe*, *felaȝschyp*, equivalent to *fellow* + *ship*; or perhaps adapted from Old Norse *félagskapr*, *félagsskapr* (“fellowship”).

senses.definition: Panel of a car which encloses the wheel area, especially the front wheels.
A shield, usually of plastic or metal, on a bicycle that protects the rider from mud or water.
senses.example: I bought new plastic fenders for my bike so the rear wheel stops splashing mud.

senses.definition: A low metal framework in front of a fireplace, intended to catch hot coals, soot, and ash.
senses.example: The fender in front of the hearth caught a spark before it reached the rug.

senses.definition: Any shaped cushion-like object normally made from polymers, rubber or wood that is placed along the sides of a boat to prevent damage when moored alongside another vessel or jetty, or when using a lock, etc. Modern variations are cylindrical although older wooden version and rubbing strips can still be found; old tires are used as a cheap substitute.
senses.example: Before docking, we hung rubber fenders along the hull to protect the paint from the pier.

senses.definition: To use fenders to protect the side of a boat.
senses.example: The deckhand fendered the hull before the ferry came alongside the crowded dock.

core.definition: In American English, the metal body panel above a car wheel, especially at the front, that covers the wheel area.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FEN. The final -er is a reduced, rhotic syllable, so say it as 'der' with a soft r. Do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, technical term for a car part.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fender for the body panel that covers the wheel on a car, and it is common in auto repair and insurance talk. British speakers normally say wing for this part, so Americans may not understand wing. Fender also refers to a bicycle guard or a fireplace guard in some contexts.

distinctions.note: A bumper is the bar at the front or back of a car that absorbs impact; a fender covers the wheel and body panel next to it.
Wing is the normal British term for the same car panel, so Americans say fender and British speakers say wing.

examples.everyday: I scraped the fender backing into the garage pillar, so I need to get it fixed.
examples.professional: The body shop quoted eight hundred dollars to replace the front fender after the collision.
examples.analytical: The fender deforms in a crash to absorb energy, which is why modern cars are designed around controlled deformation.

nuance.analogy: A fender is like a shield over the wheel, taking the first knock so the more important parts stay safe.
nuance.etymology: From the verb fend, meaning to ward off, so a fender is literally something that wards off.
common_mistakes: Using fender for the bumper, which is a different part.
Saying wing, which sounds British to American ears.

senses.definition: Someone in a nominal position of leadership who has little to no actual power.
A carved figure on the prow of a sailing ship.
senses.example: The carved figurehead on the bow of the schooner was a woman holding a lantern.

senses.definition: To lead (something) nominally and with little to no actual power.
senses.example: The board wanted a celebrity to figurehead the nonprofit while the staff ran daily operations.

core.definition: A person who holds a leadership title but has little or no real power to make decisions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FIG, with a lighter secondary stress on HEAD. Say the middle syllable as a quick 'yuh', not 'ya-ee', and keep the r in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, suggesting the person is a symbol rather than a real leader.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for a CEO's ceremonial board chair, a monarch in a constitutional system, or a celebrity who lends a name to a charity. Calling someone a figurehead can sound like a criticism of their real influence, so use it carefully about colleagues. A natural reply is simply 'Right, she's mostly the face of the company.'

distinctions.note: A puppet is controlled by someone else, while a figurehead may have no power but is not necessarily being manipulated.
A leader actually directs and decides; a figurehead mainly represents the group or organization.

examples.everyday: Our mayor is basically a figurehead; the city council runs everything.
examples.professional: The board chair is a figurehead now, so the decisions go through the executive team.
examples.analytical: A constitutional monarch may serve as a figurehead whose authority is symbolic rather than political.

nuance.analogy: Like the carved wooden figure on a ship's front that guides nothing but looks important.
nuance.etymology: From figure plus head, originally the carved ornament at a ship's bow.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'fig-yuh-HED'.
Using it as a compliment for someone who actually leads.

senses.definition: Fishing: the catching, processing and marketing of fish or other seafood.
A place related to fishing, particularly:
senses.example: The small coastal town depends on its fishery, which employs nearly half the working population.

senses.definition: A place where fish or other seafood are caught: a fishing ground (for example, a territorial one).
senses.example: Our family's trout fishery in the Ozarks sells fingerlings to lakes across the Midwest.

senses.definition: A place where fish or other seafood are raised: a fish farm.
senses.example: Our family's trout fishery in the Ozarks sells fingerlings to lakes across the Midwest.

senses.definition: A place where fish or other seafood are processed: a seafood factory.
senses.example: Our family's trout fishery in the Ozarks sells fingerlings to lakes across the Midwest.

senses.definition: A right to fish in a particular location, such as territorial fishing waters.
senses.example: The treaty granted the island nation exclusive fishery rights within two hundred miles of its coast.

senses.definition: A fishing company.
senses.example: The fishery went bankrupt after its trawlers were damaged in the winter storm.

core.definition: The industry of catching, processing, and selling fish and seafood, or an area of water where fish are regularly caught.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FISH. The end is 'uh-ree', with a clear American r, not 'airy' or 'fish-er-ee' with an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical or policy term, and it sounds professional in news and regulation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fishery in government, science, and industry contexts, such as 'Alaska salmon fishery' or 'National Marine Fisheries Service'. In everyday talk people more often say 'fishing industry' or simply 'fishing'. Fisheries in the plural is common for government agencies and fish management.

distinctions.note: Fishing is the activity, while fishery is the industry or a fishing area.
A fishery catches wild fish, while a fish farm raises fish in controlled settings.
A fishing ground is a specific area of water, while fishery can mean the whole industry or the fish stock being caught.

examples.everyday: My neighbor works on a crab fishery up in Alaska, so she's gone for months at a time.
examples.professional: The state's fishery management plan limits how many crab pots each boat can use.
examples.analytical: Economists often analyze a fishery as a common-pool resource, where unchecked harvests can deplete the stock for everyone.

nuance.analogy: A fishery is like a shared savings account: if everyone withdraws too much, nothing is left for later.
nuance.etymology: Formed from fish plus the suffix -ery, which forms nouns for a place, business, or practice.
common_mistakes: Using fishery for the activity of fishing; fishing is the normal word for the act.
Saying 'fishry' or 'fishary', which are not standard English forms.

senses.definition: A loose filmy mass or a thin chiplike layer of anything.
senses.example: There were a few flakes of paint on the floor from when we were painting the walls.

senses.definition: A scale of a fish or similar animal.
senses.example: She picked a silver flake from the trout's skin before cooking it.

senses.definition: A prehistoric tool chipped out of stone.
senses.example: The archaeologist identified the sharp flake as a tool from the Paleolithic era.

senses.definition: A person who is impractical, flighty, unreliable, or inconsistent; especially with maintaining a living.
senses.example: She makes pleasant conversation, but she's kind of a flake when it comes time for action.

senses.definition: A carnation with only two colors in the flower, the petals having large stripes.
senses.example: The nursery sold a striped flake carnation beside the red roses.

senses.definition: A flat turn or tier of rope.
senses.example: The sailor coiled the flake of rope neatly on the deck.

senses.definition: A corrupt arrest, e.g. to extort money for release or merely to fulfill a quota.
senses.example: Officers were accused of running a flake, arresting drivers to extort cash.

senses.definition: A wire rack for drying fish.
senses.example: Fishermen hung the cod on a wire flake to dry in the wind.

senses.definition: A platform of hurdles, or small sticks made fast or interwoven, supported by stanchions, for drying codfish and other things.
senses.example: The codfish were laid out on the wooden flakes to dry in the sun.

senses.definition: A small stage hung over a vessel's side, for workmen to stand on while calking, etc.
senses.example: The painter stood on a flake slung over the hull to scrape the old paint.

senses.definition: To break or chip off in a flake.
senses.example: The paint flaked off after only a year.

senses.definition: To prove unreliable or impractical; to abandon or desert, to fail to follow through.
senses.example: He said he'd come and help, but he flaked.

senses.definition: To store an item such as rope or sail in layers.
senses.example: The line is flaked into the container for easy attachment and deployment.

senses.definition: To plant evidence to facilitate a corrupt arrest.
senses.example: Detectives were caught flaking a bag of cocaine into the suspect's car.

senses.definition: To lay out on a flake for drying.
senses.example: flake a fish

core.definition: A small, thin, flat piece that breaks or peels off a surface, such as a flake of paint or a snowflake.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a glide from ay to k; don't add a vowel after the k. Watch the vowel, which is not the short a of 'flack'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the physical sense. Calling a person a flake is informal and mildly negative, meaning unreliable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use flake for thin bits of paint, skin, snow, cereal, or salt. In casual talk among younger Americans, 'don't be a flake' or 'she's such a flake' describes someone who cancels plans or doesn't follow through. It stings a little, so use it about friends with care.

distinctions.note: A chip is usually a small piece knocked off something hard, like wood or pottery, while a flake is thinner and more fragile, like paint or pastry.
A crumb is a small bit of bread, cake, or cookie; flakes are thin and flat, like cereal or pie crust.

examples.everyday: There are paint flakes all over the kitchen floor from that old window frame.
examples.professional: The inspector noted flakes of coating on the steel beams, so we need to schedule a repaint before winter.
examples.analytical: Archaeologists often study glaze flakes on pottery shards to reconstruct how a vessel was fired.

nuance.analogy: Like a single snowflake: thin, light, and easy to break off a larger surface.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English flake, probably from Old Norse flaga, meaning slab or flake.
common_mistakes: Using flake for a bit of bread or a crumb; a flake is thin and flat, not a small bit of food
Saying flake for a fish's scale in everyday talk; Americans normally say scale

senses.definition: Without flaws, defects, or shortcomings; perfect.
senses.example: The pianist’s performance this evening was flawless.

senses.definition: To win a fight against (a player) without losing health.
senses.example: I got flawlessed again. I'm so bad at this game.

core.definition: Completely perfect, with no mistakes, defects, or weaknesses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced 'luh' sound, and the ending is a weak 'us,' not 'ess.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is a strong compliment for work, appearance, or performance, though it can sound exaggerated if used too often.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flawless' to praise a performance, a dish, a presentation, or someone's appearance. In casual speech, people often say 'flawless' with enthusiasm, while in technical writing they may prefer 'error-free' or 'defect-free.' The adverb 'flawlessly' is also common.

distinctions.note: 'Perfect' is broader and can describe ideal qualities, while 'flawless' focuses on the absence of visible mistakes or defects.
'Error-free' is technical and neutral, often used for code, data, or documents, while 'flawless' is more enthusiastic and general.

examples.everyday: Her pizza crust was flawless, and everyone asked for the recipe.
examples.professional: The release went flawlessly after last week's fixes.
examples.analytical: A flawless argument must anticipate its strongest objections instead of avoiding them.

nuance.analogy: A flawless performance is like a glass of water with no smudge or crack, so the light passes through clearly.
nuance.etymology: From flaw and the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'lay' rather than a reduced 'luh'
Using 'flawless' to mean 'faultless' in legal or technical contexts without checking whether 'error-free' fits better

senses.definition: Of, related to, or resembling flesh.
senses.example: The surgeon described the tissue as pink and fleshy under the bright operating lamp.

senses.definition: Having considerable flesh; plump.
Rich and smooth, with significant body or texture.
senses.example: a fleshy wine

core.definition: Soft, plump, or thick with flesh; used for fruit and leaves that are juicy and substantial, or for a plump body.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a short 'e' in 'flesh' and a clear 'ee' ending. The 'sh' sound is a single consonant, not 'ch'.

nuance.connotation: Positive for fruit and food; neutral to negative for people, depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fleshy' comfortably for fruit, leaves, and stems, and it sounds natural in cooking or gardening. For people, it is less polite; 'fleshy arms' can sound unkind, so 'plump' or 'soft' is safer. In everyday talk, 'juicy' or 'meaty' often replaces it.

distinctions.note: 'Plump' is pleasant and round, often used for people, fruit, or cushions, while 'fleshy' emphasizes soft, meaty substance.
'Chubby' is informal and usually refers to children or cute roundness, while 'fleshy' can sound more clinical or unkind.
'Fat' is blunt and often negative for people, while 'fleshy' is milder and more descriptive.

examples.everyday: These mangoes are so fleshy and sweet, you don't need any sugar on them.
examples.professional: The produce team flagged the fleshy peaches as ready for packing because they had firm, juicy flesh.
examples.analytical: The poet's fleshy imagery pulls the reader from abstraction into the body, making the argument feel physical.

nuance.analogy: Fleshy is like a ripe peach or a thick slice of tomato: the substance under the skin is full, soft, and substantial.
nuance.etymology: From flesh plus the suffix -y; 'flesh' comes from Old English flǣsc.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'fleshy' with 'flashy', which means showy or gaudy.
Using 'fleshy' about people in a casual compliment, which can sound rude to Americans.

senses.definition: To execute or complete a commitment.
senses.example: I don't appreciate salesmen who make promises and then fail to follow through.

senses.definition: To continue moving the arms (and any held implements, such as a bat or club) or legs after striking e.g. a ball.
senses.example: Keep your eyes on the ball and follow through with your swing after contact.

senses.definition: To defecate unintentionally as a result of a cough or sneeze, etc.
senses.example: The toddler sneezed so hard that he might follow through, so Mom grabbed a towel.

core.definition: To carry out a plan, promise, or commitment until it is completely finished, not just start it.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on 'through'. The w in 'follow' is silent, and 'through' starts with a voiceless th followed by an r, so say 'throo' with a clear th sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Following through shows reliability and seriousness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use follow through often at work and in personal life, usually with 'on' before a promise or plan: 'follow through on your commitment'. Without 'on', it can also describe a motion in sports, such as a golf swing. A natural reply to a promise might be, 'I'll hold you to it', or 'Great, I'll look for the update'.

distinctions.note: Follow through means completing what you promised; follow up means checking on something or contacting someone again after an initial step.
Keep often means to maintain or continue doing something, while follow through stresses finishing a specific commitment.

examples.everyday: Dan said he'd fix the fence, and he really followed through, so we had no more loose boards.
examples.professional: Please follow through on the action items from yesterday's meeting by Friday so we can close the ticket.
examples.analytical: Moral resolve means little unless it follows through into action, which is why Aristotle stressed habituation.

nuance.analogy: Following through is like finishing a letter after you have addressed the envelope: starting is not the same as delivering.
nuance.etymology: From follow (Old English folgian) and through (Old English thurh).
common_mistakes: Leaving out 'on' before the promise: say 'follow through on your promise', not 'follow through your promise'.
Writing the noun as two words in the hyphenated form; the noun is often 'follow-through'.

senses.definition: One who follows, comes after another.
senses.example: Each of the followers lined up behind the guide on the narrow trail up the mountain.

senses.definition: Something that comes after another thing.
senses.example: Heavy rain and flooding were the followers of the long drought that summer.

senses.definition: One who is a part of master's physical group, such as a servant or retainer.
senses.example: The lord brought a dozen followers with him to the castle for the winter.

senses.definition: One who follows mentally, adherer to the opinions, ideas or teachings of another, a movement etc.
senses.example: Many of her followers embraced the new teachings after hearing her speak in person.

senses.definition: An imitator, who follows another's example.
senses.example: Young designers became followers of the minimalist style that the famous architect pioneered.

senses.definition: A pursuer.
senses.example: The fox outran its followers through the dense pine forest.

senses.definition: An account holder who subscribes to see content from another account on a social media platform.
senses.example: I have over 50 followers on Twitter, but all my tweets only get 10 likes.

senses.definition: A machine part receiving motion from another. A tappet.
senses.example: The cam's lobes push the followers up and down to open the engine valves.

senses.definition: A tappet.
senses.example: Worn followers in the old engine caused the valves to tick loudly.

senses.definition: A man courting a maidservant; a suitor.
senses.example: Years ago, a stable boy was among the followers courting the miller's daughter.

senses.definition: Young cattle.
senses.example: The farmer moved the followers into the north pasture before winter arrived.

senses.definition: A metal piece placed at the top of a candle to keep the wax melting evenly.
senses.example: The metal followers on the candle kept the wax melting evenly.

senses.definition: Any of the three players (the ruckman, ruck rover, and rover) who usually follow the ball around the ground rather than occupying a fixed position.
senses.example: In Australian rules football, the followers gather around the ball at every stoppage.

senses.definition: A debt collector.
senses.example: The bank hired followers to chase down customers who had missed several payments.

senses.definition: A tool used to remove the core from a pin-tumbler lock without causing the driver pins and springs to fall out.
senses.example: The locksmith picked up a followers and removed the core without losing any pins.

core.definition: Plural of follower: people who support a leader, or who subscribe to someone's online account.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'erz' is a reduced vowel plus a 'z' sound, so do not add an extra syllable as in 'FAH-loh-ur-ihz.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in sports culture or online contexts, it signals popularity and reach.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use followers most often for social media audiences, such as 'She has 50,000 followers.' In sports, fans may be called followers in a general sense. It is the plural form, so use it with plural verbs and when counting.

distinctions.note: Fans are enthusiastic admirers of a team or person; followers may simply subscribe or track updates without strong enthusiasm.
An audience is the group watching or listening at a moment; followers are a more persistent group who keep up with someone over time.

examples.everyday: My cousin just hit ten thousand followers, so she's pretty happy about it.
examples.professional: Our marketing team tracks followers across platforms to measure reach.
examples.analytical: The author's followers interpreted his ambiguous claims in opposing ways, which exposed the text's instability.

nuance.analogy: Followers are like a crowd trailing a parade: they stay close, watch every move, and keep marching along.
nuance.etymology: Plural of 'follower,' from 'follow' plus '-er.'
common_mistakes: Using a singular verb with a plural subject: 'The followers is growing' should be 'The followers are growing.'
Confusing 'followers' with 'following,' which is the count of accounts someone follows.

conversation.text: She has over a million followers on TikTok.
I only have a few followers, mostly family.
He bought followers, so his numbers aren't real.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of please wait for a while.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see for,‎ a,‎ while.

core.definition: For a period of time that is not very long, often used for short stays or waits.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the one-syllable word while, which sounds like wile. Reduce for a to quick weak sounds, and end with a dark l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly. It suggests a relaxed or limited period.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use for a while in casual speech to invite someone to stay or to say how long something lasts, as in Want to stay for a while? It can refer to a period now or in the past. A natural reply is Sure, I'd love to or Just for a little bit.

distinctions.note: For a while is more casual and conversational; for a time often describes a past period that has ended.
In a while means after some time in the future, so I'll see you in a while means later; for a while means during a period.

examples.everyday: Want to stay for a while? I just made coffee and there's still some cake.
examples.professional: Let's keep the pilot running for a while before we decide on a full rollout.
examples.analytical: The model performed well for a while, but its accuracy declined as the data distribution shifted.

nuance.analogy: For a while is like a song you hum for a few minutes before it fades from your mind.
nuance.etymology: From for, a and while; while comes from Old English hwīl, meaning time or period.
common_mistakes: Using in a while for for a while, which changes the meaning to later
Writing awhile after for; use for a while or just awhile, not for awhile

senses.definition: For the purpose of making money, especially in relation to an organization that was not formerly, or is not usually, run to make money.
An organization whose goal is to make a profit.

core.definition: Run to make money for its owners or shareholders, rather than as a charity or public service.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound adjective the main stress falls on FOR, with PROF secondary, and the final syllable of profit is a short, reduced 'it', not 'et'. Keep the r in 'for' clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in business; in public debates about schools, hospitals or prisons it can carry a critical tone, implying profit may conflict with public good.
nuance.usage_note: Very common in American news and policy talk, especially about for-profit colleges, hospitals and prisons. Americans contrast it with 'nonprofit' or 'not-for-profit'. As a noun, 'a for-profit' means such an organization, but the adjective is far more common in everyday use.

distinctions.note: The opposite; a nonprofit reinvests income in its mission and does not distribute it to owners, though it can still earn money.
Broader; it means connected with buying and selling and can also describe public or nonprofit activities.
Describes an activity that makes money, whereas for-profit describes an organization's purpose and legal structure.

examples.everyday: My cousin works at a for-profit hospital chain near the interstate.
examples.professional: The grant only covers nonprofit partners, so we need a for-profit vendor to build the software.
examples.analytical: The debate over for-profit colleges raises the question of whether education should be governed by market incentives.

nuance.analogy: Like a shop versus a church: both serve people, but the shop keeps its profits for its owners rather than for the community.
nuance.etymology: From the preposition 'for' and 'profit', which comes from Latin 'profectus', meaning progress or advancement, through Old French.
common_mistakes: Treating 'for-profit' and 'nonprofit' as synonyms; they describe opposite purposes and legal structures.
Stressing PROFIT in the compound, saying 'for-PROF-it', instead of putting the main stress on FOR.

senses.definition: To prevent, delay or hinder something by taking precautionary or anticipatory measures; to avert.
senses.example: Fred forestalled disaster by his prompt action.

senses.definition: To preclude or bar from happening, render impossible.
senses.example: In French, an aspired h forestalls elision.

senses.definition: To anticipate, to act foreseeingly.
senses.example: The city built higher walls to forestall another flood before the spring rains arrived.

senses.definition: To deprive (with of).
senses.example: The strict lending rules forestalled many families of a fair chance at homeownership.

senses.definition: Something situated or placed in front.
senses.example: A low stone wall served as the forestall of the castle, guarding the gate.

core.definition: To prevent or delay something bad from happening by acting first or taking precautions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STAWL, the second syllable. The vowel is the same as in 'caught' in American speech, and the final l is clear. Do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, since it describes effective prevention; it is often used when a problem is avoided.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'forestall' in formal writing, news reports, and legal or political language, such as 'The company acted to forestall a lawsuit'. In casual speech, people say 'prevent' or 'head off'. The phrase 'head off' is the closest everyday equivalent.

distinctions.note: 'Prevent' is the general, everyday word; 'forestall' is more formal and suggests acting in advance to block something.
'Avert' means to turn away a danger at the last moment; 'forestall' means to stop it before it develops.

examples.everyday: I called the mechanic early to forestall a bigger repair bill on the car.
examples.professional: We added an extra check to forestall the failure we saw in last quarter's deployment.
examples.analytical: The early reformers wrote carefully to forestall misunderstanding, though their precautions did not stop later controversies.

nuance.analogy: Like putting a fence up before the cows wander into the road: you act first to stop the problem.
nuance.etymology: From 'fore' (before) plus 'stall' (to block or delay), from an older sense of blocking an opponent.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'forestall' with 'forestall' in the sense of a noun object; the verb takes a direct object such as a crisis or lawsuit.
Using 'forestall' in very casual talk, where it sounds stiff.

forestall.etymology: From Middle English *forestallen* (“to forestall, intercept, ambush, way-lay”), from *forestalle* (“a forestalling, interception”), from Old English *foresteall* (“intervention, hindrance of justice, ambush”), from *fore-* (“ahead of, before”) + *steall*…

senses.definition: To put into a clear and definite form of statement or expression.
senses.example: He failed to formulate his ideas more clearly.

core.definition: To express an idea, plan, or question clearly in words or a precise statement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FOR. The middle syllable is a reduced myuh, and the final syllable is a clear 'late'. Do not pronounce the middle as 'mew-lay-t' or add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests careful thinking and precise wording.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use formulate in meetings, writing, and academic work, as in 'Can you formulate a clear question?' In casual talk they would say 'come up with' or 'put into words'. It sounds more deliberate than 'make up', so it fits professional speech well.

distinctions.note: State is simple and direct, while formulate implies careful work to make an idea precise.
Devise means to invent or plan a method, whereas formulate means to put an idea into clear words or a precise form.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to formulate a text to my landlord about the leak without sounding angry.
examples.professional: Let's formulate the success metrics before we start the experiment, so everyone agrees on what counts.
examples.analytical: Kant tries to formulate the moral law in a way that binds all rational agents regardless of their desires.

nuance.analogy: Formulating an idea is like shaping clay on a wheel: the rough lump becomes a clear, usable form.
nuance.etymology: From formula, from Latin formula, a small form or rule.
common_mistakes: Using 'formulate' for 'formalize' when you mean making something official.
Saying 'formulate about' instead of using 'formulate' directly with its object.

senses.definition: A person who professes to predict the future in return for money.
senses.example: "Cross my palm with silver and I'll tell you your fortune," said the fortune teller.

senses.definition: A cootie catcher.
senses.example: During recess, the kids folded a paper fortune teller and asked each other to pick a color.

core.definition: A person who claims to predict the future, usually for money, often at fairs, boardwalks or parties.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FOR in 'fortune' and on TEL in 'teller'. The 'r' in 'teller' is pronounced in American English, and the final syllable is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly skeptical. Many Americans see fortune tellers as entertainers rather than real prophets, so calling someone a fortune teller can suggest their predictions are unreliable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fortune teller' for carnival or boardwalk performers, at Halloween, and as a joke about someone who predicts outcomes. In American schools, a 'cootie catcher' is a folded paper game also called a fortune teller, which children use to reveal fortunes. A common reply to someone who claims to know the future is 'I'm not a fortune teller.'

distinctions.note: A 'psychic' claims supernatural powers such as mind reading, while a 'fortune teller' focuses on predicting the future.
An 'astrologer' predicts through the positions of the stars and planets, while a 'fortune teller' may use cards, palms or other methods.

collocations: a fortune teller at the county fair

examples.everyday: We paid ten dollars to see the fortune teller at the county fair, and she guessed I'd take a trip soon.
examples.professional: Our forecasting model is no fortune teller, so we report confidence intervals rather than promising exact numbers.
examples.analytical: Calling a predictive model a fortune teller exposes the difference between prophecy and calibrated inference.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather forecaster who gives odds instead of certainty: the prediction may be useful, but it is not a promise.
nuance.etymology: Fortune from Latin fortuna; teller from Old English tellan 'to count, relate'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'fortune-teller' with a hyphen in American sources; both spellings appear, but the unhyphenated form is common.
Using 'fortune teller' for a psychic or an astrologer without noting the difference in method.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture condemns divination and seeking fortune tellers, as in Deuteronomy 18:10-12, and Acts 16:16-18 describes a slave girl with a spirit of divination. The Hebrew word for diviner is qosem, and the Greek for the spirit of divination is pneuma pythona.

senses.definition: Consisting of fragments; disconnected; scattered.
senses.example: Fragmentary evidence suggests that he died in a foreign country.

senses.definition: Composed of the fragments of other rocks.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the sandstone looked fragmentary, with grains of older rock everywhere.

core.definition: Made up of small, broken, or incomplete pieces; not whole, connected, or complete.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a secondary stress on 'tair'. The 'ment' is weak, like 'muhn', and the final 'ary' is 'air-ee' in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes incompleteness, often in the context of evidence, memories or texts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fragmentary' most for things like ancient texts, evidence or memories that survive only in parts. In everyday speech, 'in pieces' or 'incomplete' is more natural. In professional writing, 'fragmentary' signals that the material is partial rather than broken.

distinctions.note: 'Incomplete' is general; 'fragmentary' stresses that the parts are broken off or scattered, not just missing something.
'Partial' means some part is present; 'fragmentary' suggests pieces that are disconnected from each other.
'Sketchy' is informal and often means unreliable or poorly done; 'fragmentary' is neutral and descriptive.

examples.everyday: I only have fragmentary memories of that trip, just a few pictures in my head.
examples.professional: We have only fragmentary logs from the outage, so the root cause is still unclear.
examples.analytical: Scholars must reconstruct the history from fragmentary sources that survive only in quotation.

nuance.analogy: Fragmentary evidence is like a jigsaw puzzle with half the pieces missing and the rest scattered across the table.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fragmentum, 'a piece broken off,' from frangere, 'to break.'
common_mistakes: Using 'fragmentary' for simply short or small; it means broken into pieces.
Mispronouncing the 'ment' as 'ment' with a full vowel; it is weak in American speech.

senses.definition: The ability to freely choose between different options.

core.definition: The right or ability to freely select among different options without coercion or pressure from others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FREE and CHOICE most strongly, and reduce 'of' to a weak 'uhv'. Run 'freedom of' together so it sounds like FREE-dum-uhv-CHOICE.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It appeals to individual rights, though it can be politically charged in debates about healthcare, schools or reproductive policy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'freedom of choice' in debates about health insurance, school choice, consumer products and personal decisions. It sounds formal in casual talk, so people often say 'I get to choose' instead. A natural reply in a discussion is 'Right, people should have the freedom to decide for themselves.'

distinctions.note: Freedom is the general state of being free, while freedom of choice names the specific right to select among options.
Free will is a philosophical or theological term for the capacity to make decisions, whereas freedom of choice is used in practical and political contexts.
An option is one available possibility, while freedom of choice describes the right to choose among several.

examples.everyday: At the diner you have freedom of choice between eggs, pancakes or oatmeal, so pick whatever you want.
examples.professional: The new benefits plan gives employees freedom of choice among three health networks during open enrollment.
examples.analytical: Philosophers debate whether freedom of choice requires only the absence of external constraint or also the capacity for reasoned deliberation.

nuance.analogy: Like a buffet: you pick what you want, but only from what the kitchen has put out.
nuance.etymology: Freedom from Old English freodom; choice from Old French chois, from choisir 'to choose'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'freedom of the choice' with an unnecessary article; the standard phrase is 'freedom of choice'.
Using 'freedom to choice' instead of 'freedom of choice' or 'the freedom to choose'.

senses.definition: Initialism of frontier artificial intelligence.
senses.example: The lab's safety team reviews every frontier AI model before public release.

core.definition: The most advanced general-purpose AI systems, built at the leading edge of capability, such as the newest large language models from top AI labs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TEER in frontier, and AI is said as the letters A and I, with stress on the I. Don't stress the first syllable (FRON-tier).

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound exciting or worrying depending on whether the speaker is discussing progress or risk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mainly in AI policy, company announcements and news about safety and regulation. Say the full phrase 'frontier artificial intelligence' the first time, then 'frontier AI'. In casual talk people usually say 'the newest AI models' instead.

distinctions.note: AI is the whole field; frontier AI means only the most capable, newest systems at the cutting edge.
An LLM is one type of model; frontier AI names the top tier of capability, and many frontier models are LLMs.

examples.everyday: My nephew says the newest frontier AI can write a whole essay, but I still don't fully trust it.
examples.professional: Our team is reviewing the safety evaluations for the frontier AI model before we add it to the product roadmap.
examples.analytical: Debates over frontier AI often turn on whether capability gains are outpacing our ability to verify what these systems actually do.

nuance.analogy: Like the leading edge of a jet's performance envelope: the newest, most powerful machines, still being tested at their limits.
nuance.etymology: Frontier comes from Old French frontiere, 'border', from front; the AI sense is a recent coinage.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable of frontier (FRON-tier) instead of TEER.
Treating frontier as only a geographic word; in AI it means the most advanced systems, not a border.

senses.definition: Using all the power of one's voice; communicated loudly or vociferously.
senses.example: The crowd sang the anthem in full-throated voices before the opening pitch.

senses.definition: Showing strong feelings.
(dated) Of a woman: having ample breasts.
senses.example: Her 1950s pulp novel described the heroine as full-throated, in the breathless style of its era.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Loud and forceful, using all of one's voice; or expressing strong feeling openly and without restraint.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THROAT, the second element. The final -ed is pronounced as a separate syllable, 'tid', so the word has three syllables, not two.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It usually praises enthusiasm, loyalty or strong support.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase for loud cheering, public support or an endorsement, such as 'full-throated support for the plan'. It appears often in journalism and sports writing. The older sense referring to a woman's bust is dated and can sound offensive today, so avoid using it that way.

distinctions.note: Describes sincere commitment; full-throated stresses volume or open, vocal expression of that commitment.
Means expressing opinions openly; full-throated suggests a louder, more forceful version of that.

examples.everyday: The crowd gave a full-throated cheer when the home team scored in the last minute.
examples.professional: The leadership team sent a full-throated endorsement of the proposal to the board.
examples.analytical: The prophet's full-throated condemnation of injustice leaves little room for neutral observers.

nuance.analogy: Like a bell rung at full strength instead of a light tap on a glass.
nuance.etymology: Full comes from Old English ful; throat comes from Old English throte, meaning throat.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'throated' as one syllable instead of 'THROH-tid'
Using it for quiet or hesitant support, which contradicts its meaning

senses.definition: Nonsense, gobbledygook.
A confused mixture; hodgepodge.
senses.example: The grant proposal was pure galimatias, and the reviewers couldn't tell what we actually wanted.

core.definition: Confused, meaningless talk or writing; nonsense that is hard to follow.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAY. The ending -ias is pronounced 'ee-us', not 'eye-us'. The word is pronounced as three syllables after the stressed one.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes writing or speech as confused or pretentious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use galimatias in everyday talk. It appears in literary criticism or formal writing to describe garbled prose. The everyday American equivalents are gobbledygook or double-talk.

distinctions.note: Gobbledygook is common American English for jargon-filled language; galimatias is more literary and formal.
Gallimaufry means a jumbled mixture of things; galimatias means nonsense in speech or writing.

examples.professional: The vendor's proposal was full of buzzwords and galimatias, with no clear deliverables.
examples.analytical: Much of the postmodern criticism reads as galimatias, dressing empty claims in dense jargon.

nuance.analogy: Galimatias is like static on a radio: sound comes through, but none of it makes sense.
nuance.etymology: From French galimatias, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (GAL-uh-MAY-shus).
Using it as a countable noun; it is usually uncountable.

galimatias.etymology: Borrowed from French *galimatias*, first attested in 1653 in Sir Thomas Urquhart's translation of Rabelais's works.

senses.definition: Any ploy or stratagem.
senses.example: Their promise to lower taxes is clearly an election-year gambit.

senses.definition: A remark intended to open a conversation.
senses.example: Her opening gambit about the weather got the stranger talking about his dog.

senses.definition: An opening in chess in which material is sacrificed to gain an advantage.
senses.example: Her clever gambit gave her an advantage.

senses.definition: To sacrifice (a pawn or minor piece) to gain an advantage.
senses.example: Against the young player, she gambited a knight to seize the center.

core.definition: A deliberate opening move or ploy, often risky, meant to gain an advantage; also a chess opening that sacrifices a piece.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable is short 'it', and the 'b' is clearly pronounced, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, suggesting calculated risk or manipulation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gambit for a strategic opening move in negotiation, debate or politics, as in 'an opening gambit'. It is more common in writing and news than in casual speech. In a conversation, 'opening line' or 'icebreaker' is more natural for a remark meant to start talk.

distinctions.note: Ploy is a general trick, while gambit suggests a bolder opening move that risks something to gain a bigger advantage.
Gamble is the act of risking money or outcome, while gambit is a planned first move in a contest.

examples.everyday: When my friend asked if I wanted to split the bill, that was just a gambit to get me to pay for dessert.
examples.professional: Her opening gambit in the negotiation was to offer a lower price with a longer contract.
examples.analytical: The author's opening gambit, a rhetorical question about free will, sets up everything that follows in the argument.

nuance.analogy: A gambit is like sacrificing a pawn in chess to open a line of attack.
nuance.etymology: From Italian gambetto, 'tripping up', from gamba, 'leg'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word with a long 'ee' vowel, as in 'gam-BEET'.
Using gambit for a gamble with money; it refers to a strategic move.

senses.definition: To control or limit access to something.
To limit (sometimes manipulatively, rather than directly) how much of a role another party, often a spouse, has in some task.
senses.example: Her brother tried to gatekeep the family finances, deciding which bills everyone else could see.

senses.definition: To limit another party's participation in a collective identity or an activity, usually due to undue pettiness, resentment, or overprotectiveness.
senses.example: Some longtime members tried to gatekeep the hobby, mocking newcomers who didn't know the jargon.

senses.definition: A gatekeeper.
senses.example: Those gatekeeps at the country club decided which families could join the board.

core.definition: To control who gets access to a group, activity or resource, often in a restrictive or exclusive way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, GATE, and make the second syllable a long 'ee' as in 'keep.' Do not shorten the vowel to 'kip' as in 'kip' in 'kipper.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually implies unfair, petty or exclusive control over who is allowed in.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gatekeep often in online discussions and everyday talk about hobbies, fandoms, sports teams and friend groups, as in 'stop gatekeeping the hiking group.' It criticizes someone for blocking newcomers, so it can sound confrontational. The noun gatekeeper is neutral and common in offices, news and technology, but the verb has a more pointed, informal tone.

distinctions.note: Gatekeeper is the person who controls access, while gatekeep is the action of doing so, often with a critical tone.
A bouncer physically controls entry to a club or bar, while gatekeep can describe control over information, skills or membership in any community.
Exclude is a neutral, general word for keeping someone out, whereas gatekeep usually suggests a gatekeeper's control or a pattern of blocking others.

examples.everyday: Stop gatekeeping the hiking group; anyone who wants to come along is welcome, even if they're a beginner.
examples.professional: Senior engineers shouldn't gatekeep deployment access just to protect their own workload, because that slows the whole team down.
examples.analytical: When a community gatekeeps its identity, it often defines membership by who knows the insider vocabulary rather than by what members actually do.

nuance.analogy: To gatekeep is like a bouncer at a club who decides who gets in, but applied to a hobby, a team or a group of friends.
nuance.etymology: Back-formed from gatekeeper, which combines gate and keeper.
common_mistakes: Treating gatekeep as a neutral word, when it usually implies unfair or petty control
Writing gate keep as two words in the verb form, which is wrong in standard American writing

senses.definition: Relating to genesis or origin; genetic.

core.definition: Relating to origin or genesis; an older, rare form meaning the same as genetic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NET, and the last syllable is a light, reduced kul. Americans often say the -ical ending quickly, as one syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds old-fashioned, so it can seem stiff or pedantic in modern writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use genical in modern speech; they use genetic. You may meet genetical in older books, or in scholarly writing about the history of ideas. Using it today would sound dated, so say genetic instead.

distinctions.note: Genetic is the standard modern form, while genetical is archaic and sounds stiff in ordinary and scientific writing.

examples.professional: The memo's genetical framing sounded dated, so we changed it to genetic.
examples.analytical: Older writers sometimes wrote genetical to mean relating to origin, a sense now carried by genetic.

nuance.analogy: Like an old coin that still buys something but is no longer used in daily life.
nuance.etymology: Formed from genetic with the suffix -al, from Greek genesis (origin).
common_mistakes: Using genetical in modern writing when genetic is the normal word.
Assuming genetical has a different meaning from genetic, when the difference is only style.

senses.definition: Brightly sparkling.
Valuable, desirable.
senses.example: He chased the glittering prize of a corner office, ignoring what it cost his family.

senses.definition: The appearance of something that glitters.
senses.example: The glittering of the lake under the morning sun made the hikers stop.

core.definition: Shining with many bright, sparkling points of light; also, impressively glamorous or successful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The t between vowels is a flap that sounds like a soft d, and the second syllable is a weak schwa, ending in -ing rather than -een.

nuance.connotation: Positive; suggests dazzle and glamor, though it can sound ironic when describing superficial success.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glittering to praise something shiny and lively, like a glittering city skyline or glittering jewelry, and figuratively for success, as in a glittering career. It can sound a little dramatic in everyday talk. For decorations or costumes in casual speech, glittery or sparkly is more common.

distinctions.note: Glittery is the casual word for things covered in glitter; glittering is more elegant and often figurative.
Glistening refers to a wet shine, while glittering refers to bright sparkles.
Glamorous describes attractive appeal; glittering can describe both light and glamor.

examples.everyday: The Christmas tree was glittering with ornaments, and the kids couldn't stop staring at it.
examples.professional: The dashboard looked glittering in the demo, but the underlying data was still incomplete.
examples.analytical: Many people are drawn to the glittering surface of success, yet the deeper question concerns what it costs to achieve.

nuance.analogy: Like sunlight on a lake full of sparks: many small points of light, all moving and catching the eye.
nuance.etymology: From glitter, from Middle English glitere, to shine; the -ing ending forms an adjective.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable; the stress belongs on GLIT.
Using glittering for a steady glow; glowing or shining is better there.

senses.definition: Talk about something for too long.
senses.example: My roommate goes on about her new running shoes every single morning.

core.definition: To talk about something for too long, in a way that bores or annoys the listeners.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BOUT, and the two words go and on are both fairly light. Non-native speakers often stress go and on equally, which makes the phrase sound stiff.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests the speaker is talking too long or repeating themselves, and it often implies mild annoyance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in casual talk about a person who keeps returning to a topic, such as a coworker who keeps going on about a bad meeting. You can say it about yourself with a light apology, like 'Sorry, I went on about it.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, I know, you've mentioned it.' It is too casual for formal speech or writing.

distinctions.note: Ramble on describes speech that is disorganized and wandering, while go on about focuses on one topic being repeated too long.
Harp on means to return to one complaint or grievance again and again, and it is more negative than go on about.

collocations: go on about how busy they are

examples.everyday: My uncle went on about his new boat for an hour, and I just kept nodding.
examples.professional: Sorry, I went on about the Q3 numbers longer than I meant to; let me get to the decision.
examples.analytical: Critics often go on about the decline of public trust without ever defining what trust means.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio stuck on one station, playing the same song over and over.
common_mistakes: Using 'go on about' to mean 'continue doing something' (that meaning is 'go on with' or simply 'go on').
Dropping 'about' when a topic follows, as in 'he went on the project' instead of 'he went on about the project'.

conversation.text: He keeps going on about his new car.
Sorry, I've been going on about my job all night. How are you?
She went on and on about her vacation photos.

senses.definition: To make a major effort; to be very careful when doing something, especially to an extreme or excessive degree.
senses.example: She would go to great lengths to protect her students' privacy.

core.definition: To make a very large effort or take extreme measures to achieve something. It often suggests care that goes beyond what is normal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'lengths' and pronounce its final cluster 'ŋkθs' as one unit. Many Americans drop the 't' and say something close to 'LENGKS,' but the 'th' sound is still standard.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can also imply excess when the effort seems unnecessary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for impressive effort, such as 'She went to great lengths to plan the surprise.' It can also be critical, implying someone is excessive. Use 'to' before an infinitive or a noun, and note that the phrase works in most settings from casual talk to reports.

distinctions.note: 'Make an effort' is neutral and general, while 'go to great lengths' stresses a stronger and often unusual level of effort.
'Go out of your way' emphasizes kindness or helpfulness, while 'go to great lengths' can be neutral or critical.

collocations: go to great lengths to protect
went to great lengths to hide
go to great lengths to please
go to great lengths for the team

examples.everyday: My sister went to great lengths to make my birthday a surprise, even hiding in the closet for an hour.
examples.professional: Our team went to great lengths to keep the migration from breaking the reporting dashboard, so the rollout stayed on schedule.
examples.analytical: Many people go to great lengths to justify choices they already suspect are wrong, which is why self-deception is philosophically important.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner pushing past the point where the body wants to stop, going far beyond the ordinary distance.
nuance.etymology: 'Great' comes from Old English 'grēat'; 'length' comes from Old English 'lengthu.'
common_mistakes: Using 'big lengths' instead of 'great lengths,' which is the standard collocation.
Using a singular noun, as in 'go to great length.'

synonyms: go to the ends of the earth

senses.definition: To eat hastily or greedily; to scoff or scarf.
senses.example: He gobbled four hot dogs in three minutes.

senses.definition: Of a turkey, to make its characteristic vocalisation; also, used of certain other birds.
senses.example: In the early morning, the wild turkeys gobble from the ridge above our farm.

senses.definition: To make the sound of a turkey.
senses.example: The tom turkey began to gobble as soon as the sun rose.

senses.definition: A rapid straight putt so strongly played that, if the ball had not gone into the hole, it would have gone a long way past.
