senses.example: His putt was a gobble that ran four feet past the cup.

senses.definition: The sound of a turkey; or, a similar vocalisation of another bird.
senses.example: We heard the gobble of a turkey echoing through the valley at dawn.

senses.definition: (rare) An act of eating hastily or greedily.
senses.example: He finished his sandwich in one gobble and immediately asked for dessert.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To eat quickly and greedily, taking large bites and swallowing with little chewing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, GAHB, and the second syllable is a syllabic l with no full vowel. Keep the first vowel short and open, like the vowel in cot.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting poor manners or hunger; playful when describing children or pets.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say gobble for kids, pets, or hungry adults in casual talk, as in Don't gobble your dinner. Saying it about a guest at a dinner table can sound rude. Gobble up and gobble down are more common than plain gobble, and gobble up is also used figuratively for buying or absorbing something quickly.

distinctions.note: Wolf down is also informal and stresses speed, while gobble stresses greedy swallowing with little chewing.
Devour is more formal or literary and can apply to books or ideas, while gobble is about food and usually sounds less polite.

examples.everyday: The kids gobbled their pancakes so fast that they were finished before I sat down.
examples.professional: I had to gobble my sandwich at my desk so I could finish the review before the call.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that large firms gobble up small startups before they can grow into independent competitors.

nuance.analogy: Gobbling is like a vacuum cleaner for food: fast and loud, with no time for taste.
nuance.etymology: Probably from gob, a mouthful; the turkey sense is imitative.
common_mistakes: Using gobble for slow, polite dining, where it sounds rude or childish.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a long oh, as in GOH-bul; the first vowel is a short ah.

gobble.etymology: From Middle English *gobben* (“to drink or swallow greedily”), of origin *le*.

senses.definition: Made of, or relating to, gold.
senses.example: She wore a golden crown.

senses.definition: Having a color or other richness suggestive of gold.
senses.example: Under a golden sun.

senses.definition: Of a beverage, flavored or colored with turmeric.
senses.example: The café's golden latte, flavored with turmeric and ginger, became her favorite winter drink.

senses.definition: Marked by prosperity, creativity etc.
senses.example: The Renaissance was a golden era.

senses.definition: Advantageous or very favorable.
senses.example: This is a golden opportunity

senses.definition: Relating to a fiftieth anniversary.
senses.example: It's not long until our golden wedding.

senses.definition: Relating to the elderly or retired.
senses.example: After retiring, Bob and Judy moved to Arizona to live out their golden years.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) brassy drummer, brassy chub, etc. (Kyphosus vaigiensis), a fish found in southeast Asia.
senses.example: The fisherman in Vietnam said the golden he caught would sell well at market.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of golden retriever.
To become gold or golden (in color).
senses.example: By late afternoon, the wheat fields began to golden under the setting sun.

senses.definition: To make golden or like gold.
senses.example: The jeweler used a fine brush to golden the picture frame's edges.

core.definition: Made of gold, or having the bright, warm yellow color or quality of gold.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, GOHL. The second syllable is reduced to a soft schwa-like un, and the d is often a soft flap, so it sounds close to GOHL-dun, not gol-DEN.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting warmth, value, or excellence; can be sentimental in literary or romantic contexts.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, golden describes hair, sunlight, tan skin, or a golden brown baked food, as in cook until golden brown. It also means excellent or promising, as in a golden opportunity. Americans say gold for the metal and golden for the color or quality, so do not use golden as a noun for the metal.

distinctions.note: Gold is the noun for the metal or the color; golden is the adjective meaning like gold, as in golden sunlight.
Yellow is the general color word, while golden suggests a warmer, richer yellow that looks like metal or light.

examples.everyday: Pull the chicken out of the oven when it's golden brown and the skin is crispy.
examples.professional: This is a golden opportunity to test the new model with customers who already trust us.
examples.analytical: Medieval painters used golden backgrounds to suggest divine light, which made color itself a theological statement.

nuance.analogy: Golden is gold's gentler cousin: it catches light like metal without necessarily being metal.
nuance.etymology: From gold, from Old English gold, with the -en suffix forming an adjective.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable or giving it a full vowel, as in GOLD-den, instead of a reduced ending.
Using golden as a noun for the metal; say gold for the metal.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is zahav (gold). In Scripture, golden often describes objects of worship or sacred furnishings: Exodus 32:4 describes the golden calf, Daniel 3:1 describes a golden image set up by King Nebuchadnezzar, and Exodus 25:31 describes the golden lampstand made for the tabernacle.

golden.etymology: From Middle English *golden*, a restored form (due to the noun *gold*) of earlier Middle English *gulden*, *gylden*, *gilden* "golden"; >, from Old English *gylden* (“golden”), from **gulþīn*, from Proto-Germanic **gulþīnaz* (“golden, made of gold”),…

senses.definition: An award for excellence in film and television, bestowed by the Hollywood Foreign Press Association since 1944.

core.definition: Annual American awards for excellence in film and television, given by the Hollywood Foreign Press Association since 1944.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on GLOHBZ, and the plural ending is a z sound after the b. Do not stress the first syllable of Golden or pronounce the plural as glob-us.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting prestige and glamor in entertainment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans talk about the Golden Globes in news about movies and TV, and winning one is a major honor. The ceremony is held in January and is known for a looser, more celebrity-friendly style than the Oscars, so people often say the Globes. A typical conversation might be did you watch the Golden Globes, which is usually followed by comments about speeches and red carpet outfits.

distinctions.note: The Academy Awards, or Oscars, are the most prestigious American film awards, while the Golden Globes are another major awards show with a more relaxed style and a different voting group.
The Emmys honor television and are voted on by the Television Academy, while the Golden Globes cover both film and television.

examples.everyday: Did you see who won at the Golden Globes last night?
examples.professional: Our marketing team wants the series to get a Golden Globe nomination to boost viewership.
examples.analytical: The Golden Globes are often read as a barometer of Hollywood taste, though the small size of the voting body raises questions about representativeness.

nuance.analogy: The Golden Globes are the lively cousin of the Oscars: the same family of prestige, with more champagne and less formality.
nuance.etymology: Named for the golden globe trophy; globe comes from Latin globus, meaning sphere.
common_mistakes: Saying Golden Globe for the whole show; the singular refers to one award, while the plural refers to the ceremony.
Stressing the first syllable of Globes instead of the second.

senses.definition: A golf cart.

core.definition: A small, low-speed motorized vehicle used to carry golfers and their equipment around a golf course or resort property.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAHR, the second word. The r in car is pronounced clearly in General American, and golf uses the open vowel of cot.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, descriptive term, used especially in parts of the South and Florida and by manufacturers.
nuance.usage_note: Golf car is an American term, used regionally and by some manufacturers and resorts, especially in Florida and the Southeast. Golf cart is more common across the country and is the safer choice for most listeners. Both mean the same vehicle, so you will be understood either way.

distinctions.note: Golf cart is the more widely used national term; golf car is regional and common in some manufacturer and resort contexts.
A car is a general automobile; a golf car is a specialized low-speed vehicle and is not licensed for highway use in most places.

collocations: drive a golf car to the clubhouse

examples.everyday: We rented a golf car to get from the pool to the restaurant without walking in the heat.
examples.professional: The resort approved the purchase of twelve new golf cars, and the vendor will deliver them before the season.
examples.analytical: The choice between golf car and golf cart reveals regional variation in American English, even within a single product category.

nuance.analogy: It is like the difference between soda and pop: the same thing, with the word depending on where you are.
nuance.etymology: Golf comes from Scots golf, probably from Middle Dutch kolf, a club; car comes from Latin carrus, a wheeled vehicle.
common_mistakes: Assuming golf car is wrong; it is accepted American usage, though golf cart is more common.
Pronouncing car as cah with no r; the r is pronounced in American English.

senses.definition: Relating to a government.
senses.example: governmental agency

senses.definition: Relating to governing.

core.definition: Relating to a government, or to the work, power, or actions of a government.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MEN, the third syllable, not on GUV. Americans reduce the first two syllables, so say 'guv-ern-MEN-tul' with a clear schwa in the last syllable. Avoid saying 'GUV-ern-men-tal' with equal emphasis.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds professional and precise, and it is often used in official or academic contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use governmental in writing, formal speeches, and official contexts, such as governmental agencies or governmental bodies. In casual talk, they usually say government, as in government agency or government job. The word can sound stiff in conversation, so use it when you want a formal, precise tone.

distinctions.note: Government is a noun for the institution, while governmental is an adjective describing something related to it.
Governing describes a body that is in charge, such as a governing board, while governmental describes something belonging to or relating to government.
Political is broader and can refer to parties, elections, or public debate, while governmental refers specifically to official state institutions.

examples.everyday: My cousin works for a governmental agency that handles road permits in our county.
examples.professional: Before we launch the pilot, we need approval from the governmental body that oversees data privacy.
examples.analytical: Tocqueville observes that American civic life depends on associations as much as on governmental institutions.

nuance.analogy: Governmental is to government as musical is to music: it describes things that belong to or come from the thing itself.
nuance.etymology: From government plus the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Using governmental as a noun, such as saying 'the governmentals decided'; the word is an adjective only.
Confusing governmental with governing when describing a board that is in charge of an organization.

senses.definition: A person who is recognized as having completed any of various levels of education.
senses.example: If the government wants graduates to stay in the country, they should offer more incentives.

senses.definition: A graduated (marked) cup or other container, thus fit for measuring.
senses.example: She poured the flour into a graduate before adding the milk for the pancake batter.

senses.definition: Graduated, arranged by degrees.
senses.example: The dosage plan was graduated, starting low and rising gradually each week.

senses.definition: Holding an academic degree.
senses.example: He hopes to hire a graduate engineer with a master's degree and two years experience.

senses.definition: Relating to an academic degree.
senses.example: The graduate program in statistics admits only twelve students each fall semester.

senses.definition: To be recognized by a school or university as having completed the requirements of a degree studied at the institution.
senses.example: The man graduated in 1967.

senses.definition: To be certified as having earned a degree from; to graduate from (an institution).
senses.example: Trisha graduated college.

senses.definition: To certify (a student) as having earned a degree.
senses.example: Indiana University graduated the student.

senses.definition: To mark (something) with degrees; to divide into regular steps or intervals, as the scale of a thermometer, a scheme of punishment or rewards, etc.
senses.example: The teacher graduated the rulers so students could measure each line precisely.

senses.definition: To change gradually.
senses.example: sandstone which graduates into gneiss; carnelian sometimes graduates into quartz

senses.definition: To prepare gradually; to arrange, temper, or modify by degrees or to a certain degree; to determine the degrees of.
senses.example: to graduate the heat of an oven

senses.definition: To taper, as the tail of certain birds.
senses.example: The tail of the bird graduates from a broad base to a narrow point.

senses.definition: To approve (a feature) for general release.
senses.example: We have graduated the new machine-learning features and will roll them out tomorrow.

senses.definition: Of an idol: to exit a group; or of a virtual YouTuber, to leave a management agency; usually accompanied with "graduation ceremony" send-offs, increased focus on the leaving member, and the like.
senses.example: Fans speculate that she was forced to graduate due to harassment and doxxing by stalkers and haters.

senses.definition: To bring to a certain degree of consistency, by evaporation, as a fluid.
senses.example: Cook the syrup slowly until it graduates into a thick, glossy glaze.

core.definition: A person who has successfully completed a course of study at a school, college or university and received a diploma or degree.

pronunciation.tip: The noun is stressed on the first syllable and ends in a short, reduced 'it'. The verb is different: GRAD-joo-ayt, with a long 'ay' ending, so keep them distinct.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Being a graduate usually signals achievement, completion and readiness for the next stage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'high school graduate' or 'college graduate' to name the level, and 'graduate' alone often refers to someone in graduate school, which is a master's or doctoral program. The informal shortening 'grad' is very common, as in 'grad school'. Americans also say 'graduate from' a school rather than 'graduate' a school.

distinctions.note: Alumni is a formal term for former students in general, whether or not they finished a degree; graduate specifically means someone who completed a program and received the credential.
An undergraduate is a student pursuing a bachelor's degree, while a graduate is someone who has finished a degree, or in the narrower sense a student in a master's or doctoral program.

examples.everyday: My nephew is a high school graduate, and he starts community college in the fall.
examples.professional: We're hiring recent graduates from data science programs for the summer analyst role.
examples.analytical: The modern graduate is often defined by a credential rather than by the formation the degree once claimed to provide.

nuance.analogy: A graduate is like someone who has finished a long hike and reached the trailhead: the journey is complete and a new stage begins.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin graduatus, past participle of graduare 'to take a degree', from Latin gradus 'step'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'she graduated the university'; in American English, say 'she graduated from the university'.
Pronouncing the noun with the verb's long 'ay' ending, as in 'GRAD-joo-ayt' for a person who finished school.

graduate.etymology: From Middle English *graduat* (“ a graduate of a university; graduate, having graduated”), borrowed from Medieval Latin *graduātus* (“graduated, graduate”), perfect passive participle of *graduō* (“to graduate”) (see *-ate*), from *gradus* (“step”) + *-ō*.

senses.definition: An excavation in the earth as a place of burial.
senses.example: The workers dug a narrow grave at the edge of the cemetery for the family.

senses.definition: Any place of interment.
senses.example: The family placed flowers at the grave of their grandfather every Sunday.

senses.definition: Any place containing one or more corpses.
senses.example: Investigators found the bodies in a mass grave beneath the abandoned barn.

senses.definition: Death, destruction.
senses.example: Her reckless driving nearly sent the whole family to the grave.

senses.definition: Deceased people; the dead.
senses.example: On All Souls' Day, our pastor prayed for the living and for the grave.

senses.definition: A grave accent, the diacritic mark `.
senses.example: In French class, she showed us how the grave accent changes the vowel in père.

senses.definition: (historical) A count, prefect, or person holding office.
senses.example: In the medieval charter, the grave of the shire presided over the local court.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To dig.
senses.example: They graved a deep hole in the frozen field before the storm.

senses.definition: To carve or cut, as letters or figures, on some hard substance; to engrave.
senses.example: The jeweler graved the couple's initials inside the wedding ring.

senses.definition: To carve out or give shape to, by cutting with a chisel; to sculpture.
senses.example: to grave an image

senses.definition: To impress deeply (on the mind); to fix indelibly.
senses.example: That painful afternoon in the hospital graved itself on my memory forever.

senses.definition: To entomb; to bury.
senses.example: They graved the fallen miners beneath the mountain where they had died.

senses.definition: To write or delineate on hard substances, by means of incised lines; to practice engraving.
senses.example: During the workshop, she graved fine lines into copper plates to practice her technique.

senses.definition: Characterized by a dignified sense of seriousness.
senses.example: The grave deacon nodded solemnly and asked the congregation to bow their heads.

senses.definition: Low in pitch, tone etc.
senses.example: The cellist's grave notes rumbled through the hall, low and resonant.

senses.definition: Serious, in a negative sense; important, formidable.
senses.example: The doctor warned us that the infection was a grave concern for her recovery.

senses.definition: (dated) Dull, produced in the middle or back of the mouth. (See Grave and acute on Wikipedia.Wikipedia )
senses.example: Her phonetics professor called the vowel grave, not acute, when we compared the two sounds.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A hole dug in the ground in which a dead body is buried, often marked by a stone or marker.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable that rhymes with wave. Keep the final v voiced and do not add an extra uh sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in everyday talk, but solemn and sad when used about a funeral or a loved one's burial place.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say go visit the grave of a relative, or the grave site when they mean the spot in a cemetery. Cemetery names the whole burial ground, while grave refers to one burial spot. Common idioms include turn over in his grave and dig your own grave, meaning to cause your own ruin.

distinctions.note: A tomb is usually a large structure above ground or a sealed chamber, while a grave is a dug burial place in the earth.
A cemetery is the whole area where many people are buried, whereas a grave is one individual burial place within it.
A plot is a piece of land in a cemetery that can hold one or more graves, often bought in advance by a family.

collocations: lay someone to rest in a grave

examples.everyday: We stopped by Grandpa's grave on the way home from the lake.
examples.professional: Before the renovation starts, the historical society needs to confirm that no graves are under the lot.
examples.analytical: Ancient burial customs reveal how societies understood the boundary between the living and the grave.

nuance.analogy: A grave is like a bookmark placed in the ground, marking the page where a life stopped.
nuance.etymology: From Old English græf, related to the verb grave meaning to dig.
common_mistakes: Using grave for the whole cemetery; say cemetery for the entire burial ground.
Confusing the noun grave with the adjective grave (serious), which is pronounced the same but has a different meaning.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the idea of a grave is expressed by the Hebrew she'ol, the realm of the dead, and by the Hebrew qever, a tomb or burial place. In the Greek New Testament, mnemeion means a memorial tomb. Genesis 37:35 records Jacob saying he will go down to Sheol mourning for his son. John 11:38-44 describes Jesus at the tomb of Lazarus, a cave with a stone laid across it. Matthew 27:59-60 tells how Joseph of Arimathea laid Jesus in his own new tomb cut in rock.

grave.etymology: From Middle English *grave*, *grafe*, from Old English *græf*, *grafu* (“cave, grave, trench”), from **grab*, from Proto-Germanic **grabą*, **grabō* (“grave, trench, ditch”), from Proto-Indo-European **gʰrebʰ-* (“to dig, scratch, scrape”).

senses.definition: Senses relating to seriousness.
senses.example: I hope you appreciate the gravity of the situation.

senses.definition: Of an activity, situation, words, etc.: the quality of having important or serious consequences; importance, seriousness.
senses.example: I hope you appreciate the gravity of the situation.

senses.definition: Authority, influence, weight; also, used as a title for a person with authority or influence.
senses.example: The senator's gravity in committee made her proposals hard to ignore.

senses.definition: Senses relating to physical qualities.
senses.example: Aristotelian gravity Newtonian gravity

senses.definition: Synonym of gravitation (“the fundamental force of attraction which exists between all matter in the universe that tends to draw bodies towards each other, due to matter causing the curvature of spacetime”); also, a physical law attempting to account for the phenomena of this force.
senses.example: Aristotelian gravity Newtonian gravity

senses.definition: Synonym of g-force (“the acceleration of a body relative to the freefall acceleration due to any local gravitational field, expressed in multiples of g0 (the mean acceleration due to gravity (sense 2.2.1) at the Earth's surface)”).
senses.example: Pilots in the fighter jet endured nine times normal gravity during the sharp turn.

senses.definition: Dated except in center of gravity: specific gravity or relative density (“a dimensionless measure which is the ratio of the mass of a substance to that of some reference substance (chiefly an equal volume of water at 4°C)”); also, heaviness, weight.
senses.example: The lab measured the gravity of the brine to check its salt concentration.

senses.definition: The lowness in pitch of a note, a sound, etc.
senses.example: The cellist's low notes had a warm gravity that filled the concert hall.

core.definition: The natural force that pulls objects toward each other, especially toward Earth; also the serious importance of a situation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, GRAV, and the second vowel is reduced to uh. Avoid stressing the last syllable, as in 'gra-VI-tee', and do not say 'GRAV-ih-tee' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the physical force; it can sound serious or heavy when it means the importance of a situation, which is usually a sober or negative context.
nuance.usage_note: Everyone uses gravity for the physical force, as in 'what goes up must come down because of gravity'. Americans also say 'the gravity of the situation' when they want to stress how serious something is, usually in a calm, formal tone. It is a little heavy for casual chatter, so use it when the stakes are high.

distinctions.note: Gravitas means dignified seriousness of manner, usually of a person, while gravity can describe a force or the seriousness of a situation.
Weight is the measurable force of gravity on an object's mass, while gravity is the underlying force itself.

examples.everyday: I dropped my keys and they fell straight down because of gravity, of course.
examples.professional: The team needs to recognize the gravity of this data breach before the board meeting on Friday.
examples.analytical: Newton's account of gravity as a force acting at a distance raised deep questions about how forces can act across empty space.

nuance.analogy: Like an invisible hand that keeps pulling everything back toward the ground.
nuance.etymology: From Latin gravitas, 'heaviness, weight', from gravis, 'heavy'.
common_mistakes: Using 'gravity' to mean dignified personal manner, which is 'gravitas' in English.
Stressing the last syllable, which makes the word sound like a different word.

gravity.etymology: French *gravité* (“seriousness, solemnity; severity; gravity”), or from its Latin *gravitās* (“heaviness, weight; seriousness; severity”), equivalent to *grave* + *-ity*.

senses.definition: Grazeland.
senses.example: Our cattle spent the summer on the mountain grazing above the river valley.

senses.definition: The action of animals eating, mainly of grass in a field or on other grassland.

core.definition: The action of animals eating grass in a field or pasture; also the land used for this.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, GRAY, and make the last syllable a short i sound, as in 'zing'. Do not pronounce it 'gra-zhing' or stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a normal, pastoral activity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use grazing for cattle, sheep and horses eating grass, and in rural contexts they say 'grazing land' or 'grazing rights'. In everyday speech people also use 'grazing' to mean eating small snacks throughout the day, as in 'I just grazed at the party', which is informal.

distinctions.note: Pasture is the land on which animals feed, while grazing is the activity of feeding on it or sometimes the right to use it.
Browsing is eating leaves, shoots and shrubs, while grazing is eating grass and other low plants.

examples.everyday: The cows looked peaceful out there grazing in the back pasture.
examples.professional: The county extension office recommended rotational grazing to keep the pasture from degrading over the summer.
examples.analytical: Overgrazing alters soil structure and plant diversity, which is why ecologists study grazing as a force that shapes grasslands.

nuance.analogy: Like a slow lawnmower made of cattle, moving across the field one bite at a time.
nuance.etymology: From graze, from Old English grasian, 'to feed on grass'.
common_mistakes: Using 'grazing' for any kind of eating, when it refers mainly to animals eating grass.
Misspelling 'overgrazing' by splitting it into two words.

core.definition: A country in southeastern Europe, and in the Bible the land of the Greeks, called Javan in Genesis and Hellas by the Greeks.

pronunciation.tip: Greece is a single stressed syllable with a long ee sound. Avoid adding a second syllable or pronouncing it like grease with a z ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a geographic and historical name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Greece for the country, and adjectives are Greek. Americans rarely say Hellas except in classical or Bible-scholar contexts. In Bible study the name Greece often refers to the Hellenistic world more broadly.

distinctions.note: Greece is the country; Greek is the language, people, or adjective.
Hellas is the Greek name for the country, used in classical or formal writing; Americans normally say Greece.

examples.everyday: We are going to Greece next summer, so I need to start learning a few phrases.
examples.professional: Our product team is expanding its shipping to Greece and Cyprus next quarter.
examples.analytical: Daniel 8:21 identifies the goat with the great horn as the king of Greece, which Christian interpreters have traditionally read as the empire of Alexander the Great.

nuance.analogy: Greece is like the root of a tree of Western thought: many later branches grew from its soil.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Graecia, from Greek Graikos; the Greeks called themselves Hellenes and their land Hellas.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it GREESE with a z-sound, which confuses it with grease.
Using Greece as an adjective: say Greek food, not Greece food.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew Scripture the Greek-speaking peoples are called Javan, a son of Japheth in Genesis 10:2. Daniel 8:21 and 11:2 describe a king of Greece who rises against the Persian kingdom. Zechariah 9:13 speaks of the sons of Zion being roused against the sons of Greece. In Acts 20:2-3 Luke records that Paul came to Greece, where he spent three months.

senses.definition: In a grim manner.
(rare) Grim-looking, grim-natured.
senses.example: The grimly sergeant barked orders at the recruits, his face hard and unsmiling.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: In a serious, stern, or determined way, often suggesting bad news or hard resolve.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GRIM. The final -ly is a light "lee" sound, and the vowel in grim is short, as in "big."

nuance.connotation: Negative or serious; it suggests harshness, determination in hard circumstances, or dread.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "grimly" in news reports, writing and conversation to describe serious faces, determined attitudes or bleak situations. It is not rude, but it is heavier than "seriously." A natural reply in conversation is simply to acknowledge the mood.

distinctions.note: "Seriously" can mean sincerely or gravely; "grimly" always adds a sense of bleakness or grim resolve.
"Sternly" describes a strict, disapproving manner; "grimly" suggests gloom or determination in a hard situation.

examples.everyday: The mechanic looked at my car and said grimly, "The transmission is going."
examples.professional: Our manager grimly reminded the team that the launch would slip unless we cut scope.
examples.analytical: The essayist grimly argues that modern progress has not reduced human suffering.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather forecast delivered in a serious voice: the words are plain, but the tone is heavy.
nuance.etymology: From the adjective "grim" (from Old English grimm, fierce) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using it for happy or lighthearted situations.
Pronouncing the vowel in grim as a long "ee" sound.

grimly.etymology: From Middle English *grymly*, *grimlich*, from Old English *grimliċ*, corresponding to *grim* + *ly*.

senses.definition: The act or process of guiding.
senses.example: Under her guidance, the junior analysts learned to clean messy datasets quickly.

senses.definition: Advice or counseling on some topic.
senses.example: divine guidance

senses.definition: Any process or system to control the path of a vehicle, missile, etc.
senses.example: The missile's guidance failed shortly after launch, sending it into the ocean.

core.definition: Advice, direction or counseling that helps someone make decisions or perform a task well.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, GUIDE, and reduce the ending '-ance' to a weak 'uhns'. It has two syllables, not 'gyde-AHNS'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it implies helpful direction from someone with knowledge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'guidance' often at work, in schools and in medicine, as in 'Can you give me some guidance on this?' or 'career guidance counselor.' It sounds more formal than 'advice'. A natural reply is 'Thanks, that helps' or 'I appreciate the guidance.'

distinctions.note: Advice is usually a specific suggestion, while guidance is ongoing direction over a process or decision.
Instructions tell you exactly what to do, while guidance helps you decide how to proceed.
Guidelines are written rules or recommendations, while guidance is advice given by a person or a process.

examples.everyday: Could you give me some guidance on how to set up the grill?
examples.professional: Please follow the company's travel guidance when you book flights for the conference.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that moral guidance cannot be reduced to rules, because judgment depends on contexts that rules cannot fully capture.

nuance.analogy: Guidance is like a GPS voice: it suggests the route, but you still do the driving.
nuance.etymology: From guide (verb) plus the suffix -ance, from Old French guider, to guide.
common_mistakes: Using 'guidance' with 'a' as a countable noun; say 'some guidance' or 'a piece of guidance'.
Confusing 'guidance' with 'guidelines'; guidelines are written rules, while guidance is direction given by a person or process.

senses.definition: One who gulps.
senses.example: My nephew is a fast gulper, so he always finishes his milk before the rest of us.

senses.definition: A gulper eel.
senses.example: Marine biologists photographed a gulper eel drifting in the deep Pacific waters off California.

core.definition: A person who eats or drinks very quickly, taking big, fast swallows.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the final er as a rhotic r-colored vowel, as in 'water' without the t. Do not pronounce it as 'gulp-ay'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative to playful: it describes someone who eats or drinks in a hurry, sometimes without manners.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gulper mostly in casual talk, usually for a child or a family member who eats or drinks fast. It is not a formal word and is not common in writing. In fishing or marine contexts, gulper can also mean a gulper eel, a deep-sea fish with a huge mouth.

distinctions.note: A glutton eats too much and greedily, while a gulper is focused on speed; a gulper may not eat large amounts.
Speed eater describes someone competing or training to eat quickly; gulper is a casual, everyday description.
A sipper drinks slowly and carefully, the opposite of a gulper.

examples.everyday: My little brother is a total gulper; he finishes his milk in five seconds.
examples.professional: He is a fast gulper of documentation, so I always ask him to summarize it in his own words.
examples.analytical: Ancient moralists warned that the gulper of wine often confuses appetite with true enjoyment.

nuance.analogy: A gulper is like a funnel that drains a bucket in one rush instead of letting the water flow slowly.
nuance.etymology: From gulp (verb) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using gulper as a formal term at work; say someone who reads or works very fast instead, unless it is a joke.
Misplacing the stress on the final syllable.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of hits.
senses.example: The box score showed three runs, seven H, and two errors for the home team.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of heroin.
senses.example: Police found a bag of H hidden under the seat of the stolen car.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of half-year.
senses.example: We expect the amendment to enter into force in H2 2013.

senses.definition: A pencil of grade H.
senses.example: For detailed drafting, she always reached for an H pencil before any softer grade.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of handicap.
senses.example: EOE M/F/V/H

senses.definition: Abbreviation of Hindu; mostly used by Indian Muslim netizens primarily towards Hindutva supporters.
senses.example: Online, some users shorten Hindu to H in heated arguments about religion and politics.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of hard, in reference to a grade of pencil lead.
senses.example: Draftsmen often choose an H-grade pencil with hard lead for crisp technical lines.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of high, in reference to a dialect's social status.
senses.example: An H variety usually enjoys official approval and cultural prestige.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of hinged.
senses.example: The catalog lists the bracket as H-hinged for easy installation on frameless cabinets.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of horrific, a former film classification.
senses.example: The old H rating on the poster warned parents that the film was horrific.

senses.definition: Pornographic in a way characteristic of hentai.
senses.example: H scene

senses.definition: Synonym of AH: in the year of the Hegira, used to mark dates employing the Islamic calendar.
senses.example: The manuscript is dated 450 H according to the Islamic calendar.

core.definition: The eighth letter of the English alphabet, also used in short forms like H-bomb and as a name for things shaped like it.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one syllable that rhymes with 'ache' and 'match', not as 'huh'. The final 'ch' is the sound of 'church'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a letter name with no emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'aitch' (AYCH) for the letter name, and they spell out words with 'H as in Harry' on the phone. The pronunciation 'haitch' is typical of British and Irish speech and sounds unusual in most of the United States. Americans also use H in technical codes such as the H-1B visa and H2O for water.

distinctions.note: H is the written letter, while aitch is the spoken name of that letter, which you use when you say the letter aloud.
Capital H is used at the start of a name or sentence, while lowercase h is the usual form within words.

examples.everyday: My last name starts with H, as in Harris, so please spell it with a capital H.
examples.professional: The H-1B visa petition has to go out by Friday, so please send me the final employer letter.
examples.analytical: Scholars who transliterate Hebrew use h with a dot below to mark a guttural sound that the plain English letter cannot carry.

nuance.analogy: Like a letter that sits in the middle of the alphabet, it looks simple but carries many uses.
nuance.etymology: From Phoenician heth, through Greek eta and Latin H.
common_mistakes: Saying 'haitch', which sounds British or Irish to most Americans; say AYCH.
Writing 'a H' instead of 'an H', since the name begins with a vowel sound: 'an H'.
Pronouncing H as 'huh' when spelling words aloud.

senses.definition: In AI: A confident but false or made-up statement produced by an AI model.
A sensory perception of something that does not exist, often arising from disorder of the nervous system, as in delirium tremens.
senses.example: After three days without sleep, he began to see a hallucination of a man in the hallway.

senses.definition: The act of hallucinating; a wandering of the mind; an error, mistake or blunder.
senses.example: Calling the budget a surplus was a hallucination that cost the team its credibility.

senses.definition: A confident but incorrect response given by an artificial intelligence; a confabulation.
senses.example: The chatbot's hallucination about a nonexistent court case embarrassed our legal team.

core.definition: In AI, a confident but false or made-up statement produced by a model that is not supported by its data or the input.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'NAY,' the fourth syllable. The final 'tion' is pronounced 'shun,' not 'tee-on.' Many learners add an extra syllable in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Negative in technical contexts because it describes a reliability failure. In medical settings it describes a serious symptom.
nuance.usage_note: In American data science and product discussions, 'hallucination' is the standard term for a plausible but false AI output. Medical and psychiatric uses are more serious and refer to seeing or hearing things that are not present. Use 'AI hallucination' when the context could be confused with the medical sense.

distinctions.note: An illusion is a misleading perception of something real; a hallucination is a perception of something that is not there at all.
A delusion is a fixed false belief held despite evidence; a hallucination is a false sensory experience.

examples.everyday: My friend told me the AI gave her a made-up book title, which she called a hallucination, so she double-checked everything.
examples.professional: Our evaluation shows the hallucination rate dropped by half after we added retrieval over the company knowledge base.
examples.analytical: A hallucination in a language model is not a perception but a fluent assertion without grounding, which raises questions about how we define truthfulness in machine output.

nuance.analogy: An AI hallucination is like a confident tour guide describing a monument that was never built: smooth, detailed, and wrong.
nuance.etymology: From Latin hallucinatio, from hallucinari, to wander in mind or talk idly.
common_mistakes: Using it for any AI error; it refers specifically to plausible but unsupported content.
Mispronouncing the final syllables as 'tee-on' instead of 'shun.'
Confusing it with 'illusion' in technical writing, where the two have different meanings.

conversation.text: The summary cited a paper that doesn't exist, a textbook hallucination.
Grounding answers in retrieved documents cut hallucinations noticeably in our evals.
A hallucination is when the model states something false with complete confidence.

senses.definition: In a handy manner; skillfully; conveniently.
Effortlessly; readily.
senses.example: He won the election handily.

core.definition: Easily, by a large margin, or in a skillful and convenient way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced 'uh', and the final 'y' is pronounced 'ee'. Do not stress the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests ease or a comfortable margin, especially in news or sports reporting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'handily' most often in news and sports writing, such as 'The team won handily.' In casual talk, people more often say 'easily' or 'by a mile'. It sounds a little formal, so it fits reports, essays and summaries better than everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Easily' is the everyday, general choice; 'handily' is more formal and often used for winning or succeeding by a clear margin.
'Conveniently' focuses on being suitable or close at hand; 'handily' can mean both convenient and skillful.
'Readily' means without hesitation or easily available; 'handily' often describes results, such as a win.

examples.everyday: Our team beat the other side handily, so nobody was worried about the playoff game.
examples.professional: The model outperformed the baseline handily on every validation split.
examples.analytical: The argument handily answers the objection, but it leaves open the question of how the premise itself is justified.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who crosses the finish line well ahead of the pack, with time to spare.
nuance.etymology: From 'handy' plus '-ly', from Middle English 'handy', meaning near at hand or convenient.
common_mistakes: Using 'handily' to mean 'handy' or 'useful' in casual speech, as in 'It is handily here'.
Confusing it with 'handy', which is an adjective.

senses.definition: Involving active participation.
senses.example: The internship will provide hands-on training.

senses.definition: A session of active participation, often as part of training or education.
senses.example: The workshop included a hands-on session where we built our own circuits.

core.definition: Involving direct, active participation and practice rather than only watching or reading about something.

pronunciation.tip: In a compound adjective used before a noun, the stress usually falls on HANDS, as in 'a HANDS-on class.' ON gets a weaker secondary stress, and its vowel is the American /ɑ/ sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests practical learning, engagement and getting your hands dirty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in job descriptions, school courses and workshops, and it often appears in the phrase 'hands-on experience.' The noun form, meaning a session of active practice, is common in training and education (as in 'a hands-on for new hires'). Used as a comment about a manager, it means the person is closely involved in the details, which can be praised or criticized depending on tone.

distinctions.note: 'Practical' means useful or realistic, while 'hands-on' specifically means you physically do the work or take part directly.
'Interactive' describes exchange between people or a system, while 'hands-on' emphasizes doing the activity yourself.

examples.everyday: My daughter loves the science museum because the exhibits are very hands-on.
examples.professional: The onboarding program includes a hands-on session where new engineers deploy a test service.
examples.analytical: Hands-on knowledge of a craft differs from theoretical understanding, because some skills can only be learned through repeated practice and correction.

nuance.analogy: Like learning to swim by getting in the pool instead of reading a book about it.
nuance.etymology: From hands (plural of hand) and on, formed in English in the 20th century to describe direct physical involvement.
common_mistakes: Stressing ON rather than HANDS when the phrase comes before a noun.
Using 'hands-on' to mean 'practical' in the sense of sensible; use 'practical' for that meaning.

hands-on.etymology: Possibly from the phrase *all hands on deck*.

senses.definition: An act of harmonizing.
senses.example: The committee worked for months on the harmonization of the two countries' tax rules.

core.definition: The process of making different things agree, fit together, or work consistently, such as rules, systems, or musical parts.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -ZAY-, and the -tion ending is a reduced 'shuhn.' Make the 'ni' in the middle short, and do not say 'hahr-muh-NIZE' with stress on the wrong syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually describes an effort to reduce conflict or make systems consistent, often in business, law, or policy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use harmonization in business, law, trade, and policy, such as 'harmonization of tax rules' or 'harmonization of standards.' It is more formal than 'alignment' or 'consistency,' which are common in workplace talk. In music, it refers to adding harmony to a melody.

distinctions.note: Alignment is the more common workplace word for getting teams or goals to agree, while harmonization sounds more formal and often refers to rules or standards.
Standardization means making everything the same, while harmonization means making different systems compatible without necessarily making them identical.

examples.everyday: The harmonization of the two choirs' parts made the last song sound polished and balanced.
examples.professional: Harmonization of our naming conventions across teams will cut onboarding time for new analysts.
examples.analytical: Her essay argues that the harmonization of faith and reason was a central aim of medieval scholastic thought.

nuance.analogy: Harmonization is like tuning several instruments to the same pitch so that the whole orchestra can play together.
nuance.etymology: From harmonize, from Late Latin harmonizare, from Greek harmonizein, meaning to be in tune or to agree; the noun takes the -ation suffix.
common_mistakes: Confusing harmonization with harmony; harmonization is the process, while harmony is the state or result.
Using harmonization for simple agreement between two people; 'agreement' or 'alignment' is more natural there.

senses.definition: To transport by drawing or pulling, as with horses or oxen, or a motor vehicle.
senses.example: to haul logs to a sawmill

senses.definition: To draw or pull something heavy.
To carry or transport something, with a connotation that the item is heavy or otherwise difficult to move.
senses.example: We had to haul the old piano up three flights of stairs.

senses.definition: To drag, to pull, to tug.
Followed by up: to summon to be disciplined or held answerable for something.
senses.example: The dean hauled him up before the board to explain the missing grant money.

senses.definition: To pull apart, as oxen sometimes do when yoked.
senses.example: The two oxen began to haul apart when the yoke slipped.

senses.definition: To haul ass (“go fast”).
senses.example: “How fast was he goin’?” / “I don’t know exactly, but he must’ve been haulin’, given where he landed.”

senses.definition: To steer (a vessel) closer to the wind.
senses.example: The captain ordered the crew to haul the ship closer to the wind.

senses.definition: Of the wind: to shift fore (more towards the bow).
senses.example: By dawn the wind had hauled forward, so we tacked to hold our course.

senses.definition: An act of hauling or pulling, particularly with force; a (violent) pull or tug.
senses.example: With one hard haul on the rope, the anchor finally broke free.

senses.definition: The distance over which something is hauled or transported, especially if long.
senses.example: Getting to his place was a real haul.

senses.definition: An amount of something that has been taken, especially of fish, illegal loot, or items purchased on a shopping trip.
senses.example: The robber’s haul was over thirty items.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of haul video (“video posted on the Internet consisting of someone showing and talking about recently purchased items”).
A bundle of many threads to be tarred.
senses.example: The rope-maker set aside a haul of yarn to be dipped in hot tar.

core.definition: To pull or carry something heavy, often by vehicle or with great effort, from one place to another.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable with the 'aw' vowel of 'caught' and a clear, final 'l'. Do not add a 'w' or 'ow' glide.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes the effort of moving something heavy, and can be used casually or in a business sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'haul' often for trucks, trailers or heavy loads, as in 'hauling furniture' or 'the truck hauls gravel'. It is very common in casual talk about moving things. For ordinary carrying of light items, Americans usually say 'carry' or 'bring'.

distinctions.note: Carry is the general word for moving something in your hands or on your back, while haul implies heavier loads or a vehicle.
Tow means pulling a vehicle behind another one using a hitch or cable, whereas haul covers any kind of heavy transport.

examples.everyday: Can you help me haul this old couch out to the curb on Saturday?
examples.professional: Our logistics partner hauls the server racks to the new data center every quarter.
examples.analytical: The argument hauls its heavy conceptual baggage through several chapters before arriving at its conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Haul is like dragging a loaded wagon up a hill: the weight is the point, and the effort is visible.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English halen, from Old French haler, meaning to haul or pull, of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Using 'haul' for light objects, when 'carry' is more natural.
Pronouncing it like 'hall' with a short vowel instead of the long 'aw' sound.

haul.etymology: From Middle English *hālen*, *hailen*, *haulen*, *halien* (“to drag, pull; to draw up”), from Old French *haler* (“to haul, pull”), from **halōn* (“to drag, fetch, haul”) or Middle Dutch *halen* (“to drag, fetch, haul”), possibly merging with Old English…

senses.definition: A gravestone, a grave marker: a monument traditionally made of stone placed at the head of a grave.
The cornerstone or principal stone of a building.
senses.example: The workers laid the headstone first, and every other wall was measured from it.

core.definition: A stone marker placed at the head of a grave, usually inscribed with the dead person's name and dates.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HED, and the d in the middle is pronounced before the s, so it sounds like HEDS-tone. Keep the long o of stone clear, not a short aw sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to solemn. It refers to death and memory, so speakers use it with respect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say headstone or gravestone for a marker at a grave, and tombstone is also common, especially in cemeteries and old-fashioned speech. Headstone is most typical for a stone at one specific grave. Visiting a cemetery and talking about someone's headstone is a natural everyday situation.

distinctions.note: Gravestone is a broader and very common term for any grave marker, while headstone emphasizes the stone at the head of a grave.
Tombstone is also common in the US, but it can suggest a stone over an above-ground tomb or a more old-fashioned tone.
A cornerstone is a stone at the corner of a building's foundation, not a grave marker, so the words should not be confused.

examples.everyday: We walked over to Grandma's headstone and left some flowers by the grass.
examples.professional: The cemetery office needs the final approval form before we can install the headstone.
examples.analytical: The inscription on a headstone shows what a family chose to remember, which shapes how the dead are understood by later generations.

nuance.analogy: A headstone is like a name tag for the dead: it marks where someone rests and says who they were.
nuance.etymology: From head plus stone, referring to the stone set at the head of a grave.
common_mistakes: Confusing headstone with cornerstone, which is a building term.
Pronouncing the vowel of stone as in stun, instead of the long o.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture does not use the English word headstone for a grave marker, but it describes stones at tombs. Genesis 23 records Abraham buying the cave of Machpelah as a burial place for Sarah. Matthew 27:60 describes Joseph of Arimathea rolling a great stone to the door of the tomb of Jesus. The Greek word behind stone there is lithos.

senses.definition: Any food that is considered to be especially beneficial to health.

core.definition: Food regarded as especially good for your health, often natural, whole, or minimally processed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FOOD, the second word, and the first word's stress is lighter. The th in health is voiceless, so do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests wholesome and good for you, though some people use it ironically to mean bland or expensive food.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use health food for products sold in stores like Whole Foods or a health food store, and it often covers organic, gluten-free, or low-sugar items. Saying you eat health food is a casual way to describe your diet. A natural reply is Oh, what do you usually buy there?

distinctions.note: Organic describes how food was grown, without synthetic pesticides; health food describes a general perception of healthfulness.
Whole food means unprocessed, like brown rice or fresh vegetables; health food is a broader marketing term.

collocations: a bag of health food snacks

examples.everyday: I know it's health food, but these kale chips are actually pretty good.
examples.professional: Our wellness campaign targets shoppers who buy health food but don't read the labels.
examples.analytical: The phrase health food assumes that a single category of food can be good for the body, which obscures the role of total diet.

nuance.analogy: Health food is like a label on a box that says trust me; the label helps you choose, but you still need to check what's inside.
nuance.etymology: Health comes from Old English hǣlth, meaning wholeness or soundness; food comes from Old English fōda.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the th in health as a t or d sound.
Using health food as a countable noun in the singular for a single item; say a health food product or a health food item.

conversation.text: That store sells mostly health food and vitamins.
Granola is sold as health food, but it's full of sugar.
She's really into health food lately.

senses.definition: In a hearted manner.

core.definition: In a sincere, warm, wholehearted way; with real feeling and enthusiasm.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HEART. The spelling ea is pronounced like the vowel in 'hart,' not like 'heat,' and the final -ly is a short 'lee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests genuine warmth and sincerity, but the word is rare, so Americans usually choose 'wholeheartedly' instead.
nuance.usage_note: Heartedly is a rare adverb built from the adjective 'hearted,' as in 'kind-hearted' or 'warm-hearted.' Americans almost always say 'wholeheartedly' or 'with all my heart.' You will mostly meet 'heartedly' in older or literary writing, so you do not need it in daily speech.

distinctions.note: Wholeheartedly is the common American form and carries the same meaning of full commitment, so it is the better choice in nearly every situation.
Sincerely stresses honesty about what you say, while heartedly stresses warmth and emotional commitment in how you act.

examples.everyday: My aunt welcomed us into her home so warmly that we felt heartedly at ease from the moment we arrived.
examples.professional: Our manager endorsed the new onboarding process heartedly, and the whole team followed her lead.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the medieval author embraced the virtues of humility heartedly, not merely as a rhetorical convention.

nuance.analogy: Heartedly is like a rarely used tool in a toolbox: it works, but you will almost always reach for the more common one, wholeheartedly.
nuance.etymology: From 'heart' (Old English heorte) plus the suffix '-ed' and the adverbial '-ly.'
common_mistakes: Using 'heartedly' in everyday speech where Americans say 'wholeheartedly' or 'with all my heart.'
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'heart-ED-ly.' Keep the stress on HEART.

senses.definition: In a hectic manner.

core.definition: In a busy, rushed, and chaotic way, with very little time to relax or slow down.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HEK, the first syllable, and the final -ly is the easy sound 'lee'. Learners often make the middle syllable too strong or add an extra 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or tiring. It describes a rushed, stressful pace, usually with a sense of disorder.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hectically mainly to describe how people spend their time, such as 'We worked hectically all week'. It is casual and common in everyday talk, but in formal writing you might say at a frantic pace or with great urgency. It usually appears with verbs such as work, run, or schedule.

distinctions.note: Busily is neutral and describes steady activity. Hectically adds a sense of rush and disorder.
Frantically is stronger and suggests panic or desperation, while hectically describes a chaotic pace that may still be controlled.

examples.everyday: We've been running around hectically all weekend, so I'm ready for a nap.
examples.professional: The team has been working hectically to finish the release before the client demo.
examples.analytical: The writer describes city life as moving hectically, with every hour divided into obligations that never quite fit.

nuance.analogy: Moving hectically is like juggling plates while someone keeps adding new ones to the pile.
nuance.etymology: English adverb formed from hectic, from Late Latin hecticus and Greek hektikos.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in heck-TIK-lee.
Using hectically when you mean busily, which lacks the sense of rush and stress.

senses.definition: A person who treats diseases by means of medicinal herbs.

core.definition: A person who uses medicinal herbs to treat illness or promote health, rather than prescribing synthetic drugs.

pronunciation.tip: The h is usually silent, and the stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ist is a clear 'ist' like 'list', not 'last'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive when people admire natural remedies, but skeptical when used about treating serious disease. The tone depends heavily on the speaker.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use herbalist for people who sell or prescribe herbal remedies, often in health food stores, farmers markets, or community clinics. Doctors and pharmacists may be skeptical of herbalists making medical claims. In everyday talk, people might say my aunt is an herbalist or go to an herbalist for a tea.

distinctions.note: A naturopath is usually a licensed or trained practitioner using a broader set of natural methods, while an herbalist focuses specifically on plant remedies.
A pharmacist is a licensed professional who dispenses regulated medications; an herbalist typically works outside that system.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is an herbalist, and she makes a tea for my sore throat every winter.
examples.professional: The clinic partners with a local herbalist for patient education, but any medical claims still go through the pharmacist.
examples.analytical: The herbalist's authority rests on inherited practice rather than controlled trials, which is why its claims remain contested.

nuance.analogy: Like a home cook who knows every spice in the pantry, an herbalist knows plants but may not know the lab tests behind them.
nuance.etymology: From herb plus the suffix -ist, 'one who practices' a particular art or craft.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable, as in 'her-BAL-ist'.
Confusing herbalist with pharmacist, which implies a licensed professional who dispenses regulated drugs.

senses.definition: Under this.
Under this (within the document being read).

core.definition: Below or later in this document or text, under the terms or provisions being discussed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, UN, and the first syllable is reduced to 'hih'. Keep the final syllable short as 'der'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and formal, used in legal and business writing to refer to provisions below.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hereunder almost exclusively in contracts, insurance policies, and legal or financial documents, usually with words like obligations hereunder or rights hereunder. In speech, people say below or under the terms instead. It is rarely appropriate in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Herein means within the document in general, while hereunder means under or below a specific provision or section.
Thereunder refers to something under that, usually earlier in the text, while hereunder refers to something under this, later in the text.

examples.everyday: Everything you need for the trip is listed hereunder, so check the packing list before Friday.
examples.professional: Any payments due hereunder must be made within thirty days of the invoice date.
examples.analytical: The objections raised hereunder fail because they confuse ontological priority with temporal order.

nuance.analogy: Like a footnote at the bottom of a page, hereunder points the reader to the provisions that follow below.
nuance.etymology: From here plus under, from Old English her and under.
common_mistakes: Writing hereunder as two words, under here, which sounds casual and misses the legal sense.
Using hereunder in conversation where below or under the terms is more natural.

senses.definition: Having to do with hermeneutics; that explains, interprets, illustrates or elucidates texts, especially holy texts.
senses.example: Her hermeneutic approach to the Gospel of John emphasized the historical context of each passage.

senses.definition: A particular theory of hermeneutics; a particular method of interpretation of text, especially holy texts.
senses.example: The seminar compared a literal hermeneutic with a historical-critical one for reading Paul.

core.definition: Relating to hermeneutics, the theory and method of interpreting texts, especially sacred texts.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NOO, with a light secondary stress on hur. The final syllable is a short 'tik', and the y-glide before the u is optional in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hermeneutic in academic writing and seminars about interpretation, literature, philosophy, or theology. In everyday speech it would sound too technical. People sometimes say 'interpretive' instead, which is more common and easier to understand.

distinctions.note: Interpretive is the common everyday word for relating to interpretation, while hermeneutic is a specialized term for formal theories of interpretation.
Exegetical refers specifically to the critical explanation of a text, especially Scripture, while hermeneutic refers to the broader theory behind such interpretation.

examples.everyday: My professor's hermeneutic approach made the poem feel completely different to me.
examples.professional: We need a hermeneutic framework for reading the user feedback before we label it.
examples.analytical: Gadamer's hermeneutic account holds that every interpreter brings a horizon of prior understanding to the text.

nuance.analogy: A hermeneutic approach is like a set of lenses for reading: it changes how you see the text and its context.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hermeneutikos, relating to interpretation, from hermeneuein, to interpret.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; the main stress is on NOO, not on hur.
Using hermeneutic as a noun for a single interpretation when the noun means a theory or method.

hermeneutic.etymology: Ancient Greek *ἑρμηνευτικός* (“of or for interpreting”), from *ἑρμηνεύς* (“interpreter”).

senses.definition: Hermetic philosophy or practice; hermetics.
A form of obscure poetry with subjective use of language and imagery.
senses.example: The professor's hermeticism made her poems nearly impossible for undergraduates to decipher.

core.definition: The philosophy and practice of the hermetic tradition, a set of esoteric teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus that focus on alchemy and secret knowledge.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, MEH. The -ic- of hermetic changes to -is- before -ism, and the final syllable is reduced to 'um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in popular use the word can suggest mystery, secrecy or the occult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hermeticism mainly in the history of religion, Renaissance studies and the history of science. In everyday English people would say 'the occult' or 'alchemy' for something similar. Scholars often distinguish the philosophical texts from later popular occultism.

distinctions.note: Alchemy is the practice of trying to transform metals, while hermeticism is a wider philosophy in which alchemy is one part.
Esotericism is the broad category of hidden or inner knowledge traditions, and hermeticism is one tradition within it.

examples.everyday: My neighbor has a shelf of old books about alchemy and hermeticism.
examples.professional: The library digitization project includes Renaissance texts on hermeticism, so the metadata needs careful review.
examples.analytical: Frances Yates argued that hermeticism shaped Renaissance thought more deeply than historians had once admitted.

nuance.analogy: Like a locked cabinet of old recipes whose instructions are written in symbols that only initiates can read.
nuance.etymology: From Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the hermetic writings, whose name combines the Greek god Hermes with Latin megistus, 'greatest'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'HER-muh-tiz-um'; the stress is on the second syllable.
Confusing hermeticism with the adjective hermetic, which is used in phrases like 'hermetic seal'.

senses.definition: An ancient Greek priest who interpreted sacred mysteries, especially the priest of the Eleusinian Mysteries.
An interpreter of sacred mysteries or arcane knowledge.
One who explains or makes a commentary.
senses.example: The hierophant gave a long commentary on each passage of the ancient ritual text.

core.definition: A priest in ancient Greek religion who explained sacred mysteries, or someone who teaches secret or hidden knowledge.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HY, and the middle syllables are quick and unstressed. The final 'ant' rhymes with 'can't'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly grand; it suggests religious authority or mysterious knowledge and is rarely used casually.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in classical studies, religious history or literary writing. In everyday speech, people would say 'priest' or 'religious leader' instead. Calling a teacher a hierophant is a deliberate, somewhat playful choice.

distinctions.note: Priest is the common everyday word for a religious minister; hierophant specifically means an interpreter of sacred mysteries, especially in ancient Greece.
A mystic seeks direct experience of the divine; a hierophant is an authorized interpreter who explains the sacred to others.
An oracle gives prophetic answers from a god; a hierophant explains established sacred rites and mysteries.

examples.everyday: Our history teacher loves to act like a hierophant when she explains the old Greek festivals.
examples.professional: In the seminar paper we described the hierophant's role in the Eleusinian ceremonies as a public teacher of ritual meaning.
examples.analytical: The author treats the scholar as a modern hierophant, whose authority rests on access to texts that ordinary readers cannot interpret.

nuance.analogy: A hierophant is like a museum docent for sacred mysteries: someone who holds the key and guides you through what would otherwise be hidden.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hierophantes, from hieros 'sacred' and phainein 'to show'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in hy-er-OH-fant; the primary stress belongs on HY.
Confusing it with 'hierophany', which is a different noun for a manifestation of the sacred.

hierophant.etymology: From Latin *hierophanta*, from Ancient Greek *ἱεροφάντης*, from *ἱερός* + *φαίνω*.

senses.definition: Important or well publicized.

core.definition: Attracting a lot of public attention, media coverage, or notice, often because of importance or fame.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PRO, with a secondary stress on FILE, but in ordinary speech the second part is quieter. Learners often pronounce the -file ending as 'fil,' missing the long i sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting importance or prestige. It can be negative when the attention is unwelcome, such as scandal or controversy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for people, cases, projects, and events that receive a lot of media attention, as in 'It's a high-profile lawsuit that everyone is following.' It is common in business, politics, and news. Using it about private life can sound surprising, but it works for public figures and well-known projects.

distinctions.note: Prominent describes someone or something that stands out in importance, while high-profile emphasizes public visibility and media attention.
Famous describes being well known, while high-profile describes a current situation that attracts attention, which may be temporary.

examples.everyday: My sister is going to a high-profile wedding in Los Angeles, so she's nervous about the photographers.
examples.professional: The team is handling a high-profile product launch, so every email needs to be reviewed by legal before it goes out.
examples.analytical: A high-profile trial can shape public opinion before the evidence is fully examined, which raises questions about fairness.

nuance.analogy: A high-profile person is like a lighthouse on a dark coast: everyone can see it from far away, which is useful but also means it cannot hide.
nuance.etymology: From high plus profile; 'profile' comes from Italian profilo, from profilare, 'to outline.'
common_mistakes: Using high-profile to mean 'high-quality' or 'important in quality,' when the word refers to public attention.
Missing the hyphen when the word is used before a noun, as in 'a high profile case,' where American style normally uses 'high-profile case.'

senses.definition: To flirt with; to approach and speak to (someone), seeking romance, love, sex, etc.
senses.example: That's the third guy that has hit on her tonight.

senses.definition: To discover, pinpoint; to think up; to realize.
senses.example: He hit on a great idea for improving the design.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see hit,‎ on.

core.definition: To approach someone and show romantic or sexual interest in them, usually by flirting or making a direct move.

pronunciation.tip: 'On' is often stressed here and uses the 'ah' vowel of cot and caught, not the 'oh' vowel. Keep the final n clear and short.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It can be friendly flirting, but when the interest is unwelcome it can be seen as harassment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hit on' in casual talk about dating and bars, often with a note of disapproval if the person was not interested. In a professional setting, it can cause real problems. Also, Americans say 'hit on an idea' or 'hit on a solution' to mean that they discovered or thought of something, which is positive. A natural reply might be 'Did he get the message?' or 'That's a great idea you hit on.'

distinctions.note: 'Flirt with' suggests lighter, often mutual playfulness, while 'hit on' often describes a more direct approach that may be unwelcome.
'Come on to' means much the same and is slightly more slangy, so 'hit on' sounds a bit more neutral.
'Ask out' means to invite someone on a date, which is more specific and less likely to be seen as harassment.

collocations: hit on someone at a bar

examples.everyday: A guy at the bar kept trying to hit on my friend, so we decided to leave early.
examples.professional: We hit on a fix during the review: caching the query results so the dashboard stops timing out.
examples.analytical: Historians note that the author hit on the key concept only after rejecting two earlier drafts.

nuance.analogy: It works like a fishing line that lands near a fish: you make contact, and the response decides whether something happens.
common_mistakes: Using 'hit on' in a professional setting, where it can be read as harassment.
Confusing it with 'hit upon,' which is more formal and means to discover or think of something.

core.definition: In Christian belief, the third person of the Trinity, God present and active, giving life and guiding believers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPIR, which has a long ee-like vowel before the r (SPEER-it). Many learners say 'spy-rit' or add a vowel.

nuance.connotation: Reverent and positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "Holy Spirit" most commonly, and "Holy Ghost" is now mainly older or traditional. It is capitalized. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians speak often of experiences of the Spirit, while other traditions are more reserved.

distinctions.note: Holy Ghost is an older English name for the same person, common in older hymns.
A spirit is any nonphysical being; the Holy Spirit is God.
Paraclete is a Greek title meaning helper or advocate, used for the Spirit in John.

collocations: the gift of the Holy Spirit
the work of the Holy Spirit
the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit

examples.everyday: She says she felt the Holy Spirit leading her to change jobs.
examples.professional: Tonight's class will cover the role of the Holy Spirit in Paul's letters.
examples.analytical: Western and Eastern churches differ over whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son.

nuance.analogy: Like the wind or breath: unseen, but its effects can be seen.
nuance.etymology: Holy from Old English halig; spirit from Latin spiritus, breath. It translates Greek pneuma and Hebrew ruach.
common_mistakes: Saying 'spy-rit' or pronouncing three syllables, 'spir-i-it'.
Omitting the: use "the Holy Spirit."
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew ruach (breath, wind, spirit) in Genesis 1:2 describes the Spirit of God over the waters. In the New Testament the Greek pneuma hagion appears at Jesus' baptism (Mark 1:10), is promised by Jesus as the Counselor in John 14:26, and comes at Pentecost in Acts 2:1-4. Romans 8 describes the Spirit as giving life and bearing witness that believers are children of God.

traditions.view: The Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and the Orthodox reject the filioque added to the Creed in the West.
The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (filioque), and is active through the sacraments such as baptism and confirmation.
Most accept the filioque. Reformed and Lutheran traditions stress the Spirit's work through Word and sacrament; Pentecostals emphasize baptism in the Spirit and spiritual gifts.

senses.definition: Humankind; human beings as a group.
The human condition or nature.
senses.example: Augustine wrestled with the fallen nature of humanity long before modern psychology.

senses.definition: The quality of being benevolent; humane traits of character; humane qualities or aspects.
Any academic subject belonging to the humanities.
senses.example: Philosophy is a humanity while psychology is a science.

core.definition: All human beings as a group; humankind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAN, the second syllable. In American speech the t between vowels is often a quick flap that sounds almost like a d, so the ending can sound like 'ih-dee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it can refer to all people, or to compassion, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'humanity' for all people in serious or broad statements, such as 'for the good of humanity.' In everyday speech, people more often use it to mean kindness, as in 'he showed real humanity.' It is less casual than 'people' or 'everyone,' so use it when you want a larger or more moral tone.

distinctions.note: Humankind refers neutrally to all people as a group, while humanity can also suggest the quality of compassion.
Humanity can mean all people, but humaneness refers only to the quality of kindness and mercy.

examples.everyday: After the hurricane, I was amazed by the humanity of the neighbors who brought food to people they had never met.
examples.professional: Our product will help the humanity of customer support, since it frees agents to handle the hardest cases with care.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that humanity in our own person must always be treated as an end, never merely as a means.

nuance.analogy: Like a shared language that every person speaks, whatever their country or culture.
nuance.etymology: From Latin humanitas, human nature or kindness, through Old French humanite.
common_mistakes: Using humanity to mean a single person, which is not natural.
Pronouncing the t as a sharp t in casual speech, when Americans usually flap it.
